title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
text:
Preface
A first-principles course in Python and PyTorch.
Much of modern deep learning can be understood as familiar machinery, made learnable, placed inside the right structure, and run on hardware that makes matrix multiplication absurdly fast.
Text and figures licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; all code MIT. Source on GitHub. The graduate companion is Deep Learning: Making It Trainable.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
text:
Why now
For many readers trained in classical statistics, a foundational lesson was to keep the model small relative to the data. Too many adjustable parameters would fit noise as readily as signal, and high-dimensional estimation demanded defensive care. Deep learning steps squarely into the regime that classical intuition warned against: overparameterized models with millions or billions of parameters, optimized across vast, non-convex loss landscapes. Yet on unseen data, these models routinely generalize.
The deeper surprise is that additional capacity can improve out-of-sample prediction. In many measured regimes, scaling parameters, data, and compute together can produce systematic reductions in held-out loss that are well described by power laws. Generalization need not collapse when a network interpolates its training sample. Architecture, data distribution, and optimization dynamics still govern success, but parameter count alone no longer marks where useful learning must stop.
We will encounter this surprise in Chapter 6 and examine empirical scaling laws in Chapter 19. A complete theoretical account of why these high-dimensional learners generalize remains an active research frontier.
The computation itself is more concrete. Linear algebra organizes the workload into batched matrix operations that modern accelerators execute efficiently, while backpropagation computes gradients for all those parameters in a single reverse sweep. Our task here is to master these mechanics: how to design the architecture, how to wire the computation, and how to audit what it has learned.
As my math PhD advisor used to remind me: sometimes you just have to follow your nose. When a model or an objective feels overwhelming, you do not wait for an epiphany. You pick up a pencil, work through the derivations line by line, check the shapes, and trust the mathematical mechanics to carry you forward. The intuition is earned through the work, not before it. Understanding the computation should make its success more interesting, not make that success seem inevitable.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
section: What the mechanics explain, and what they do not
text:
What the mechanics explain, and what they do not
Building, wiring, and running these models takes familiar mathematics: the chain rule, matrix products, vector–Jacobian products, and probability for the losses. Explaining why they work so well at scale is a different matter. Networks with far more parameters than training examples can fit random labels, yet on real data they generalize; the double descent met in Chapter 6 is one face of this. Gradient descent on a nonconvex loss in millions or billions of dimensions routinely finds solutions that generalize. Over wide ranges of scale, loss falls roughly as a power law in parameters, data, and compute, a regularity that Chapter 19 examines. Accounting for these facts draws on high-dimensional probability, random matrix theory, dynamical systems, and statistical physics, and much of it is still active research.
This book neither pretends those questions are settled nor waits for them. It is a builder’s and auditor’s manual: fluency in the mechanics and the inductive biases lets you read that theory, and the claims made in its name, critically.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
section: A continuation, not a fresh start
text:
A continuation, not a fresh start
You own more of this subject than you think. If you know linear regression, empirical risk minimization, gradient descent, and why squared error is the maximum-likelihood loss for Gaussian noise, you are not starting over. Each architecture in this book keeps the model before it and makes one more piece learnable, shared, or reused.


Each rung keeps the model below it and adds one move, shown in orange. The grey tags name the Part of the book where each move is made.

Take a linear model and let it learn its own nonlinear features: the core of a multilayer perceptron. Take fixed convolutional filters and learn them from data: the core of a convolutional network. Take a one-shot summary and learn how to update it step by step: recurrence. Take similarity-weighted averaging and learn how to compare and mix: the core of attention. Learn a representation once and adapt it many times: the pretrained era.
The underlying mathematical move, in its simplest instance:
\[
\underbrace{f_{\vect{w}}(x) = \vect{w}^\top \phi(x)}_{\text{linear model on fixed features}}
\qquad\longrightarrow\qquad
\underbrace{f_{\vect{w},\theta}(x) = \vect{w}^\top \phi_\theta(x)}_{\text{linear readout on learned nonlinear features}}.
\]
What we build in, through architecture, objectives, data, or training, is inductive bias: regularities the model should not have to rediscover from scratch. Three questions organize everything that follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\textbf{What is learned?} &\quad \text{features, filters, comparisons, representations} \\
\textbf{What is built in?} &\quad \text{locality, sharing, order, invariance, visibility} \\
\textbf{What is reused?} &\quad \text{pretrained representations and models}
\end{aligned}
\]
With these questions in hand, architectures stop looking like a zoo of named models and start reading as a short sequence of design moves. When an idea feels half-familiar, it usually is. Follow your nose backward: the cross-references first, then Appendix A for linear algebra and the SVD, Appendix B for tensors, and Appendix E for statistical learning.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
text:
Open the hood
This book spends little time persuading you that deep learning matters. It spends its time on how learning works. Treat a network as an engine to assemble, tune, and repair:


Forward, data flows left to right; backward, sensitivities flow right to left. Every layer holds learnable parameters (orange), and the loss compares the prediction (green) with the target (purple).


Forward, left to right. Data flows through linear maps, one batched matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer, each followed by a nonlinear bend.
Backward, right to left. Reverse-mode differentiation carries the loss’s sensitivity back to every parameter, one vector–Jacobian product per layer.
The design goal. As much representational power as possible from as few parameters as possible, obtained by building the data’s known structure into the architecture.

When training stalls, we do not guess. We check shapes and strides, gradient norms layer by layer, what each position is allowed to see, and whether the numbers are well conditioned.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
text:
Who this book is for
This book is for builders and auditors: engineers, students, and researchers who want to understand deep learning well enough to implement it from scratch, diagnose why it fails, and evaluate its claims critically.
You do not need previous deep learning experience, but working fluency with multivariable calculus, linear algebra, basic probability, and standard Python will let you focus on the architecture rather than the background math. The opening chapters revisit the necessary optimization and loss mechanics, while the appendices provide self-contained reference contracts: linear algebra and the SVD (Appendix A), tensors and PyTorch layout (Appendix B), numerical precision and the Roofline model (Appendix C), notation (Appendix D), and statistical learning contracts (Appendix E).
Although our executable code uses PyTorch, the principles are framework-independent. Tensor shapes, vector–Jacobian products, memory hierarchies, and broadcasting rules apply identically whether you write PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow.

title: Deep Learning: Making It Learnable
text:
How to read this book
Use the same loop throughout: read → predict → run → audit. Before executing an example, write down the shape, direction, or trend you expect. Then compare the result with your prediction. When they disagree, reduce the problem to one batch or one example and find where your mental model of the computation broke down.
Five questions organize every audit:

Function class. What family of functions does the code implement, and what structure is built in (locality, weight sharing, order, causality)?
Objective. What does the loss reward, and which conditional noise model justifies it?
Estimator. What does each batch compute: an unbiased per-example mean, a biased plug-in of an aggregate, or an objective defined by the batch itself? Chapter 4 separates the three cases.
Visibility. What information reaches the prediction? Check padding, causal masks, and leakage across data splits.
Claim. What does the evidence establish, and which tempting conclusions remain unproven?

Apply these questions whether you wrote the code by hand, borrowed it from a repository, or generated it with an AI assistant. Capable AI assistants are valuable tools, and because they now write plausible PyTorch in seconds, syntax is no longer the bottleneck: insight and auditing are. Building through these chapters step by step gives you the leverage to use those tools effectively: to prompt them with precision, spot silent bugs in their output, and judge whether the computation matches your intent. An assistant that writes code you cannot audit costs you the competence you came here to build.
The code is plain Python and PyTorch and runs on an ordinary laptop CPU because the data are small. If you are taking the course, the lecture videos and course-site self-checks complement this loop.
For a first pass, read the opening problem, study the figures, run the single cell that tests the central claim, and answer the Check yourself prompts without looking back. Then return for the derivations, code, and exercises. The Trap and tip boxes help diagnose common bugs.
When you encounter an unfamiliar architecture in a newly published paper, you should be able to identify what it changes, trace its computation, and design a diagnostic test of its claims. That is the fluency this book asks you to build.

Why this book
Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville’s Deep Learning is the encyclopedic reference; Prince’s Understanding Deep Learning emphasizes visual explanation; Dive into Deep Learning ranges broadly across frameworks and tools; Bach’s Learning Theory from First Principles develops generalization theory from the ground up. This book is narrower on purpose. It follows one question through every architecture, what if we made this learnable?, and prints only code that ran, so reading, predicting, running, and auditing form one loop.
This book is complete on its own terms. It tells the architecture story as one arc, from linear regression to the pretrained era, and teaches exactly the training mechanics its experiments need: loss and stochastic gradient descent, backpropagation, and numerical precision. It also leaves you ready for the research literature. With these mechanics in hand, current papers on test-time learning, state-space sequence models, diffusion, and preference optimization become readable.
Readers who want the theory of training will find it in Shakeri (2026), Deep Learning: Making It Trainable, a separate, self-contained treatment of initialization, optimization dynamics, numerical contracts, and the spectra of high-dimensional data that shares this book’s notation.
Make the right parts learnable. Build in the structure you trust. Reuse what transfers.

Plan a reading session
Time depends more on whether you stop to derive and run than on page count. As a planning range, allow roughly 45–90 minutes for a careful first read of most chapters, with the experiment-heavy later chapters often taking the longer end or a second sitting. Once the environment and data are ready, reproducing a few key cells commonly adds 20–45 minutes; rerunning every training cell from scratch can take substantially longer and varies by machine. Exercises are best treated as their own work session.
If you have one short sitting, read the opening problem, study the figures, run one cell that tests the main claim, and answer any closing Check yourself prompts without looking back. Return for the derivations and exercises when you can explain what failed, what changed, and what evidence supports the repair.


Exercises, hints, and solutions
The book supports both enrolled and self-paced readers. For-credit assignment rules on the course site and in the syllabus take precedence. To protect those assignments, the public book does not publish full worked solutions to overlapping graded work. Public Check yourself prompts are retrieval practice, not answer banks; the chapter recap and course-site self-check feedback provide the first layer of hints.
For self-paced work, use these acceptance criteria:

A conceptual answer names the mechanism, predicts a direction or limiting case, and states one condition under which the claim could fail.
A shape derivation labels every axis before the operation and checks the resulting shape against the code.
A code exercise runs from a fresh session, fixes its seed, prints or asserts the important shapes, and reproduces the requested qualitative relationship. Small machine-dependent numerical differences are not failures unless the exercise sets a tolerance.
An experiment states the question before the run, separates tuning from final evaluation, keeps the comparison recipe fixed, reports seed variation when requested, and ends with a limitation rather than a universal claim.

When stuck, inspect the nearest Trap: or tip callout, write the expected shape or trend before running anything, and reduce the code to one batch or one example. Enrolled students should use the course’s approved help channels for assignment-specific hints; complete graded solutions stay there rather than in the public text.

title: From Lines to Networks
text:
Skip to main content




We begin with the smallest complete learning system: a model, a loss, and an update rule. In the first two chapters the features are given, so a linear or logistic model can only recombine what someone chose to measure. Interleaving linear layers with hinges keeps the stack from collapsing into one linear map and makes the intermediate representations learnable: within each activation region the network applies an affine map, and every region’s map comes from the same shared parameters. Stochastic gradient descent moves those parameters downhill on the loss, and backpropagation computes the gradient it needs. The flexibility is real, but it carries no knowledge of the world: a well-fitted MLP loses nearly thirty points of accuracy when its validation images are shifted two pixels to the right. An interlude on experimental method sets the protocol under which that claim, and every later comparison, is made. The failure itself points to the next move: build what we know about the data into the architecture.

title: 1  Linear Regression, the Mother Model
text:
1.1 Learning from examples
Machine learning replaces hand-written rules with functions fitted to data. Every method in this book does this with three components: a model that makes predictions, a loss that scores them, and an update rule that improves the model. Before we can see what is deep about deep learning, we need all three working together on the smallest model that contains them. Linear regression is that model. By the end of this chapter we will fit it with two methods: a direct solve and gradient descent. We will write gradient descent twice, once by hand and once with PyTorch modules. All three implementations agree, and we will see why.
We start with a dataset of examples,
\[
\mathcal{D}
= \{(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i},\targetpart{y_i})\}_{i=1}^{n},
\]
where each \(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i}\in\R^d\) is an input with \(d\) features and \(\targetpart{y_i}\) is the output observed for that input, called the target or the supervision signal. Stacking the inputs as rows gives the blue data matrix \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\in\R^{n\times d}\): \(n\) examples down, \(d\) features across, with the purple targets in \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\).
Our goal is a flexible function \(f\) such that
\[
\predictionpart{f(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i})}
\approx \targetpart{y_i}
\quad \text{and } f \text{ generalizes to unseen data.}
\]
The second requirement, generalization to unseen data, is the central objective. Training fit alone is not sufficient. We assume that the training pairs \((\featurepart{\vect{x}_i}, \targetpart{y_i})\) are independent draws from one fixed but unknown probability distribution \(P\) over input–target pairs. A new input–target pair comes from the same \(P\), and what matters is how well \(f\) predicts the target from the input.
In statistical notation, training minimizes the empirical risk
\[
\hat R_{\mathcal D}(\parameterpart{\theta})
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\ell\!\left(
  \predictionpart{f_{\parameterpart{\theta}}(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i})},
  \targetpart{y_i}
\right),
\]
while the quantity we ultimately care about is the population risk
\[
R_P(\parameterpart{\theta})
= \E_{(\featurepart{X},\targetpart{Y})\sim P}\!\left[
  \ell\!\left(
    \predictionpart{f_{\parameterpart{\theta}}(\featurepart{X})},
    \targetpart{Y}
  \right)
\right].
\]
Here \(\ell\) scores one prediction against its target (the loss section chooses a concrete \(\ell\)), and \(\parameterpart{\theta}\) is the vector of all the model’s adjustable parameters. The empirical risk is the average loss on the \(n\) examples we have. The population risk is the expected loss on a fresh pair drawn from \(P\), which we can only estimate. We will use this distinction throughout the book. An independent validation set drawn from \(P\) estimates performance under \(P\). After deployment, a model may meet inputs from a different distribution \(Q\), in which, for instance, every image is shifted by a few pixels. Performance under \(P\) need not predict performance under \(Q\). Chapter 6 makes that difference visible, and Appendix E gathers these statistical distinctions in one reference.

This chapter covers regression, and Chapter 2 handles classification with the same machinery.



Why is this hard?
Learning a function from examples sounds simple, but it hides a difficulty: for any finite set of examples, there are infinitely many functions that fit them perfectly. We want the one best suited to our problem, so the learning algorithm needs a nudge in the right direction: an assumption about which functions to prefer. That guiding assumption is called its inductive bias.

A linear model restricts its predictions to a weighted sum of the supplied features plus a constant. That strong assumption keeps it simple. It can follow a curve such as \(y = x^2\) only if \(x^2\) is one of the supplied features.
A deep neural network can learn nonlinear features of its own, while its architecture and training still impose assumptions about which solutions to prefer. Its flexibility lets it learn complex patterns. It can also memorize the training set without learning the underlying rule, and then perform poorly on new data.

The key to modern deep learning is to use a flexible model and limit overfitting with more data, regularization, and inductive biases matched to the structure of the problem. That last principle is the subject of Chapter 6.
To make any of this concrete, we parameterize a family of functions \(f_{\vect{w}}\) by a vector \(\vect{w}\) of adjustable parameters, the \(\parameterpart{\theta}\) of the risks above. Think of each parameter as a knob. Learning is finding a good setting \(\hat{\vect{w}}\) of the knobs. Inference is using \(f_{\hat{\vect{w}}}\) to predict on unseen data. That is the vocabulary we will use throughout the book.

title: 1  Linear Regression, the Mother Model
section: 1.2 The linear model and its geometry
text:
1.2 The linear model and its geometry
Linear regression assumes a linear relationship:
\[
\predictionpart{\hat y}
= \parameterpart{\vect{w}^\top}\featurepart{\vect{x}} + \parameterpart{b} .
\]
The second term, \(\parameterpart{b}\), is the prediction at \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}=\vect{0}\). The first term, \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}^\top}\featurepart{\vect{x}}\), adjusts that baseline up or down based on how the input matches the weight vector. In linear algebra, a linear map plus a constant is called affine. Machine learning usually says “linear” for both, and we will say “affine” when the constant matters.






Figure 1.2: The dot product measures the signed shadow of an input along the weight vector. Aligned inputs raise the prediction above \(\parameterpart{b}\), orthogonal inputs leave it at \(\parameterpart{b}\), and opposing inputs lower it.



Figure 1.2 draws the first term and shows the principle behind it: a dot product is a similarity score. With \(\varphi\) the angle between \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\) and \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}\),
\[
\parameterpart{\vect{w}^\top}\featurepart{\vect{x}}
= \norm{\parameterpart{\vect{w}}}_2\norm{\featurepart{\vect{x}}}_2\cos\varphi .
\]
For normalized vectors it measures directional similarity directly: positive when \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}\) points along \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\), zero when they are orthogonal, and negative when they oppose. Without normalization, the two norms also control the score, so a large dot product can mean strong alignment, large magnitude, or both. A linear model is therefore a learned pattern scorer: \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\) is a template whose direction and scale both matter.1
To simplify notation, we absorb \(\parameterpart{b}\) into the weights by appending \(1\) to the input vector, \(\featurepart{\vect{x}} = (x_1, \dots, x_d, 1)^\top\), and \(\parameterpart{b}\) to \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}} = (w_1, \dots, w_d, \parameterpart{b})^\top\).2 Then
\[
\predictionpart{\hat y}
= \parameterpart{\vect{w}^\top}\featurepart{\vect{x}}
\qquad \text{(bias included)}.
\]
With the bias absorbed, \(d\) counts the constant feature as well.

section: 1.4 Finding the best weights, method 1: solve it exactly
text:
1.4 Finding the best weights, method 1: solve it exactly
For this one special problem we do not need to search: we can characterize the exact minimizer. Differentiate the MSE of Equation 1.1 with respect to \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\) and set the gradient to zero:
\[
\nabla_{\parameterpart{\vect{w}}}\loss
= -\frac{2}{n}\,\featurepart{\matr{X}}^{\top}
\bigl(\targetpart{\vect{y}}-\featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\bigr)
= -\frac{2}{n}\,\featurepart{\matr{X}}^{\top}\residualpart{\vect{e}}
= \vect{0}.
\]
The condition \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^{\top}\residualpart{\vect{e}}=\vect{0}\) says the residual is orthogonal to every feature column. Substituting \(\residualpart{\vect{e}}=\targetpart{\vect{y}}-\featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}}\) and moving the known term to the right gives the normal equations:
\[
\featurepart{\matr{X}^\top\matr{X}}\,
\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}}
=
\featurepart{\matr{X}^\top}\targetpart{\vect{y}} .
\tag{1.2}\]
The normal equations characterize the minimizer. To compute it, we do not form \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) and invert it: the inverse \((\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}})^{-1}\) is mathematical shorthand, and numerical libraries solve the system by more stable means (Implementation 1 below).
Direct inversion also requires full column rank (\(n \ge d\), with no redundant features). When parameters outnumber training examples (\(d > n\)), the matrix \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) is singular, and infinitely many weight vectors achieve the same minimum error. Classical statistics treated \(d > n\) as a pathology. In deep learning, having more parameters than training examples (overparameterization) is common.3
Even if direct inversion is impractical at scale, setting the gradient to zero gives a geometric picture of the solution. As the next subsection shows, the normal equations describe an orthogonal projection, and that projection can be read in two ways. The first reads a prediction as a weighted sum of features, as in every linear model. The second reads it as a weighted sum of training targets, the form that attention takes in Part IV.

Two sides of the same projection
Each column \(\featurepart{\matr{X}_{:j}}\) of the data matrix holds the values of feature \(j\) for all \(n\) examples. The prediction vector is a weighted combination of these columns, with the weights as coefficients:
\[
\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}}
= \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}}
= \sum_{j=1}^{d}\parameterpart{\hat w_j}\featurepart{\matr{X}_{:j}} .
\]
It therefore lies in the column space of \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\). If \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\) lies outside that space, the closest point to it inside the space is found by dropping a perpendicular: \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}}\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\) onto the column space. The residual \(\residualpart{\vect{e}}=\targetpart{\vect{y}}-\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}}\) is then orthogonal to every column, which is the condition \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^{\top}\residualpart{\vect{e}}=\vect{0}\) derived above. No adjustment of the weights can shorten it further. Figure 1.3 draws the picture.






Figure 1.3: The normal equations, geometrically: the optimal prediction \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}}\) is the projection of \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\) onto the column space of \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\). The residual \(\residualpart{\vect{e}}\) is orthogonal to it.



Now read the same projection from the other side. Let \(\featurepart{\matr{X}^{+}}\) be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\). It equals \((\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}})^{-1}\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\) when \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) has full column rank. In general it is \(\matr{V}\matr{\Sigma}^{+}\matr{U}^\top\), where \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}=\matr{U}\matr{\Sigma}\matr{V}^\top\) is the SVD of \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) (Appendix A) and \(\matr{\Sigma}^{+}\) inverts the nonzero singular values and keeps the zero ones. One least-squares solution is \(\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}^{+}}\targetpart{\vect{y}}\), and it is the only one when \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) has full column rank. Substituting it into \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}}\) gives \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}\matr{X}^{+}}\targetpart{\vect{y}}\). The \(n\times n\) matrix \(\featurepart{\matr{X}\matr{X}^{+}}\) is the projection matrix, often called the hat matrix because it puts the hat on \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\). Entry \(i\) of the product is one fitted value:
\[
\predictionpart{\hat y_i}
= \sum_{j=1}^{n}
\featurepart{\bigl(\matr{X}\matr{X}^{+}\bigr)_{ij}}\,
\targetpart{y_j}.
\]
Read this way, every prediction is a weighted combination of the training targets \(\targetpart{y_j}\).4
This dual perspective will return often. The column-space reading predicts by weighting the features with learned weights. The hat-matrix reading predicts by mixing observed training targets. Under full column rank, the weight on \(\targetpart{y_j}\) is the inner product \(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i^\top(\matr{X}^\top\matr{X})^{-1}\vect{x}_j}\), which measures how the training input \(\featurepart{\vect{x}_j}\) aligns with the input \(\featurepart{\vect{x}_i}\) at which we predict.5
The normal equations define the optimal destination. What they do not provide is a scalable way to get there. A direct solution is available for the small linear models considered here. To train modern models, we trade the one-shot solve for an iterative search: start with an initial guess, measure how bad it is, and take a local step downhill.

section: 1.5 Finding the best weights, method 2: walk downhill
text:
1.5 Finding the best weights, method 2: walk downhill
Here is the geometric intuition. Picture the loss as a landscape over the parameter space, and imagine standing on it blindfolded, trying to find the lowest valley. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you feel the slope, take a small step downhill, and repeat. The mathematical expression of this procedure is gradient descent:

\[
\parameterpart{\vect{w}^{(t+1)}}
= \parameterpart{\vect{w}^{(t)}}
- \eta\,\nabla_{\parameterpart{\vect{w}}}
\loss\!\left(\parameterpart{\vect{w}^{(t)}}\right),
\tag{1.3}\]

where the learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size.
Recall from our derivation of the normal equations that the gradient of the MSE loss is already in hand. With \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\in\R^{n\times d}\), \(\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\in\R^d\), and \(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\in\R^n\), the gradient is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla_{\parameterpart{\vect{w}}}
\loss(\parameterpart{\vect{w}})
&= -\frac{2}{n}\,\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\residualpart{\vect{e}} \\
&= \frac{2}{n}\,\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top
\left(
  \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\vect{w}}
  -\targetpart{\vect{y}}
\right)
\in\R^d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.4}\]




Create a two-parameter regression problem and its loss surface.
Follow the gradient from a deliberately poor starting point.
Show the same landscape in perspective and from overhead.



import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
x1 = torch.randn(60)
y1 = 2.5 * x1 - 1.0 + 0.3 * torch.randn(60)

def mse(w, b):
    return ((y1 - (w * x1 + b)) ** 2).mean()

W, B = np.meshgrid(
    np.linspace(-1.5, 5.5, 100),
    np.linspace(-4.0, 3.0, 100),
)
L = np.vectorize(lambda wi, bi: float(mse(wi, bi)))(W, B)

# [2]
w, b, path = -0.5, 2.0, []
for _ in range(20):
    path.append((w, b))
    err = (w * x1 + b) - y1
    w -= 0.25 * float(2 * (err * x1).mean())
    b -= 0.25 * float(2 * err.mean())

pw, pb = zip(*path)
path_loss = [float(mse(wi, bi)) for wi, bi in path]

# [3]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9.2, 3.8))
ax3d = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1, projection="3d")
ax3d.plot_surface(W, B, L, cmap="Blues", alpha=0.78, linewidth=0)
ax3d.plot(pw, pb, path_loss, "o-", color="#E57200", ms=3, lw=1.5)
ax3d.set(xlabel="$w$", ylabel="$b$", zlabel="MSE")
ax3d.view_init(elev=27, azim=-58)

ax2d = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2)
ax2d.contour(W, B, L, levels=25, cmap="Blues", alpha=0.85)
ax2d.plot(pw, pb, "o-", color="#E57200", ms=4, lw=1.5,
          label="descent path")
ax2d.plot(2.5, -1.0, "k*", ms=12, label="data-generating parameters")
ax2d.set(xlabel="$w$", ylabel="$b$")
ax2d.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1.4: One loss landscape, two views. The surface makes the scalar height of MSE visible; the contour view makes the update path legible. Gradient descent needs only the local slope, not a view of the whole bowl.






This iterative loop (predict \(\rightarrow\) evaluate the loss \(\rightarrow\) compute the gradient \(\rightarrow\) update the parameters) is what modern deep learning frameworks automate, at billion-parameter scale. When the dataset is huge, we will not even evaluate the loss on every example at each step: a small random batch provides an unbiased gradient estimate that is accurate enough to make steady progress. That refinement, stochastic gradient descent, is the subject of Chapter 4.

section: 1.6 Build the complete model three ways
text:
1.6 Build the complete model three ways
The 60-point problem above had two parameters, so we could draw its landscape and the path of gradient descent. Now we fit a regression model with two features and a bias to a new dataset, using both methods. Implementation 1 is the direct solve. Implementations 2 and 3 are gradient descent, written by hand and then with the PyTorch modules we will reuse for every later model. We then check whether the three computations give the same estimate.






TipCoding hygiene



Two habits are worth forming from the first cell: fix seeds so runs are reproducible, and annotate functions with types so shapes and interfaces stay readable. The cells in this book are short teaching examples that expose the mechanism and the checks behind each claim.





Load the chapter dependencies and establish reproducible state.



import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050);


First, synthetic data. We know the data-generating weights and bias, so we can compare each method’s estimate against them.



Define the reusable make_synthetic_data helper.
Generate noisy targets from known weights, then check the batch shapes.



# [1]
def make_synthetic_data(
    weights: torch.Tensor, bias: float, n_samples: int, noise: float = 0.1
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """y = Xw + b + noise.  Returns X: (n, d) and y: (n,)."""
    X = torch.randn(n_samples, len(weights))
    y = X @ weights + bias + noise * torch.randn(n_samples)
    return X, y

# [2]
true_w, true_b = torch.tensor([2.0, -3.4]), 4.2
X, y = make_synthetic_data(true_w, true_b, n_samples=200)
X.shape, y.shape        # always check your shapes

(torch.Size([200, 2]), torch.Size([200]))




Implementation 1: least squares
First append a column of ones to \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\), so that the bias becomes the weight of a constant feature (the linear model section). Then call the least-squares routine:



Append a constant feature to represent the bias.
Solve least squares with a rank-aware library routine.
Compare the estimate with the planted parameters.



# [1]
X_aug = torch.cat([X, torch.ones(X.shape[0], 1)], dim=1)

# [2]
w_ols = torch.linalg.lstsq(X_aug, y).solution

# [3]
print(f"closed form:      w = {w_ols[:2].numpy().round(3)},  b = {w_ols[2]:.3f}")
print(f"ground truth:     w = {true_w.numpy()},  b = {true_b}")

closed form:      w = [ 2.01  -3.402],  b = 4.196
ground truth:     w = [ 2.  -3.4],  b = 4.2



These two lines compute the least-squares estimate, which we compare with the planted parameters here and with the two iterative estimates below. lstsq handles rank and conditioning more reliably than explicitly forming \(\matr{X}^{\top}\matr{X}\).


Implementation 2: manual gradient descent
We write the model as a small class: a forward pass and an update step. Each step predicts, forms the error, and moves both parameters against the gradient of Equation 1.4, which we derived by hand.



Store the parameters and define the linear prediction.
Convert batch residuals into the exact MSE update.
Repeat that update until the loss settles.
Compare the learned parameters with the other solution.



# [1]
class LinearRegressionScratch:
    """Linear regression trained with manually derived gradients."""

    def __init__(self, input_size: int, lr: float = 0.1):
        self.w = 0.01 * torch.randn(input_size)
        self.b = torch.zeros(1)
        self.lr = lr

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return X @ self.w + self.b

    def step(self, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> float:
        # [2]
        err = self.forward(X) - y            # 1. predict, 2. measure   (n,)
        self.w -= self.lr * 2 * X.T @ err / len(y)   # 3. feel the slope,
        self.b -= self.lr * 2 * err.mean()           # 4. step downhill
        return float((err ** 2).mean())

# [3]
model = LinearRegressionScratch(input_size=2)
losses = [model.step(X, y) for _ in range(100)]

# [4]
print(f"gradient descent: w = {model.w.numpy().round(3)},  b = {model.b.item():.3f}")

gradient descent: w = [ 2.01  -3.402],  b = 4.196





Implementation 3: PyTorch modules
Finally, we adopt the idiom you will use for every model from here on: nn.Linear stores the parameters, autograd computes their gradients, and the optimizer applies the update.






NoteA deliberate framework preview



This cell shows the complete PyTorch training loop so you can recognize its shape. We use the three framework calls as black boxes here: Chapter 3 introduces modules, Chapter 4 opens the optimizer, and Chapter 5 explains what backward() computes. Until then, the manual implementation above shows what the three calls do.





Pair a linear module with MSE and an SGD optimizer.
Repeat the framework forward, backward, and update sequence.
Detach and report the learned parameters.



from torch import nn

# [1]
net = nn.Linear(in_features=2, out_features=1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
nn_losses = []

# [2]
for _ in range(100):
    optimizer.zero_grad()              # clear old gradients: they accumulate!
    loss = loss_fn(net(X).squeeze(-1), y)   # (n, 1) -> (n)
    nn_losses.append(float(loss.detach()))
    loss.backward()                    # autograd feels the slope for us
    optimizer.step()

w_nn = net.weight.detach().squeeze()
b_nn = net.bias.item()
# [3]
print(f"nn.Linear:        w = {w_nn.numpy().round(3)},  b = {b_nn:.3f}")

nn.Linear:        w = [ 2.01  -3.402],  b = 4.196



Each method leaves a loss record we can compare:



Collect the direct-solve and iterative loss records.



# [1]
closed_losses = [
    float((y ** 2).mean()),
    float(((X_aug @ w_ols - y) ** 2).mean()),
]
records = [closed_losses, losses, nn_losses]
titles = ["closed form", "scratch gradient descent", "PyTorch module"]










Figure 1.5: Three routes to the same loss floor. The closed form is a before-and-after solve, not an optimization trajectory; both gradient methods expose the sequence of corrective steps.





Loss-versus-step plots will recur throughout the book. They reveal whether an optimization process is descending, stalling, or diverging, and they make competing update rules comparable.
Three implementations, one answer:



Choose a one-dimensional slice through the two-feature data.
Evaluate each learned model along that same slice.
Plot the adjusted observations and all three fits.



# [1]
grid = torch.linspace(X[:, 0].min(), X[:, 0].max(), 50)
x2_mean = X[:, 1].mean()

# [2]
def prediction_slice(weights: torch.Tensor, bias: float) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Predictions along x1 while x2 is held at its sample mean."""
    return weights[0] * grid + weights[1] * x2_mean + bias

y_on_slice = y - true_w[1] * (X[:, 1] - x2_mean)

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 3.6))
# [3]
plt.scatter(X[:, 0], y_on_slice, s=12, alpha=0.4, label="data adjusted to slice")
plt.plot(grid, prediction_slice(w_ols, float(w_ols[2])), lw=3, label="closed form")
plt.plot(grid, prediction_slice(model.w, model.b.item()), "--", lw=2,
         label="gradient descent")
plt.plot(grid, prediction_slice(w_nn, b_nn), ":", lw=2, label="nn.Linear")
plt.xlabel("$x_1$"); plt.ylabel("$y$"); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1.6: All three methods find the same line on the slice \(x_2 = \bar{x}_2\). Because this is synthetic data, the points can be adjusted to that same slice using the known true coefficient; line and points now show the same question.






The computation shared by all three implementations can also be drawn as a small circuit:






Figure 1.7: A linear model as a computation circuit: each blue input is scaled by an orange learnable weight, the signals and orange bias are added, and the green prediction leaves the circuit.

section: 1.7 Why squared error? The maximum-likelihood view
text:
1.7 Why squared error? The maximum-likelihood view
Mean squared error is not an arbitrary penalty. Assume targets are generated by a linear process with additive Gaussian noise.6
\[
\targetpart{y}
= \parameterpart{\vect{w}^\top}\featurepart{\vect{x}}
+ \parameterpart{b}
+ \residualpart{\epsilon},
\qquad
\residualpart{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
\]
The conditional distribution of \(\targetpart{y}\) given \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}\) is therefore a Gaussian centered at the deterministic prediction \(\predictionpart{\hat y}
=\parameterpart{\vect{w}^{\top}}\featurepart{\vect{x}}+\parameterpart{b}\):
\[
p(\targetpart{y}\mid\featurepart{\vect{x}};
  \parameterpart{\vect{w}},\parameterpart{b})
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\!\left(
  -\frac{\bigl(\targetpart{y}-\predictionpart{\hat y}\bigr)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\right).
\]
Maximum likelihood asks which \((\parameterpart{\vect{w}},\parameterpart{b})\) make the observed dataset most probable. Independence makes the dataset likelihood the product of the per-example densities, \(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p(\targetpart{y_i}\mid\featurepart{\vect{x}_i};\parameterpart{\vect{w}},\parameterpart{b})\). The logarithm turns that product into a sum and brings the Gaussian exponent down:
\[
\log p(\targetpart{\vect{y}}\mid\featurepart{\matr{X}};\parameterpart{\vect{w}},\parameterpart{b})
= C-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\bigl(\targetpart{y_i}-\predictionpart{\hat y_i}\bigr)^2.
\]
Maximizing this log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared residuals. A likelihood-derived loss is a probability model in disguise: we state how targets may vary around a prediction and take the negative log-likelihood.






Figure 1.8: The target type changes the conditional distribution and link function, but the maximum-likelihood recipe stays fixed. Gaussian continuous targets yield MSE, and Bernoulli binary targets yield binary cross-entropy.



The same recipe carries over to classification in Chapter 2. Continuous targets suggest a Gaussian likelihood and MSE. Binary and categorical targets suggest Bernoulli and categorical likelihoods and cross-entropy. A Laplace likelihood would instead produce absolute error. Choosing a loss is therefore a modeling decision: we make it by choosing a distribution for the targets.

title: 1  Linear Regression, the Mother Model
section: 1.8 A first look at bias and variance
text:
1.8 A first look at bias and variance
A fitted model depends on the training set we happened to collect. To judge a fitting recipe, we therefore ask how its predictions would change if we collected the data again. A simulation answers this question. Take the curve \(f^*(x) = 0.25 + 0.75x + 0.85x^2\) as the truth, and repeat three steps 200 times:

draw 12 inputs uniformly from \([-1, 1]\);
set each target to \(f^*(x)\) plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.32;
fit a straight line to the 12 points by least squares.

Each repetition gives a different line (the left panel of Figure 1.9). At a fixed input such as \(x_0 = 0.65\), the 200 predictions form a green distribution with a center and a spread (the middle panel, a vertical slice through the left one). The center can miss the black true curve, because a line cannot follow a parabola. The spread comes from the changing training sets. Fresh targets at \(x_0\) also scatter around the true curve, because of the noise.








Figure 1.9: Bias and variance from repeated fits. Left: forty of the 200 fits, each a straight line fitted to a fresh noisy dataset. One dataset is purple, the mean prediction is green, and the data-generating curve is black. The dotted line marks the slice at \(x_0=0.65\). Middle: on the same vertical scale, that slice becomes two distributions, the predictions at \(x_0\) (green) and fresh targets at \(x_0\) (gray). Bias is the distance from the truth to the mean prediction. The green and gray arrows each span \(\pm 1\) sample standard deviation, and the squares of these spreads are the variance and the irreducible noise. Right: the familiar U-curve, a schematic of the classical trade-off between the three terms as the model grows more flexible. Modern models can depart from it.





Now we formalize what the figure shows. Our learned predictor \(\predictionpart{\hat f_{\mathcal D}}\) depends on the random training set \(\mathcal D\). Let \(f^*(\featurepart{\vect{x}})
=\E[\targetpart{Y}\mid\featurepart{X}=\featurepart{\vect{x}}]\) be the regression function, and write the average learned prediction as \(\predictionpart{\bar f}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})
=\E_{\mathcal D}[\predictionpart{\hat f_{\mathcal D}}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})]\). Now fix an input \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}\) and draw a fresh target \(\targetpart{Y}\) at that input, independently of the training set. The error \(\predictionpart{\hat f_{\mathcal D}}(\featurepart{\vect{x}}) - \targetpart{Y}\) is random for two reasons: the training set \(\mathcal D\) varies, and so does \(\targetpart{Y}\). The average of its square over both sources of randomness has three parts:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\E_{\mathcal D,\targetpart{Y}}\!\Bigl[\bigl(\predictionpart{\hat f_{\mathcal D}}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})-\targetpart{Y}\bigr)^2\Bigr] \\[4pt]
&\quad = \underbrace{\bigl(\predictionpart{\bar f}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})-f^*(\featurepart{\vect{x}})\bigr)^2}_{\residualpart{\text{bias}^2}} \\[4pt]
&\qquad + \underbrace{\E_{\mathcal D}\!\Bigl[\bigl(\predictionpart{\hat f_{\mathcal D}}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})-\predictionpart{\bar f}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})\bigr)^2\Bigr]}_{\predictionpart{\text{variance}}} \\[4pt]
&\qquad + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\bigl(\targetpart{Y}\mid\featurepart{X}=\featurepart{\vect{x}}\bigr)}_{\targetpart{\text{irreducible noise}}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{1.5}\]

The \(\residualpart{\text{bias}}\) term measures how far the \(\predictionpart{\text{average prediction}}\) is from the truth because of limiting assumptions like linearity: a simple model on complex data is systematically wrong (underfitting). The \(\predictionpart{\text{variance}}\) term measures how much the prediction would change if we collected a fresh training set (the model’s sensitivity to sampling noise). A complex model can fit the noise itself (overfitting). The \(\targetpart{\text{irreducible noise}}\) belongs to the data-generating process and cannot be learned away.
This is why we split data into training, validation, and test sets. We fit the model on the training set. The validation set is an independent sample from \(P\), so its average loss estimates each fitted model’s population risk \(R_P\) and referees the bias–variance trade-off. The test set stays untouched until the end.






WarningTrap: treating the U-shaped curve as a universal law



The textbook picture shows validation error falling and then rising as complexity grows. It is a helpful first mental model, but bias and variance need not move in opposite directions. In classical fixed-dimensional, well-specified settings, variance often falls roughly like \(1/n\) as data grows, and modern models need not follow that rate. Regularization and inductive biases matched to the problem can allow more capacity without a sharp rise in variance. An overparameterized network can even pass the interpolation threshold, the capacity at which it first fits the training set exactly, and then improve again as capacity grows. This second fall is called double descent. Chapter 6 tests the classical U-curve in a small width sweep and discusses double descent.



Regularization, briefly
We can already reduce variance with one change to the loss: a penalty on large weights. Ridge regression adds an \(L_2\) penalty,
\[
\loss_\lambda(\parameterpart{\vect{w}})
= \frac{1}{n}\norm{
  \targetpart{\vect{y}}-\featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\vect{w}}
}_2^2
+ \lambda\norm{\parameterpart{\vect{w}}}_2^2,
\qquad
\parameterpart{\hat{\vect{w}}_{\text{ridge}}}
= \left(
  \featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}}+n\lambda I
\right)^{-1}
\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\targetpart{\vect{y}},
\]
nudging the model toward smaller, more stable weights: it accepts a little bias in exchange for less variance.7 The factor \(n\) is there because our data-fit term is a mean. This displayed solution applies when there is no intercept or when features and targets have been centered so the intercept is recovered separately. We normally do not penalize that intercept. In augmented-matrix notation, replace \(I\) by \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0)\) so the final bias coordinate remains free.
To see the effect, we construct a dataset on which least squares is unstable. It has \(n = 25\) examples, each with \(d = 20\) features drawn from a standard normal distribution, so there are barely more examples than weights to fit. Only the first 5 features have nonzero planted weights. The other 15 have weight zero, the bias is zero, and Gaussian noise is added to each target. With so few examples per weight, the ordinary least-squares (OLS) estimate varies a lot from one dataset to the next, and it can give sizable weights to the 15 features that do not affect the target.



Create a small-sample problem with many irrelevant features.
Solve the same data with unregularized and ridge estimators.
Compare both estimates with the planted weights.



# [1]
n, d = 25, 20                            # barely more samples than knobs!
w_true = torch.zeros(d)
w_true[:5] = torch.tensor([3.0, -2.0, 1.5, 2.5, -1.0])   # only 5 real features
Xh, yh = make_synthetic_data(w_true, bias=0.0, n_samples=n, noise=2.0)

# [2]
w_ols_h = torch.linalg.lstsq(Xh, yh).solution
lam = 0.4
w_ridge = torch.linalg.solve(Xh.T @ Xh + n * lam * torch.eye(d), Xh.T @ yh)

# [3]
def report(name: str, w_hat: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    err = ((w_hat - w_true) ** 2).mean()
    print(f"{name:>6}:  weight MSE = {err:.4f}")

report("OLS", w_ols_h)
report("ridge", w_ridge)

   OLS:  weight MSE = 1.2347
 ridge:  weight MSE = 0.4400



We score each estimate by its weight MSE, the mean squared difference between the estimated and planted weights. Ridge shrinks every weight toward zero and reduces the weight MSE from 1.2347 for OLS to 0.4400. These numbers come from a single draw of the data, taken from the random stream of the runs above, with \(\lambda\) set by hand. Another draw would give other numbers, and separating the gain into bias and variance would require repeating the experiment across fresh datasets, as in Figure 1.9. (Rerun this cell with n = 100 and watch OLS become more stable, as classical fixed-dimensional theory predicts.) In later chapters, the same \(L_2\) idea returns as weight decay in large neural networks.

title: 1  Linear Regression, the Mother Model
text:
In Part II, an image filter will slide this same dot product across an image. In Part IV, attention will build learned similarities between queries and keys from the same primitive.↩︎
Across all \(n\) examples stacked in the data matrix \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\in\R^{n\times d}\), the predictions \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\vect{w}} + \parameterpart{b}\vect{1}\) likewise become \(\predictionpart{\hat{\vect{y}}} = \featurepart{\matr{X}}\parameterpart{\vect{w}}\) after appending a column of ones \(\vect{1}\) to \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}\). This is called bias augmentation or homogeneous coordinates. Geometrically, lifting the problem to \(\R^{d+1}\) anchors the hyperplane to the origin. Every model adjustment then rotates or rescales one weight vector about the origin, with no separate translation.↩︎
Two additional numerical hurdles make forming and inverting \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) impractical in software. You can skip these details without losing the conceptual thread. First, forming \(\featurepart{\matr{X}}^\top\featurepart{\matr{X}}\) explicitly squares the condition number, doubling the digits of precision that rounding can destroy (Appendix A and Appendix C). Second, exact inversion scales cubically as \(O(d^3)\) and storing the square matrix takes \(O(d^2)\) memory. At a million parameters, that matrix alone would hold a trillion entries. Robust numerical libraries therefore bypass the normal equations and factor rectangular data directly, as in Implementation 1 below.↩︎
The same reading holds for kernel ridge regression in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space: each prediction is again a fixed weighted combination of the training targets, and, as in least squares, some of those weights can be negative.↩︎
In ordinary least squares, these mixing weights are fixed globally, and some can be negative. In Part IV (Chapter 14 and Chapter 17), we reopen this exact target-mixing equation. Replacing this rigid projection with a localized, positive similarity score connects linear regression directly to Nadaraya–Watson kernel regression and the modern attention mechanism, which forces the mixing weights to be nonnegative and sum to one.↩︎
This is more than algebraic convenience. A residual often aggregates many small, unobserved effects, such as sensor variation, environmental fluctuations, omitted features, and rounding. Under the conditions of the central limit theorem, sums of many independent or weakly dependent finite-variance effects become approximately Gaussian. There is also an informational argument: among continuous distributions with a fixed mean and variance, the Gaussian has maximum differential entropy, so it adds no further structure beyond those two constraints. Neither argument makes every residual Gaussian. The assumption is a useful model, and its fit to the data should be checked.↩︎
For a small update nearly perpendicular to \(\vect{w}\), the rotation angle is \(\Delta\varphi\approx
\norm{\Delta\vect{w}_{\perp}}_2/\norm{\vect{w}}_2\): the same nudge rotates a larger vector less. The \(L_2\) penalty adds \(2\lambda\vect{w}\) to the gradient, so a gradient step becomes \(\vect{w}\leftarrow(1-2\eta\lambda)\vect{w}
-\eta\nabla\loss_{\mathrm{data}}\). The first factor shrinks \(\vect{w}\) along its own direction. A shorter weight vector turns further under the same nudge, so the shrink keeps later updates able to change the weight’s direction.↩︎

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
2.1 From regression to classification
Regression predicts numbers. Many tasks ask for categories instead: cat or dog, spam or not, which of ten digits. This chapter turns the linear machinery of Chapter 1 into a classifier and keeps its parts: the same weighted sums, the same maximum-likelihood recipe for the loss, the same gradient descent. The new element is a probability transformation at the output.
In the computation circuit of Figure 1.7, the affine combination of inputs and bias defines a raw score \(o\) for each example. A classifier adds one operation after that score, and the linear map that produces the score stays the same.
In regression, \(y \in \R\) and the Gaussian noise model led to the MSE objective (Chapter 1). In classification, \(y\) is a label from \(\{0, \dots, K-1\}\). A binary label is a Bernoulli draw, so the Gaussian noise model no longer applies. Maximum likelihood with a Bernoulli model yields a different loss, the cross-entropy.
We need two things:
crumbs: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
a way to turn the model’s raw score (its logit, \(o \in \R\)) into a probability;
a loss that evaluates the predicted probabilities against the observed labels.
crumbs: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
2.2 Binary classification

From score to probability: the sigmoid
Our linear model produces \(o = \vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\), an unbounded score. The sigmoid maps it to a probability:
\[
\sigma(o) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-o}} .
\tag{2.1}\]



Evaluate the sigmoid across a range of logits.



import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
o = torch.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
sigmoid_response = torch.sigmoid(o)


Figure 2.1 shows the sigmoid in two views. On the left is the curve itself, \(\hat p = \sigma(o)\) as a function of the score. On the right is a binary problem with two input features, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Each marker is one example, and the shading shows the predicted probability \(\sigma(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b)\) at every point of the plane.








Figure 2.1: The sigmoid maps any real score to \((0,1)\) and crosses \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) exactly at \(o=0\) (left). In input space (right), the inputs with score zero form the straight line \(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x}+b=0\) between the circles and the squares, and the dashed contours \(\hat p = 0.1\) and \(0.9\) are parallel to it. Near the line \(\hat p\) stays close to \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), and far from it \(\hat p\) saturates toward 0 or 1.

Far from the line, the probability saturates toward 1.

The scrubber, the speed menu and the score slider also work by keyboard; the slider's own keys never move the timeline. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat's state instead of moving between them.
    
  


The decision boundary is still a hyperplane. It is the set where \(\hat{p} = \tfrac{1}{2}\). Since \(\sigma\) is increasing and \(\sigma(0) = \tfrac{1}{2}\), the boundary is the set where \(o = 0\), the hyperplane \(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b = 0\). This is the hyperplane geometry of Chapter 1, and \(\vect{w}\) is still the template against which the input is scored. The sigmoid leaves the boundary flat and assigns probabilities on either side of it.


The loss: cross-entropy from maximum likelihood
Apply maximum likelihood with the Bernoulli noise model. If the labels \(y_i \in \{0, 1\}\) are independent Bernoulli draws with \(P(y{=}1 \mid \vect{x}) = \hat{p}\), the likelihood of the dataset is \(\prod_i \hat{p}_i^{\,y_i}(1-\hat{p}_i)^{1-y_i}\). Taking the negative logarithm gives a sum of per-example binary cross-entropies. For one example,
\[
\loss_{\text{BCE}} = -\bigl[\, y \log \hat{p} + (1 - y)\log(1 - \hat{p}) \,\bigr].
\tag{2.2}\]
The loss measures surprise: if the true label is 1, the loss is \(-\log \hat{p}\). It is small when the predicted probability of the observed outcome is high and diverges as that probability approaches zero. The more confidently wrong the model is, the larger the loss.



  
  Watch the mechanism: the price of being sure and wrong

The gradient with respect to the logit
Differentiating through the sigmoid and cross-entropy with respect to the logit gives (Exercise 1 derives it step by step):
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial o} = \hat{p} - y .
\tag{2.3}\]
The logarithms and exponentials cancel, and the gradient is the prediction error, the same form that mean squared error gave for regression. Because \(o = \vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\), the chain rule gives the gradients with respect to the parameters: \(\partial\loss/\partial\vect{w} = (\hat{p} - y)\,\vect{x}\) and \(\partial\loss/\partial b = \hat{p} - y\). Softmax with cross-entropy gives the same cancellation (Equation 2.6).

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
2.3 Multiclass classification: softmax
With \(K\) classes, score \(K\) templates at once: \(\matr{W} \in \R^{K \times d}\) produces a score vector \(\vect{o} = \matr{W}\vect{x} + \vect{b}\), one logit per class.






TipThe first architectural block: the classification head



The linear map from an incoming representation to class scores is the classification head, also called a linear readout:
\[
\operatorname{head}(\featurepart{\vect{h}})
= \parameterpart{\matr{W}}\featurepart{\vect{h}} + \parameterpart{\vect{b}},
\qquad
\parameterpart{\matr{W}} \in \R^{K \times d},\quad \parameterpart{\vect{b}} \in \R^{K}.
\]
Its role is narrow: map a \(d\)-dimensional representation \(\featurepart{\vect{h}}\) of the input to \(K\) logits \(\vect{o}\) and pass them to the loss. In this chapter the representation is the raw input itself, \(\featurepart{\vect{h}} = \featurepart{\vect{x}}\), and the whole model is the head. Chapter 3 adds layers that compute \(\featurepart{\vect{h}}\) from \(\featurepart{\vect{x}}\).
Later models split into two parts. A backbone (also called the trunk) turns raw inputs such as pixels or tokens into a representation \(\featurepart{\vect{h}} = \phi_{\theta}(\featurepart{\vect{x}})\), and a small task-specific head maps that representation to the required outputs. The backbone changes dramatically across the book, from multilayer perceptrons (Chapter 3) to convolutional stacks (Chapters 9 and 10) and Transformers (Chapters 16, 18, and 19). The head usually stays this small linear map. Because the two are separate, either can be swapped. Adapting a pretrained model to new classes often keeps its backbone and trains only a fresh head (Chapters 10, 18, and 20), and one backbone can feed several heads at once: a softmax head for a label beside a linear-regression head for a coordinate.


To turn \(K\) scores into a probability distribution, exponentiate (making everything positive) and normalize:
\[
\hat{y}_j = \mathrm{softmax}(\vect{o})_j = \frac{e^{o_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{o_k}} .
\tag{2.4}\]
Softmax has three properties: every output is positive, the outputs sum to one, and it is invariant to constant shifts. Adding the same \(c\) to every logit changes nothing, because \(e^{o_j + c} = e^c e^{o_j}\) and \(e^c\) cancels between numerator and denominator. Only the differences between scores matter.



Compare softmax probabilities before and after a common logit shift.



# [1]
logits = torch.tensor([2.0, 0.5, -1.0, 1.0])
softmax_cases = [(shift, torch.softmax(logits + shift, dim=0))
                 for shift in (0.0, 100.0)]










Figure 2.2: Softmax turns scores into a distribution. Shifting every logit by the same constant (right panel) leaves the probabilities unchanged: only the differences between scores carry information.

    Transcript and keyboard help

        Divide by the one shared sum: 0.6095, 0.1360, 0.0303, 0.2242, which add to 1.
        Add c to every score, sweeping c from 0 to 100: the score ticks slide up together, the blue bars scale by the same factor, and the green bars stay on their c = 0 dashes. At c = 100 the ruler is relabelled 99 to 107 and the same marks stand where they stood: only the differences between scores matter.
        Why: adding c to a score multiplies its exponential by one shared factor, and the same factor multiplies every term of the denominator, so it cancels top and bottom.
        Return to c = 0: the same four probabilities, 0.6095, 0.1360, 0.0303, 0.2242; o₀ stays the largest throughout.

The scrubber and speed menu also work by keyboard. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat’s state: c snaps straight from 0 to 100 on the relabelled ruler for the shift and cancel beats and back to 0 for the last, never a value in between.
    
  









TipSoftmax: from scores to normalized weights



Softmax is a differentiable way to turn a list of scores into positive weights that sum to one, giving larger scores more weight. Here the scores are class logits. In Part IV the scores measure how well one request matches several stored candidates, and the resulting weights blend what those candidates contain. The reusable machine is the same: scores \(\rightarrow\) positive weights that sum to one.








NoteDifferentiable relaxation: softening hard decisions



Gradient descent needs informative derivatives.
To turn scores into one predicted class, we could take the index of the largest score, the \(\operatorname{argmax}\), and output a one-hot vector: 1 for that class and 0 for the others. This rule is hard. A small change to a losing logit leaves the output unchanged, and a change large enough to pass the winner makes the output jump. Its derivative is therefore zero almost everywhere, so gradient descent receives no signal about how close each losing score was or how the weights should change. (The scalar \(\max\) of the scores behaves differently: its gradient passes through the winning input.)
Softmax is a smooth relaxation of that one-hot selection, a soft max. Instead of selecting one winner, it distributes probability according to the scores, so the loss can be differentiated through every logit. The resulting gradient still depends on the loss and the probabilities: with cross-entropy, each logit’s gradient is its predicted probability minus its target, as Equation 2.6 below shows. Softmax plays two roles at once: its output is a proper categorical distribution, which cross-entropy scores below, and it is a smooth surrogate for a discrete choice that makes the model trainable.
A temperature \(\tau > 0\) sets how sharp or flat the softmax output is:
\[
\operatorname{softmax}(\vect{o}/\tau)_j = \frac{e^{o_j/\tau}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{o_k/\tau}} .
\]
As \(\tau \to 0\) the distribution sharpens toward the hard winner, and as \(\tau \to \infty\) it flattens toward a uniform distribution. Every value in between gives a smooth output (Figure 2.3). Text generators use the same division: they divide next-token logits by \(\tau\) and sample from the result, so \(\tau\) sets the entropy of the sampling distribution. Near \(\tau = 0\) sampling approaches greedy decoding, which is predictable and prone to repetition. At large \(\tau\) it approaches uniform noise. In between, lower-ranked but plausible tokens are sometimes drawn.
Other discrete operations, such as a lookup, a yes/no branch, or even sorting a list (differentiable sorting exists), can be softened the same way: replace the hard decision with a smooth, temperature-controlled relaxation, train with gradients, and sharpen later if needed. One such relaxation recurs in this book. A hard memory lookup reads one stored row and ignores the others. Part IV replaces it with a softmax-weighted read across all the stored rows, an operation called attention.





Compare one hard selection with three temperature-softened distributions.



# [1]
logits_demo = torch.tensor([2.0, 1.0, 0.2, -0.5])
klasses = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]
hard = torch.zeros(4); hard[logits_demo.argmax()] = 1.0
temperatures = [0.5, 1.0, 4.0]
soft_cases = [torch.softmax(logits_demo / temp, dim=0) for temp in temperatures]










Figure 2.3: The softening move, in one row. The same four logits (left) pass through the hard argmax-plus-one-hot selection (piecewise constant, with zero gradient almost everywhere) and through softmax at three temperatures. Small \(\tau\) sharpens toward the hard winner, and large \(\tau\) flattens toward a uniform distribution. Every version in between is smooth, so the loss can be differentiated through every logit. Chapter 15 returns to this same normalization pattern.






Multiclass cross-entropy
With one-hot labels \(\vect{y}\) (all zeros except a 1 at the true class), the cross-entropy is
\[
\loss_{\text{CE}} = -\sum_{j=1}^{K} y_j \log \hat{y}_j = -\log \hat{y}_{\text{true class}},
\tag{2.5}\]
the surprise at the true class, again. And the gradient has the same form:
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial o_j} = \hat{y}_j - y_j ,
\tag{2.6}\]
prediction minus target, one more time. This recurrence has a reason. Taking the logarithm of Equation 2.4 gives \(\log\hat{y}_j = o_j - \log\sum_{k} e^{o_k}\): each log-probability is its own logit minus a term shared by all classes. Logits with this property are called the distribution’s natural parameters, and the sigmoid is the two-class case. Differentiating \(-\log\hat{y}_{\text{true class}}\) with respect to \(o_j\) gives \(-y_j\) from the first term and \(\hat{y}_j\) from the shared term, so the gradient is the predicted probability minus the observed indicator.






NoteThe information-theory reading: coding and surprise



Probability and compression are two readings of the same objective. A code writes each symbol as a string of digits, and a good code gives frequent symbols short strings. The best code gives a symbol of probability \(p_j\) a length of about \(-\log p_j\). (The word has another meaning in Chapter 11, where a code is a learned representation of the input.) With natural logs, lengths are measured in nats.

Entropy \(H(P) = -\sum_j p_j \log p_j\) is the uncertainty in a distribution: the shortest average code length possible for symbols drawn from \(P\).
Cross-entropy \(H(P, Q) = -\sum_j p_j \log q_j\) is the average code length when symbols from \(P\) are encoded with a code built for the model’s belief \(Q\).

The gap between them is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, the extra length incurred by using the wrong code:
\[
H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \,\|\, Q),
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \,\|\, Q) = \sum_j p_j \log \frac{p_j}{q_j} \;\ge\; 0 .
\]
A one-hot label puts probability 1 on the true class, so it has no uncertainty: \(H(P) = 0\). For one-hot labels, then, cross-entropy is the KL divergence, and both reduce to the surprise at the truth, \(-\log q_{\text{true}}\) of Equation 2.5. Minimizing this loss is at once maximizing the categorical likelihood, minimizing the expected code length, and minimizing the KL divergence from the labels to the model.
When the target is itself a soft distribution, \(H(P)\) no longer vanishes. If \(P\) is fixed, cross-entropy and KL still differ only by that constant. The distinction matters when the first argument moves too, as in the alignment penalty of Chapter 21 and the variational autoencoder of Chapter 22. Appendix E compares KL with other ways to compare distributions.










Figure 2.4: Cross-entropy splits into the target’s own entropy plus the KL divergence, the extra code length incurred by using the model’s belief \(Q\). The model belief is the same in both rows. A soft target (top) carries entropy of its own. A one-hot target (bottom) carries none, so its whole cross-entropy is KL divergence, the surprise \(-\log q_{\text{true}}\).







Numerical stability of softmax
Computing \(e^{o_j}\) overflows once a logit exceeds roughly 88.7 in float32 (about 709 in float64), a scale training easily reaches. The fix exploits shift invariance: subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiating forces every exponent to be at most zero. This safeguard (the core of the log-sum-exp trick) preserves the mathematical result while avoiding overflow in the exponentials. We put it to work from scratch in the code below. Appendix C examines floating-point limits and hardware representations in depth.

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
2.4 Implementing a three-class classifier
We now assemble the full classifier on three Gaussian clusters from four pieces of the preceding sections: three templates, the stable softmax, the cross-entropy loss, and the gradient. The template of class \(k\) is its weight vector \(\vect{w}_k\), which is row \(k\) of \(\matr{W}\). The score \(\vect{w}_k^\top\vect{x} + b_k\) measures how well \(\vect{x}\) matches it (Chapter 1). Because Equation 2.6 reduced the gradient to \(\hat{\vect{y}} - \vect{y}\), we can implement it by hand, without autograd:



Fix the seed, draw three Gaussian clusters of 150 points each, and one-hot encode the labels.
Define the reusable stable_softmax helper.
Apply the softmax cross-entropy gradient to all three templates.
Print the final cross-entropy and accuracy on the training clusters.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
centers = torch.tensor([[-2.0, 0.0], [2.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.5]])
X = torch.cat([c + 0.7 * torch.randn(150, 2) for c in centers])   # (450, 2)
y = torch.arange(3).repeat_interleave(150)                        # (450,)
Y = torch.nn.functional.one_hot(y, 3).float()                     # (450, 3)

# [2]
def stable_softmax(logits: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    z = logits - logits.max(dim=-1, keepdim=True).values   # shift invariance at work
    e = torch.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)

W, b = torch.zeros(3, 2), torch.zeros(3)
# [3]
for step in range(400):
    P = stable_softmax(X @ W.T + b)          # (450, 3) predicted probabilities
    G = (P - Y) / len(X)                     # the beautiful gradient, eq. (6)
    W -= 1.0 * G.T @ X                       # residual out x signal in
    b -= 1.0 * G.sum(0)

P = stable_softmax(X @ W.T + b)              # evaluate the final updated parameters
ce = -(Y * torch.log(P)).sum(1).mean()
acc = (P.argmax(1) == y).float().mean()
# [4]
print(f"cross-entropy {ce:.3f}   accuracy {acc:.1%}")

cross-entropy 0.033   accuracy 98.9%






Score a dense grid with the trained classifier, then fill class regions and shade by confidence.
Overlay each class’s points and label the axes.



import numpy as np

# [1]
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 300), np.linspace(-2.5, 5, 300))
grid = torch.tensor(np.stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()], 1), dtype=torch.float32)
Pg = stable_softmax(grid @ W.T + b)
cls = Pg.argmax(1).reshape(gx.shape).numpy()
conf = Pg.max(1).values.reshape(gx.shape).numpy()

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4.4))
plt.contourf(gx, gy, cls, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5],
             colors=["#DCE6F2", "#FDE3C8", "#E3EEE3"])
plt.contourf(gx, gy, 1 - conf, levels=12, cmap="Greys",
             alpha=0.25, antialiased=True)
# [2]
for k, color in enumerate(["#232D4B", "#E57200", "#6B8E6B"]):
    plt.scatter(X[y == k, 0], X[y == k, 1], s=8, c=color, label=f"class {k}")
plt.xlabel("$x_1$"); plt.ylabel("$x_2$"); plt.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 2.5: Three templates, three linear boundaries. Color shows the predicted class; shading shows confidence (the max softmax probability): crisp deep in each region, washed out along the boundaries where classes compete.






PyTorch provides the same cross-entropy as a built-in loss, nn.CrossEntropyLoss, which takes raw logits and integer labels. The warning below explains its one trap. The loss object only evaluates the loss: the parameter updates still come from the manual loop above, and optimizers and automatic differentiation remain black boxes until Chapters 4 and 5.



Create the framework loss object loss_fn from torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss.
Compare the hand-computed cross-entropy with PyTorch’s fused loss.



# [1]
loss_fn = torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
# [2]
print(f"ours: {ce:.6f}   torch: {loss_fn(X @ W.T + b, y):.6f}")

ours: 0.033425   torch: 0.033425









WarningLet PyTorch do the logits-to-probabilities conversion



nn.CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits by design. It fuses the softmax and the logarithm with the log-sum-exp trick, which is more stable numerically than a softmax followed by a separate logarithm. Have the model output logits, pass them directly to the loss, and apply softmax only when probabilities are needed for reporting. In PyTorch a classification head is an nn.Linear(d, K), and its contract is to emit raw logits \(\vect{o} \in \R^K\) without applying softmax internally. (The same goes for binary problems: prefer binary_cross_entropy_with_logits over sigmoid-then-BCE.) The classic bug is feeding softmax outputs into CrossEntropyLoss. The loss then treats probabilities as logits and computes a different objective, without necessarily producing a shape error. If a classifier is mysteriously mediocre, check this first.








NoteCheck yourself



Close the book for one minute and reconstruct the classifier.

What remains linear before sigmoid or softmax is applied?
Why does the target distribution determine the negative-log-likelihood loss?
Why does PyTorch’s cross-entropy loss take raw logits as its input?

section: 2.5 Okay, so: classification keeps the linear geometry
text:
2.5 Okay, so: classification keeps the linear geometry

The linear geometry holds. Logits are still template similarities \(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\). Sigmoid and softmax act only at the output, where they turn scores into probabilities. Both preserve the order of the scores, so the boundary between any two classes is still a hyperplane, and the multiclass decision regions are bounded by pieces of those hyperplanes.
The loss comes from the noise model. As in Chapter 1, maximum likelihood turns a Bernoulli model into BCE and a categorical model into cross-entropy. Both read as surprise at the truth.
The gradient is the error. For both models, the gradient of the loss with respect to the logits is the prediction error \(\hat{\vect{y}} - \vect{y}\), because the logits are the natural parameters of the Bernoulli and categorical distributions.
Softmax turns scores into weights. It is shift-invariant, and log-sum-exp keeps it numerically stable. It returns unchanged as the normalizer of attention.

Next, we let the templates themselves be built out of other templates: Chapter 3 stacks these linear units into a backbone beneath the same head, and shows why a nonlinear activation between them is necessary.

title: 2  Linear Classification: Logistic Regression and Softmax
text:
Sources and further reading

Cox, “The Regression Analysis of Binary Sequences” (1958) develops the logistic model as a principled tool for binary outcomes.
Bridle, “Probabilistic Interpretation of Feedforward Classification Network Outputs” (1990) connects normalized exponential outputs to probabilistic multiclass classification.
Shannon, “A Mathematical Theory of Communication” (1948) is the original source behind the entropy and information vocabulary used to read cross-entropy.
Kullback and Leibler, “On Information and Sufficiency” (1951) introduces the divergence that separates cross-entropy from entropy. 
Jaynes, “Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics” (1957) shows that the distribution with the most entropy at a given expected score has the exponential form of softmax.
Blondel, Teboul, Berthet, and Djolonga, “Fast Differentiable Sorting and Ranking” (2020) is one example of replacing a hard, discrete operation with a trainable relaxation.
