title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
3.1 The four points a hyperplane cannot separate
Our linear models can regress (Chapter 1) and classify (Chapter 2). Stacking them, so that the output of one linear layer feeds into another, gives
\[
\matr{W}_2\bigl(\matr{W}_1\vect{x} + \vect{b}_1\bigr) + \vect{b}_2
= (\matr{W}_2\matr{W}_1)\,\vect{x} + (\matr{W}_2\vect{b}_1 + \vect{b}_2)
= \matr{W}_{\text{new}}\,\vect{x} + \vect{b}_{\text{new}} .
\tag{3.1}\]
The stack collapses. Two linear layers, or twenty, are equivalent to one linear layer with different parameters, so stacking alone does not increase expressive power. We need a nonlinear operation between the linear layers. This chapter studies one such operation, the hinge, and what it adds.
Four points in the plane suffice to show the limits of a linear model. The XOR function outputs 1 exactly when its two binary inputs differ:
Among the four points, no single line separates the 1s from the 0s. The two points labeled 1, \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\), sit on one diagonal of the unit square, and the two labeled 0, \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), sit on the other. Both diagonals pass through the center \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\) of the square. A line that puts both 1-points on one side also puts the midpoint between them, the center, on that side. A line that puts both 0-points on the other side puts the same center there too. No line can do both, so every line misclassifies at least one point. A linear classifier cannot represent this function, no matter how it is trained.
With the four points weighted equally, each input on its own carries no evidence about the label. Whether \(x_1\) is 0 or 1, the label is 1 half the time, and the same holds for \(x_2\). The correlation between either input and the label is therefore zero. The label depends only on the interaction of the two inputs. Because a linear score \(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\) sums separate per-coordinate contributions, it has no term that can capture that interaction.
We confirm the linear model’s limit empirically. We train two models on the four XOR points using the binary cross-entropy loss from Chapter 2: a single linear layer, nn.Linear(2, 1), and a two-layer network with a hidden layer of four units between two linear transformations. Each hidden unit applies the ReLU nonlinearity of the next section, and the layer is hidden because its outputs are neither inputs nor targets. Such a network is the simplest multilayer perceptron (MLP). We train both models by full-batch gradient descent, in which every step uses all four points. Both runs reuse the training loop structure introduced in Chapter 1 (we formally analyze the optimizer and backward() in Chapter 4 and Chapter 5).
The trained linear model converges to the cross-entropy optimum for this symmetric dataset: it assigns a probability of exactly 0.5 to all four points, for a loss of \(\log 2 \approx 0.693\). Its logits differ from zero only by floating-point rounding, so thresholding them at 0 can report an apparent accuracy of 25%, 50%, or 75%. That number reflects rounding alone. At best, a line classifies three of the four points correctly (75%). The network with four hidden units classifies all four correctly.

NoteHistorical context: the credit assignment problem



In 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons, proving that single-layer models cannot solve XOR. Multilayer networks could already represent XOR. What was missing was a reliable way to find their parameters.
A hidden unit, one that sits between the input and the output, has no target of its own. When the output is wrong, it is unclear how much each hidden weight contributed to the error and how it should change. Assigning each hidden weight its share of the output error is the credit assignment problem. Chapter 5 develops backpropagation, which solves it by computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight.






Fix the seed and write out the four XOR inputs and their labels.
Define the reusable train helper.
Run xor training.
Print the linear model’s probabilities and binary cross-entropy, then the MLP’s accuracy.



import torch
from torch import nn
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
X_xor = torch.tensor([[0., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.]])
y_xor = torch.tensor([0., 1., 1., 0.])

# [2]
def train(
    model: nn.Module, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor,
    steps: int = 4000, lr: float = 0.5
) -> nn.Module:
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(model(X).squeeze(-1), y)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    return model

# [3]
linear = train(nn.Linear(2, 1), X_xor, y_xor)
mlp = train(nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 1)),
            X_xor, y_xor)

with torch.no_grad():
    linear_p = torch.sigmoid(linear(X_xor).squeeze(-1))
    linear_bce = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy(linear_p, y_xor)
    mlp_acc = ((mlp(X_xor).squeeze(-1) > 0).float() == y_xor).float().mean()

# [4]
print(f"trained linear: probabilities {linear_p.numpy().round(3)}, "
      f"BCE {linear_bce:.3f}")
print(f" MLP (4 hidden): accuracy {mlp_acc:.0%}")

trained linear: probabilities [0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5], BCE 0.693

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

grid = torch.tensor(np.stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()], 1), dtype=torch.float32)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.4), sharey=True)
# [2]
for ax, model, title in [(axes[0], None, "best linear rule (75%)"),
                         (axes[1], mlp, "trained MLP (100%)")]:
    with torch.no_grad():
        if model is None:
            Z = (grid.sum(1) - 0.5 > 0).float().reshape(gx.shape)
        else:
            Z = (model(grid).squeeze(-1) > 0).float().reshape(gx.shape)
    ax.contourf(gx, gy, Z, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5],
                colors=["#DCE6F2", "#FDE3C8"], alpha=0.9)
    for cls, marker, color in [(0, "o", "#232D4B"), (1, "s", "#E57200")]:
        pts = X_xor[y_xor == cls]
        ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], marker=marker, s=120, c=color,
                   edgecolors="white", linewidths=1.5, zorder=3,
                   label=f"class {cls}")
    ax.set_title(title); ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("$x_2$"); axes[0].legend(loc="center right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

section: 3.2 The neuron: a threshold with a hinge
text:
3.2 The neuron: a threshold with a hinge
A neuron keeps the weighted-sum circuit of Figure 1.7 and places a hinge at its output.
The artificial neuron takes its conceptual inspiration from biology: a cell integrates incoming signals and fires only when the accumulated stimulus crosses a threshold. Early models formalized this as a hard step function, but step functions have zero derivatives almost everywhere, which halts gradient descent. The rectified linear unit (ReLU) is a computationally simple alternative. It keeps the threshold at zero and lets the response grow linearly above it:
\[
\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z), \qquad
f(\vect{x}) = \mathrm{ReLU}(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b).
\tag{3.2}\]
The affine combination \(\vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\) is the stimulus. Recall from Chapter 1 that it measures the similarity between the input and the template \(\vect{w}\), shifted by the bias \(b\). Below threshold, the neuron remains silent with an output of zero. Above threshold, it fires with an intensity proportional to the stimulus.



Evaluate one neuron’s stimulus and rectified response.
Evaluate the same neuron over the input plane.



# [1]
z = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 300)
response = torch.relu(z)
# [2]
axis = torch.linspace(-2.4, 2.4, 220)
x1, x2 = torch.meshgrid(axis, axis, indexing="xy")
w, b = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.65]), -0.25
surface = torch.relu(w[0] * x1 + w[1] * x2 + b)

The chapter's own straight rule, x₁ + x₂ = 0.5, is drawn across them; the corner it gets wrong wears a wine ring and the readout says 3 of 4.
        The line turns. The corner it gets wrong changes, and partway round two corners are wrong at once, so the readout falls to 2 of 4 and climbs back to 3. It never reads 4. The turn comes to rest with the line lying exactly along this neuron's own threshold, x₁ + 0.65x₂ = 0.25.
        That resting line is now the neuron's, and it turns orange. One side is OFF, where the neuron is silent, and it is shaded; the other is ON. A weight arrow grows out of the line, pointing straight across it.

        A hollow ghost drops out of that pinned corner to −0.25, the stimulus the rectifier threw away. Without the clip the four heights would be −0.25, 0.40, 0.75 and 1.40, and every one of them would lie on a single plane.
        A flat plane arrives horizontal — a rule that reads the activation alone — and gets 2 of 4. It tilts, keeping perfectly flat, bringing the two input coordinates back in. At 3 of 4 the (1,0) square passes below it; at 4 of 4 the (0,0) ring passes above it, and the tilt stops.
        Where that flat cut crosses the tilted sheet, a line is drawn in the air, and it falls to the input plane beneath it. A second piece of the boundary was already lying flat inside the OFF region.

In one dimension, a single neuron turns a straight line into a hinge. In two dimensions, it divides the plane into a flat zero-floor and a rising ramp separated by a crease. The neuron stays silent on the inactive half-space and fires on the active one, and \(\vect{w}\) stands perpendicular to the dividing boundary. That threshold boundary is the elementary building block of everything that follows.
At the corner \(z = 0\), the derivative is undefined, and any slope in the interval \([0, 1]\) is a valid subgradient. Frameworks settle the choice by convention, and PyTorch sets the derivative at zero to 0. The pre-activation \(z = \vect{w}^\top\vect{x} + b\), the input to the activation, is exactly zero more often than one might expect. A ReLU layer outputs many exact zeros, so a unit in the next layer can receive an all-zero input. With a zero-initialized bias, that unit’s pre-activation is then exactly \(z = 0\). Under this convention, such a unit passes no gradient back for that input. Chapter 5 analyzes the gradient through this derivative, and Exercise 3 inspects units that stay permanently silent.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
section: 3.3 Layers of hinges: bumps and polytopes
text:
3.3 Layers of hinges: bumps and polytopes
One neuron makes one boundary. A layer of \(k\) neurons makes \(k\) boundaries. Their intersections partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions (bounded ones are polytopes), and within each region the layer computes an affine function, a linear map plus a constant (Chapter 1). For fixed input dimension \(d\), the maximum region count of one generic hyperplane arrangement grows on the order of \(k^d\): polynomial in the width \(k\), and quadratic on a two-dimensional plane (Exercise 4 derives the exact count).
The simplest compact constructive example is one-dimensional. Combine three hinges so the slopes cancel again after the third breakpoint:



Combine three shifted hinges into a compact bump.



# [1]
xs = torch.linspace(-3, 5, 400)
h1 = torch.relu(xs + 1.5)
h2 = torch.relu(xs - 0.5)
h3 = torch.relu(xs - 2.5)
bump = h1 - 2 * h2 + h3










Figure 3.3: Three hinges make a compact triangular bump: the first starts the rise, the second reverses the slope, and the third cancels it back to zero.

The pale green shape standing from the first frame is the declared bump drawn ahead of its own construction — a target to aim at, not a second measurement — which is why it is the same green as the sum that aims at it; it stays while the control can still miss it, and only its dashed edge disappears, under the sum, when the sum lands. Play or a timeline seek returns c to the recorded sweep. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat’s state: the sum is complete, and the coefficient stands at +1 or at −2, never in between.
    
  


Before the first hinge, all units are silent and the output is zero. After the first breakpoint, \(h_1\) starts the climb. The coefficient \(-2\) on \(h_2\) reverses the slope at the peak, and \(h_3\) cancels that downward slope at the final breakpoint. Four linear pieces yield one compact bump.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
3.4 The universal approximation theorem
A layer of hinges can place many bumps, at any position and height. In one dimension, sums of these bumps give an intuitive route to approximating continuous functions. The universal approximation theorem extends the representational claim to higher dimensions: a network with a single hidden layer can, in principle, approximate any continuous function on a closed and bounded region to any desired accuracy. For ReLU and other continuous non-polynomial activations, this is the theorem of Leshno et al. (1993).
Fit one hidden layer at widths 2, 8, and 64:



Place 200 evenly spaced inputs on [-3, 3] and compute a sine-plus-quadratic target.
Define the reusable fit helper.
Implement the width sweep.



# [1]
xs1 = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)[:, None]
target = torch.sin(1.5 * xs1) + 0.08 * xs1 ** 2

# [2]
def fit(width: int, steps: int = 3000, lr: float = 0.05) -> torch.Tensor:
    torch.manual_seed(6050)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, width), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(width, 1))
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        ((net(xs1) - target) ** 2).mean().backward()
        opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return net(xs1).squeeze(-1)

plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
plt.plot(xs1, target, color="#232D4B", lw=2.5, label="target")
# [3]
for width, color in [(2, "#B8B8A8"), (8, "#5379AA"), (64, "#E57200")]:
    plt.plot(xs1, fit(width), color=color, lw=1.6, label=f"width {width}")
plt.xlabel("$x$"); plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 3.4: One hidden ReLU layer approximating a continuous curved target. Width 2 misses much of the curvature, width 8 follows the broad shape, and width 64 follows it closely. More width gives more hinge locations, but the theorem itself says nothing about where the optimizer places them.






The theorem guarantees less than is often assumed:






WarningTrap: universal approximation is not a training guarantee




It does not tell you how to find the weights. The theorem proves only that suitable weights exist. Finding them is the job of the loss and the optimizer, and nothing guarantees that gradient descent reaches such weights.
It does not say the network is small. Tiling a complicated function with one-layer bumps can require astronomically many units.
In its usual uniform-approximation form, it speaks of continuous functions on closed and bounded regions. It guarantees that an approximation exists over the whole region. It does not promise that fitting finitely many samples will find one, and it says nothing about inputs beyond the region. A step function that jumps from 0 to 1 at \(x = 0\) lies outside that class. A ReLU network computes a continuous function \(g\). If \(g\) stays on one side of \(\tfrac12\), it misses one side of the step by at least \(\tfrac12\). Otherwise \(g\) crosses \(\tfrac12\) somewhere. The step is 0 or 1 at that point, so the error there is \(\tfrac12\). The worst-case error therefore stays at least half the jump size. Under a mean-square (\(L_2\)) criterion, however, the network can squeeze the transition into a narrow interval, and the average error becomes arbitrarily small. Approximation and generalization are separate questions, and Chapter 6 takes up the second.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
3.5 Why depth: boundaries that bend
One hidden layer suffices in principle, yet depth matters for efficiency and for geometry. A second hidden layer receives the piecewise-linear outputs of the first, so in input space its boundaries are no longer single hyperplanes. They bend wherever the first layer’s boundaries cut the space: each layer folds the partition produced by the layer below it.
A ReLU network is affine inside each region of input space where the on/off pattern of its units is constant, and those regions are polyhedra whose walls are the units’ boundaries. Deeper layers add walls that kink wherever they cross earlier ones. Exercise 4 has you draw this tiling and count its cells.
One dimension already shows how this folding compounds. A single hidden layer of \(k\) ReLU units cuts a line into at most \(k+1\) linear pieces, so the pieces grow linearly with width. Now let two units fold the interval \([0,1]\) into a tent, \(t(x) = 2\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x) - 4\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x - \tfrac{1}{2})\), which rises and then falls. Composing the tent with itself \(L\) times (Telgarsky (2016)) gives a sawtooth with \(2^L\) linear pieces from only \(2L\) units, because each fold doubles the pieces of everything beneath it. A single hidden layer needs at least \(2^L - 1\) units to supply the required breakpoints.
The same holds beyond one dimension: for suitable ReLU constructions at fixed input dimension, achievable region counts grow exponentially with depth, while a single hidden layer’s count grows polynomially with width (Montúfar et al. (2014)). Gradient descent need not find such networks or use all their regions. The construction is an argument for the representational efficiency of depth: deep networks fold space recursively and represent partitions that a shallow network would need exponentially more units to match.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
3.6 Implementing a multilayer perceptron
We now build the model as a reusable class.






TipCoding hygiene: call the base-class initializer first



Every model you write from now on subclasses nn.Module, and the first line of your __init__ is always super().__init__(). The base-class initializer sets up parameter registration, .parameters(), and everything the optimizer and autograd need. Forget it and PyTorch raises an exception at once.





Register the hidden and output layers, then compose them in forward.



# [1]
class MLP(nn.Module):
    """A multilayer perceptron: linear layers with bends between them."""

    def __init__(self, input_dim: int, hidden_dim: int, output_dim: int):
        super().__init__()                      # the foundation
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim)
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, output_dim)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.out(torch.relu(self.hidden(x)))


The problem is two interleaved moons, the classic shape no line can separate well. The training loop is unchanged, and only the model is new:



Fix the seed, draw 200 noisy points on each of two interleaved moons, and reseed before fitting.
Fit a linear model and an MLP to the same moons.
Evaluate both decision rules on a dense grid.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
n = 200
t = torch.rand(n) * torch.pi
moon1 = torch.stack([torch.cos(t), torch.sin(t)], 1) + 0.12 * torch.randn(n, 2)
moon2 = torch.stack([1 - torch.cos(t), 0.4 - torch.sin(t)], 1)
moon2 = moon2 + 0.12 * torch.randn(n, 2)
X_m = torch.cat([moon1, moon2])
y_m = torch.cat([torch.zeros(n), torch.ones(n)])

torch.manual_seed(6050)
# [2]
lin_m = train(nn.Linear(2, 1), X_m, y_m, steps=3000, lr=0.8)
torch.manual_seed(6050)
mlp_m = train(MLP(2, 16, 1), X_m, y_m, steps=3000, lr=0.8)

gx3, gy3 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.6, 2.6, 240), np.linspace(-1.1, 1.6, 240))
grid3 = torch.tensor(np.stack([gx3.ravel(), gy3.ravel()], 1), dtype=torch.float32)

# [3]
moon_panels = []
for model in (lin_m, mlp_m):
    with torch.no_grad():
        accuracy_value = (
            (model(X_m).squeeze(-1) > 0).float() == y_m
        ).float().mean()
        boundary_values = (
            model(grid3).squeeze(-1) > 0
        ).float().reshape(gx3.shape)
    moon_panels.append((accuracy_value, boundary_values))










Figure 3.5: Two moons: with one line, the linear model classifies about 90% of the points correctly here, whereas the MLP’s boundary passes through the gap and separates the classes without error.





The MLP’s output layer is still linear. The network bends the boundary in input space by learning features on which a linear readout suffices: a space in which the boundary is straight. In the vocabulary of Chapter 2, the hidden layer forms a backbone \(\phi_\theta\), and the output layer is its classification head, the linear model \(\vect{w}^\top \phi_\theta(\vect{x}) + b\). Project the hidden activations onto the readout direction \(\hat{\vect{w}} = \vect{w}/\lVert\vect{w}\rVert\) (here the hat marks a unit vector), and the decision boundary sits at the single coordinate value \(-b/\lVert\vect{w}\rVert\). Figure 3.6 plots the moons in these learned coordinates.



Compute the hidden activations phi and their coordinate a1 along the unit readout direction.
Project the moons into learned readout and orthogonal coordinates.



# [1]
with torch.no_grad():
    phi = torch.relu(mlp_m.hidden(X_m))              # phi_theta(x): (400, 16)
    w = mlp_m.out.weight.squeeze(0)
    b = mlp_m.out.bias.item()
    w_hat = w / w.norm()
    a1 = phi @ w_hat                                 # readout coordinate
# [2]
    resid = phi - a1[:, None] * w_hat                # remove readout direction
    resid = resid - resid.mean(0)
    a2 = resid @ torch.linalg.svd(resid, full_matrices=False).Vh[0]
    boundary = -b / w.norm()                         # the line, exactly
    field = (torch.relu(mlp_m.hidden(grid3)) @ w_hat).reshape(gx3.shape)










Figure 3.6: The learned feature space, on the trained moons MLP from Figure 3.5. Left: the scalar feature \(\hat{\vect{w}}^\top\phi_\theta(\vect{x})\) over the input plane. The dashed contour is the decision boundary, kinked wherever hidden units switch on or off. Right: the same points with coordinates (readout direction, top orthogonal principal component of \(\phi_\theta\)): the classes separate, and the boundary is the exact vertical line \(\hat{\vect{w}}^\top\phi = -b/\lVert\vect{w}\rVert\). The network learns nonlinear features on which a linear readout suffices.

On XOR, two hidden units suffice in principle. The units \(\mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 - x_2)\) and \(\mathrm{ReLU}(x_2 - x_1)\) respond to \(x_1 > x_2\) and to \(x_2 > x_1\), and their sum \(\lvert x_1 - x_2\rvert\) is 1 on the two 1-points and 0 on the two 0-points. Trained from random starting weights, such a minimal network often fails. If one of its two units becomes silent on all four points, its output and its gradient are zero there, so it stops learning. The remaining unit and the readout then draw a single straight boundary, which cannot represent XOR. Across random seeds, two-unit networks often stall at 50% accuracy with silent units (Exercise 3). With more hidden units, the network keeps enough active units even if some fall silent. Extra units cost little and make training more reliable. Chapter 4 examines how stochastic gradients aid exploration, though noise alone does not guarantee escape.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
3.7 Representation without spatial structure
Consider image classification. A popular story is often told about the hidden layers of a deep network: the first layer detects edges, the next combines them into textures and parts, and the next assembles objects, forming a tidy hierarchy of increasingly abstract features.
A fully connected network on raw images does not impose that hierarchy. An MLP treats its input as one long, flat vector. In a dense weight matrix, neighboring pixels are no closer than pixels in opposite corners of the frame: every first-layer unit reads the whole frame, with a separate coefficient for each pixel. The network may still learn spatial regularities, but locality is not built in, and nothing in the architecture encourages a local-to-global hierarchy. Such a hierarchy is not a property of depth itself. Architectures that build locality in encourage it, and Part II builds one.
The MLP can represent nonlinear rules, but its architecture does not encode the spatial transformations that should preserve an image’s label. Chapter 6 tests that distinction.






NoteCheck yourself



Close the book for one minute and explain the hinge.

Why does stacking linear layers without an activation still produce one linear map?
What geometric object does one ReLU neuron introduce?
How can a nonlinear feature map make a curved input-space problem linearly separable?

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
section: 3.8 Okay, so: nonlinear features, linear readout
text:
3.8 Okay, so: nonlinear features, linear readout

Linear stacks collapse. Without a nonlinearity, any stack of linear layers is one linear layer (Equation 3.1), and no line separates the four XOR points.
A neuron is a thresholded similarity score. It is silent below its boundary and proportional to the score above it. One neuron yields one boundary, a layer forms a polyhedral partition, and three hinges make a compact bump.
Sums of bumps approximate functions. The universal approximation theorem promises only existence: it says nothing about how to learn the weights, how many units are needed, or how the network generalizes.
Depth folds boundaries. Suitable deep constructions create region counts that grow exponentially with depth, far beyond what comparable shallow constructions reach.
The MLP is a module. It subclasses nn.Module, calls the base-class initializer first, and separates what no line can.

title: 3  Nonlinearity and the MLP
text:
Sources and further reading

Cybenko, “Approximation by Superpositions of a Sigmoidal Function” (1989) gives a foundational uniform universal-approximation result on compact domains.
Hornik, “Approximation Capabilities of Multilayer Feedforward Networks” (1991) makes the distinction between uniform and \(L_p\) approximation explicit, addressing the jump-function nuance treated in this chapter.
Nair and Hinton, “Rectified Linear Units Improve Restricted Boltzmann Machines” (2010) is an early empirical account of rectifiers preserving useful signal through multiple layers.
Minsky and Papert, Perceptrons: An Introduction to Computational Geometry (MIT Press, 1969) is the rigorous analysis of single-layer perceptrons behind the historical callout.
Minsky, “Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence” (1961) describes the credit assignment problem that hidden units pose for learning.
Telgarsky, “Benefits of Depth in Neural Networks” (2016) gives the composed-tent construction whose \(2^L\) pieces a shallow network matches only with exponentially many units.
Montúfar et al., “On the Number of Linear Regions of Deep Neural Networks” (2014) develops the architecture-dependent region-count argument behind the chapter’s case for depth.
Lin, Tegmark, and Rolnick, “Why Does Deep and Cheap Learning Work So Well?” (2017) studies multiplication as a reusable compositional primitive and proves that there are settings in which flattening that computation requires exponentially more units.

text:
Exercises

(Pencil.) Generalize Equation 3.1: show by induction that any stack of \(L\) linear layers equals a single linear layer. Where does inserting \(\mathrm{ReLU}\) between layers break your proof?
(Pencil.) Using the hinge construction, give explicit weights and biases for a one-hidden-layer network that outputs exactly 1 on \([0,1]\) and 0 outside \([-0.2, 1.2]\), a trapezoid. How many hidden units did you need?
(Code.) Retrain the XOR network with 2 hidden units in place of 4 across ten different seeds. How often does it reach 100%? Inspect a failed run: what happened to its hidden units? (Hint: check how many are permanently silent.)
(Pencil.) For \(k\) lines in general position in two dimensions, derive the maximum region count \(1+k+\binom{k}{2}=\sum_{i=0}^{2}\binom{k}{i}\). (Code.) Record the activation signs of every hidden layer, and color the input plane by this complete on/off pattern for a random \(2 \to 8 \to 8 \to 1\) network initialized from a fixed seed. On successively finer grids, count the distinct activation patterns that appear (torch.unique(patterns, dim=0)). A complete fixed pattern defines a convex polyhedral region, so a pattern that seems to occupy several disconnected cells on a sampled grid should be checked as a discretization effect, for example by labeling connected components with scipy.ndimage.label at a finer resolution. Compare with a parameter-matched wide network, \(2 \to 26 \to 1\): both have 105 parameters. Report the grid resolution with each count, because a sampled count is only a lower bound on the true count.
(Code.) Replace the moons MLP’s ReLU with nn.Identity() and retrain. Explain the resulting boundary in one sentence using Equation 3.1.
(Pencil.) Let \(\sigma\) be smooth and choose an offset \(c\) with \(\sigma''(c)\ne0\). Use Taylor expansion to show that \[
m_\lambda(u,v)=
\frac{\sigma(c+\lambda(u+v))+\sigma(c-\lambda(u+v))
-\sigma(c+\lambda(u-v))-\sigma(c-\lambda(u-v))}
{4\sigma''(c)\lambda^2}
\longrightarrow uv
\] as \(\lambda\to0\). (Code.) Use the logistic sigmoid with \(c=1\), sweep \(\lambda\) over \([10^{-6}, 1]\) on a logarithmic grid, and plot \(|m_\lambda(u,v)-uv|\) in float64 at \(u=0.6\), \(v=0.4\). Explain both the approximation-error regime and the eventual roundoff regime, and estimate the \(\lambda\) where they balance. Optional extension: compose seven of these approximate products into a balanced tree for \(x_1x_2\cdots x_8\). How does depth change the error, and how would you choose \(\lambda\) at each level? Common misconception: “expand the logistic sigmoid at \(c=0\).” That is its inflection point, where \(\sigma''(0)=0\) and the proposed denominator vanishes.

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.1 Likelihood-derived loss functions
We now have models for practical tasks: linear regressors (Chapter 1), classifiers (Chapter 2), and multilayer perceptrons (Chapter 3). We have losses that score their predictions against truth, and we know the direction of improvement is the negative gradient. What remains is the central engineering challenge: how to run the descent when the dataset has a million examples, the model has millions of parameters, and the loss landscape is no longer a convex bowl.
Stochastic gradient descent is the basic optimization method, augmented by minibatching, momentum, and adaptive per-parameter scaling. These refinements turn a simple theoretical concept into the practical algorithm that trains every network in this book.
Before optimizing a loss, we recall why we choose the loss we do. In Chapter 1 we saw that assuming Gaussian noise on a linear process reduces maximum likelihood to least squares, and in Chapter 2 the same argument with a categorical distribution produced cross-entropy. Both follow one principle: a likelihood-derived loss is a noise model in disguise. Specifying the conditional distribution of targets around predictions determines how errors are penalized, and negative log-likelihood turns that model into the scalar objective that training minimizes.
With the loss fixed, training minimizes the average loss:
\[
\hat{\vect{w}} = \argmin_{\vect{w}} \; \loss(\vect{w})
= \argmin_{\vect{w}} \; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_i(\vect{w}),
\tag{4.1}\]
where \(\ell_i\) is the loss on example \(i\). The rest of this chapter addresses how to minimize this objective when \(n\) is massive: making rapid, reliable progress without evaluating every term at every step.
crumbs: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.2 The computational bottleneck
Gradient descent, as we left it in Chapter 1, updates with the full gradient:
\[
\vect{w}^{(t+1)} = \vect{w}^{(t)} - \eta \, \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \nabla \ell_i(\vect{w}^{(t)}).
\tag{4.2}\]
One step touches every example. Modern datasets have millions to billions of examples, models have millions to billions of parameters, and training needs thousands of steps. At this scale, computing an exact gradient at every step is too expensive.
crumbs: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.3 Stochastic gradient descent
We can estimate the gradient without evaluating every training example. Instead of the expensive sum over all \(n\) examples, average over a small random minibatch \(\mathcal{B}\), e.g., 32 examples against a million:
\[
\vect{w}^{(t+1)} = \vect{w}^{(t)} - \eta \, \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \nabla \ell_i(\vect{w}^{(t)}).
\tag{4.3}\]
Why does this work? At a fixed parameter vector, a uniformly sampled minibatch gradient is unbiased: the expected contribution of example \(i\) to a batch equals its contribution to the full average, so
\[
\E\bigl[\nabla \loss_{\mathcal{B}}(\vect{w})\bigr] = \nabla \loss(\vect{w}).
\tag{4.4}\]
Here the expectation is over the random draw of the minibatch from the fixed training set. The identity holds for independent draws with replacement and also for one uniformly chosen subset without replacement.1 In either case, the minibatch gradient equals the full-data gradient in expectation.
There is a second, physical reason to batch. The hardware that trains networks is built around batched general matrix multiplication (GEMM). A dense layer applied to \(B\) examples is one matrix product in which every weight, once read from memory, is reused for all \(B\) examples. Batching lets several examples share the cost of moving the weights. The resulting throughput depends on the shapes and the hardware, so it should be measured. Batch size therefore trades gradient noise against hardware efficiency, and we return to both sides below and in Section 4.6.1.
In practice the algorithm runs as follows:

Shuffle the training data.
Split it into minibatches of size \(B\).
For each batch: compute the average gradient, update the parameters.
One pass through all batches is an epoch. Repeat for multiple epochs.
crumbs: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.4 Gradient-dominated and noise-dominated behavior
On the noisy least-squares problem below, fixed-step SGD illustrates two regimes, a pattern often called semi-convergence: gradient-dominated progress early, then persistent variation near the solution. The mechanism is a shifting balance between signal and noise. At any parameter vector, split the minibatch gradient into the full gradient plus a noise vector \(\vect{\xi}_{\mathcal{B}}\) whose mean is zero by the unbiasedness in Equation 4.4:
\[
\nabla\loss_{\mathcal B}(\vect{w})
= \nabla\loss(\vect{w}) + \vect{\xi}_{\mathcal B},
\qquad
\E[\vect{\xi}_{\mathcal B}]=\vect{0}.
\]
On our convex least-squares bowl the two regimes are easy to see:

Far from the optimum, signal dominates. The full gradient is large relative to the batch noise, so most batch directions make useful progress, and their mean is the full descent direction.
Near the optimum, noise dominates. The full gradient shrinks toward zero (recall Figure 1.4), but individual batches still disagree because different examples pull in different directions. With a fixed learning rate the iterate keeps bouncing inside what we will call the region of confusion:




Generate one least-squares problem and solve for its empirical optimum.
Partition the examples into equal batches and define their gradients.
Compare batch descent directions far from and at the optimum.
Verify that their fixed-point mean equals the full descent direction, then plot both regimes.



import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
x1 = torch.randn(80)
y1 = 2.5 * x1 - 1.0 + 0.4 * torch.randn(80)
A = torch.stack([x1, torch.ones_like(x1)], dim=1)
optimum = torch.linalg.lstsq(A, y1).solution

# [2]
batch_size = 4
batches = torch.randperm(len(x1)).reshape(-1, batch_size)

def gradient_at(theta: torch.Tensor, idx=slice(None)) -> torch.Tensor:
    residual = A[idx] @ theta - y1[idx]
    return 2 * A[idx].T @ residual / len(residual)

def batch_descent_directions(theta: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return torch.stack([-gradient_at(theta, idx) for idx in batches])

# [3]
points = [torch.tensor([-0.5, 2.0]), optimum]
titles = ["far away: agreement in expectation",
          "at the optimum: batches disagree"]
arrow_lengths = [0.72, 0.46]

                   np.linspace(-4.0, 3.0, 100))

    full_direction = -gradient_at(theta)

        mean_unit = full_direction / full_direction.norm()

                    arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->", "lw": 3, "color": "#232D4B"})

                "mean direction $\\approx 0$", ha="center", color="#232D4B")

    ax.plot(*theta, marker="o", ms=5, color="#232D4B")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="$w$", xlim=(-1.5, 5.5), ylim=(-4, 3))

             label="batch directions")

             "region of confusion", ha="center", color="#722F37")

In some regimes the bouncing is an advantage. A noisy step may push the iterate away from a saddle point, where the loss rises in some directions and falls in others, or out of a narrow basin or a shallow trap that exact descent would follow more predictably. Minibatch noise can also bias training toward different solutions, and smaller batches sometimes improve generalization. None of these outcomes is guaranteed. The effect depends on the model and the data, and on training choices such as the initialization, the order of the batches, the learning rate, and the batch size. title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.5 The learning rate
The learning rate \(\eta\) is a hyperparameter, a setting we choose before training instead of learning it, and few hyperparameters matter more. It scales every step, and its failure modes are asymmetric: too small a learning rate can produce slow progress, while one that is too large overshoots the valley and diverges.



Define the reusable losses_for helper.
Open one figure for the three loss curves.
Implement the learning-rate triptych.
Add a legend naming each learning rate and show the figure.



# [1]
def losses_for(lr: float, steps: int = 60) -> list[float]:
    w, b, out = torch.tensor(-0.5), torch.tensor(2.0), []
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = (w * x1 + b) - y1
        out.append(float((err ** 2).mean()))
        w = w - lr * 2 * (err * x1).mean()
        b = b - lr * 2 * err.mean()
    return out

# [2]
plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
# [3]
for lr, style, color in [(0.005, "-", "#5379AA"), (0.12, "-", "#E57200"),
                         (1.1, "--", "#722F37")]:
    plt.semilogy(losses_for(lr), style, color=color, label=f"$\\eta = {lr}$")
plt.xlabel("step"); plt.ylabel("loss (log scale)")
# [4]
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 4.2: Same problem, same steps, three learning rates. The smallest makes slow progress, the largest makes the loss climb at every step, and the middle one converges quickly.












TipSelecting and scheduling the learning rate



For plain SGD on normalized toy problems like these, \(\eta = 0.1\) is a reasonable first try. That value is calibrated to the scale of these problems: Adam, unnormalized features, and deep models can need very different values. Read the training curves. If the loss decreases slowly, try a larger learning rate, and if it oscillates or explodes, try a smaller one.
A rule that changes the learning rate during training is a learning-rate schedule. The most common schedule is decay, which lowers the learning rate later in training so that the final steps are smaller. Warmup changes it in the other direction at the start: it begins with a small learning rate and gradually increases it. Recipes for training Transformers commonly begin with warmup and then decay.

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.6 The batch size
The batch size \(B\) sets the operating point on the noise–efficiency trade-off:








Batch size
Character
Trade-off




Small (1–32)
Noisy, exploratory
Sometimes a generalization benefit; slow and less hardware-efficient


Medium (32–256)
Balanced
The usual default; hardware-efficient


Large (256+)
Smooth, high throughput
Less gradient noise; often needs learning-rate and schedule retuning



With independent sampling, gradient standard deviation scales like \(1/\sqrt{B}\): quadrupling the batch roughly halves the jitter. For a uniform subset without replacement, multiply by \(\sqrt{(n-B)/(n-1)}\), which makes the noise exactly zero when \(B=n\). For \(B \ll n\) the correction is near one, which is why the simpler rule is useful. The batch size is a dial that links statistics and hardware, and its best setting depends on both.

What a batch may estimate, and what it may not
The unbiasedness of Equation 4.4 holds because the full loss is an average of per-example terms, and a batch average estimates an average without bias. Some quantities computed on a batch are not averages of per-example terms. Three cases cover the ones in this book, and a small example shows each.
Case 1: an average of per-example losses. The squared error and cross-entropy used so far average one term per example, \(\loss(\vect{w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell_i(\vect{w})\). A batch average of the \(\ell_i\) has the same expected value as the full average, and so does its gradient. Changing \(B\) then changes only the noise and the cost of each step, and the objective stays the same. This requires each example’s prediction to be independent of the other examples in its batch. BatchNorm in training mode (Chapter 10) breaks that condition, and so does a loss that averages over all the tokens in a batch of sequences with different lengths (Chapter 13).
Case 2: a nonlinear function of an average. Some quantities apply a nonlinear function \(R\) to an average, \(R(\E[s])\). Plugging in the batch mean \(\bar{s}_B\) gives \(R(\bar{s}_B)\), whose expected value is generally different from \(R(\E[s])\). Take \(R = \log\) and let \(s\) be 1 or 3 with equal probability, so \(\E[s] = 2\) and \(\log\E[s] = 0.693\). With \(B = 1\), the plug-in estimate \(\log s\) averages \((\log 1 + \log 3)/2 = 0.549\). With \(B = 2\), drawn with replacement, the batch mean is 1, 2, 2 or 3 with equal probability, and \(\log\bar{s}_2\) averages 0.621. The bias shrinks as \(B\) grows, but it remains at every finite batch size, and the average over many batches converges to the biased value (0.621 at \(B = 2\)). Jensen’s inequality gives the direction of the bias whenever \(R\) is convex or concave: the logarithm is concave, so the plug-in estimate is too low on average. The logarithm of a mean, the KL divergence between aggregate distributions, and correlation-style diagnostics belong to this case. For such a quantity, either estimate it in a way that avoids the bias or report the bias.
Case 3: an objective defined by the batch. In some losses the batch sets the task itself. A contrastive loss (Chapter 23) asks the model to pick each example’s true partner among the \(B\) candidates in its batch. A model that guesses uniformly has loss \(\log 64 = 4.16\) at \(B = 64\) and \(\log 256 = 5.55\) at \(B = 256\). The two batch sizes pose different problems, so neither loss estimates the other. Here \(B\) is part of the training protocol and should be reported with the other design choices.
A call to .mean() computes a number, and what that number means statistically depends on how the loss is built and how the batch is drawn. Changing \(B\) can change the sampling noise (Case 1), the bias of a plug-in estimate (Case 2), or the objective itself (Case 3). Before changing the batch size for speed, check which case applies. Appendix E connects these distinctions to population risk and statistical uncertainty.

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.7 Momentum and accumulated gradients
At a fixed batch size, plain SGD uses one scalar learning rate \(\eta\), and in narrow, curved valleys that is not enough: the iterate zigzags across the steep direction while inching along the shallow one. Momentum gives the update a memory. A running velocity accumulates gradients, and each step follows the velocity instead of the raw gradient:
\[
\vect{v}^{(t)} = \beta\,\vect{v}^{(t-1)} + \nabla \loss(\vect{w}^{(t)}), \qquad
\vect{w}^{(t+1)} = \vect{w}^{(t)} - \eta\,\vect{v}^{(t)},
\tag{4.5}\]
with \(\beta \in [0.9, 0.99]\). The comparison below uses \(\beta = 0.9\), a common choice. This is the ball rolling downhill. In directions where gradients keep agreeing, speed builds. In directions where they flip sign every step, they cancel. The zigzag is damped, and momentum can reduce the influence of short-lived changes in the gradient.
The ball analogy can be made precise. A ball of mass \(m\) moving through a viscous fluid with drag coefficient \(\gamma\) over the loss landscape obeys
\[
m\,\ddot{\vect{w}} = -\gamma\,\dot{\vect{w}} - \nabla\loss(\vect{w}):
\]
acceleration comes from the downhill force minus friction. Step it forward with time step \(\Delta t\) and write \(\Delta\vect{w}^{(t)} = \vect{w}^{(t+1)} - \vect{w}^{(t)}\) for the displacement:
\[
\Delta\vect{w}^{(t)} = \beta\,\Delta\vect{w}^{(t-1)} - \eta\,\nabla\loss(\vect{w}^{(t)}),
\qquad
\beta = 1 - \frac{\gamma\,\Delta t}{m},
\quad
\eta = \frac{\Delta t^{2}}{m}.
\]
This is Equation 4.5 with \(\Delta\vect{w}^{(t)} = -\eta\,\vect{v}^{(t)}\). So \(\beta\) is the fraction of velocity that survives one step of friction: \(\beta = 0\) is a ball in syrup, which is plain gradient descent, and \(\beta \to 1\) is a frictionless ball that never settles.
Unrolled, the velocity is a geometrically weighted sum of past gradients, \(\vect{v}^{(t)} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \beta^k\,\nabla\loss(\vect{w}^{(t-k)})\), which makes momentum a low-pass filter: it passes slow, steady changes and damps fast ones. Once many steps have accumulated, a gradient component that keeps its sign is multiplied by \(\sum_k \beta^k = 1/(1-\beta)\), a factor of 10 at \(\beta = 0.9\). A component that flips sign every step is multiplied by \(\sum_k (-\beta)^k = 1/(1+\beta)\), a factor of about \(0.53\). The steady downhill signal therefore grows relative to the zigzag across the valley and to the minibatch noise, which has no preferred sign from step to step.

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.8 Adam: adaptive per-parameter steps
Momentum uses the same learning rate for every parameter, yet the loss can be steep along some parameters and nearly flat along others. Adam (adaptive moment estimation, Kingma and Ba (2015)) combines three ideas.2 Momentum accumulates past gradients. Per-parameter step sizes scale each parameter’s step by the size of its own recent gradients. Bias correction removes the pull toward zero that comes from starting both accumulators at zero. Adam applies these elementwise updates:
\[
\vect{m}^{(t)} = \beta_1 \vect{m}^{(t-1)} + (1-\beta_1)\,\vect{g}^{(t)}, \quad
\vect{s}^{(t)} = \beta_2 \vect{s}^{(t-1)} + (1-\beta_2)\,\vect{g}^{(t)\,2}, \quad
\vect{w}^{(t+1)} = \vect{w}^{(t)} - \eta\,\frac{\hat{\vect{m}}^{(t)}}{\sqrt{\hat{\vect{s}}^{(t)}} + \epsilon},
\tag{4.6}\]
where \(\vect{g}^{(t)} = \nabla \loss_{\mathcal{B}}(\vect{w}^{(t)})\) is the minibatch gradient at step \(t\), and the bias-corrected accumulators are
\[
\hat{\vect{m}}^{(t)} = \frac{\vect{m}^{(t)}}{1 - \beta_1^t}, \qquad
\hat{\vect{s}}^{(t)} = \frac{\vect{s}^{(t)}}{1 - \beta_2^t}.
\]
To see the bias, unroll the first accumulator from \(\vect{m}^{(0)} = \vect{0}\): \(\vect{m}^{(t)} = (1-\beta_1)\sum_{k=1}^{t}\beta_1^{t-k}\,\vect{g}^{(k)}\). Suppose the gradients have a constant mean \(\E[\vect{g}]\). The averaging coefficients \((1-\beta_1)\beta_1^{t-k}\) sum to \(1-\beta_1^t\), so \(\E[\vect{m}^{(t)}] = (1-\beta_1^t)\,\E[\vect{g}]\). At the first step with \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\E[\vect{m}^{(1)}]\) is one tenth of the expected gradient. Dividing by \(1-\beta_1^t\) removes this factor, and the same argument applied to the squared gradients gives the correction for \(\vect{s}^{(t)}\). As \(t\) grows, \(\beta_1^t\) and \(\beta_2^t\) approach zero and the corrections fade.
The next experiment compares the three update rules on a least-squares problem with unequal feature scales, using declared learning rates and a shared update budget.

text:
4.9 Comparing optimizers under unequal feature scales
This comparison fixes the data, the starting point and the budget, draws the minibatches at random from one shared seed, and compares each optimizer’s full-batch loss with the loss of the least-squares solution. The second feature has ten times the scale of the first, which gives the loss very different curvature in the two parameter directions. We give all three optimizers the same 120-step, 16-example-batch budget, while using learning rates chosen for this toy: \(0.003\) for SGD and momentum, small enough for the steep direction, and \(0.1\) for Adam. This is a mechanism comparison: it shows how each rule responds to unequal curvature and supports no ranking of the optimizers at a shared learning rate.
The cell gets the comparison’s gradients from backward(), as in Chapter 1. Chapter 5 derives the backward computation.



Fix the seed, draw 256 inputs with feature scales 1 and 10, and form noisy targets from w_true.
Define the reusable race helper.
Implement the optimizer comparison.
Add a legend naming each optimizer and show the loss curves.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
n = 256
Xr = torch.randn(n, 2) * torch.tensor([1.0, 10.0])   # ill-conditioned by design
w_true = torch.tensor([3.0, 0.3])
yr = Xr @ w_true + 0.1 * torch.randn(n)

# [2]
def race(kind: str, steps: int = 120, B: int = 16) -> list[float]:
    torch.manual_seed(1)                             # same batches for everyone
    w = torch.zeros(2, requires_grad=True)
    opt = {"SGD":      torch.optim.SGD([w], lr=3e-3),
           "momentum": torch.optim.SGD([w], lr=3e-3, momentum=0.9),
           "Adam":     torch.optim.Adam([w], lr=0.1)}[kind]
    hist = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        idx = torch.randint(0, n, (B,))
        opt.zero_grad()
        ((Xr[idx] @ w - yr[idx]) ** 2).mean().backward()
        opt.step()
        hist.append(((Xr @ w.detach() - yr) ** 2).mean().item())
    return hist

plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))
# [3]
for kind, color in [("SGD", "#5379AA"), ("momentum", "#232D4B"),
                    ("Adam", "#E57200")]:
    plt.semilogy(race(kind), color=color, label=kind)
plt.xlabel("step"); plt.ylabel("full-batch loss (log scale)")
# [4]
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 4.3: Full-batch loss after each step of the optimizer comparison, on a logarithmic axis. The feature scales are 1 and 10, the step budget is equal, and the learning rates suit each optimizer (\(0.003\) for SGD/momentum, \(0.1\) for Adam). Plain SGD progresses slowly along the shallow direction, momentum damps the zigzag, and Adam’s per-parameter scaling largely neutralizes the difference in feature scales.






The trajectories isolate how each update rule responds to unequal curvature. Per-direction memory (momentum) and per-parameter scaling (Adam) reach a loss orders of magnitude below plain SGD’s within the same step budget. Normalizing the inputs removes much of this sensitivity to feature scale at the source (Exercise 5).

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.10 Regularization during training
Regularization is any change to training that aims to reduce overfitting, usually by preferring simpler or more stable solutions. Chapter 1 met one form, the ridge penalty. Weight decay, dropout, and early stopping regularize training in different ways. Weight decay modifies parameter updates, dropout randomly masks activations, and early stopping uses validation performance to determine training duration.

Weight decay
Under plain SGD, adding an \(L_2\) penalty \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\vect{w}\|_2^2\) to the loss gives
\[
\vect{w} \leftarrow
(1-\eta\lambda)\vect{w} - \eta\nabla\loss.
\]
Here \(\lambda\) sets the strength of the penalty, and the factor \(\tfrac12\) makes its gradient \(\lambda\vect{w}\). The penalty introduces a shrinkage term, connecting weight decay to the ridge regression of Chapter 1.
Many PyTorch optimizers expose a weight_decay argument, but its implementation matters. Under Adam, an \(L_2\) penalty contributes \(\lambda\vect{w}\) to the gradient. This contribution is processed through the moment estimates and the coordinate-wise scaling of Equation 4.6, so it does not produce the same uniform shrinkage. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter (2019)) applies \(\vect{w} \leftarrow (1-\eta\lambda)\vect{w}\) separately from the adaptive gradient update. Training recipes often exclude bias and normalization parameters from this decay.


Dropout
Dropout (Srivastava et al. (2014)) randomly sets activations to zero during training. Let \(h_i\) be one hidden activation, \(p\) its drop probability, and \(q=1-p\) the probability that it is retained. With inverted dropout, an independent mask \(r_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)\) gives
\[
\widetilde{h}_i = \frac{r_i}{q}h_i.
\tag{4.7}\]
A masked activation becomes zero, and a retained activation is multiplied by \(1/q\). This scaling preserves the conditional mean:
\[
\E[\widetilde{h}_i\mid h_i]
= \frac{\E[r_i]}{q}h_i
= h_i.
\tag{4.8}\]
At evaluation time, dropout is disabled and the activation remains \(h_i\), with no rescaling. PyTorch’s nn.Dropout(p) uses this convention: model.train() enables its masking, and model.eval() disables it. The mode therefore changes what the network computes.
Here is the mechanism written directly, followed by a small seeded check. The empirical training mean is close to the input, while evaluation is deterministic and leaves the input unchanged:



Define the reusable inverted_dropout helper.
Fix the seed and average 20,000 inverted_dropout draws of the four-entry h at p = 0.25.
Implement inverted dropout and verify its scale.



# [1]
def inverted_dropout(
    h: torch.Tensor, p: float, training: bool = True
) -> torch.Tensor:
    if not training:
        return h
    if not 0.0 <= p < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("p must satisfy 0 <= p < 1")
    q = 1.0 - p
    mask = (torch.rand_like(h) < q).to(h.dtype)
    return mask * h / q

# [2]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
h = torch.tensor([1.0, -2.0, 4.0, 0.5])
draws = torch.stack([inverted_dropout(h, p=0.25) for _ in range(20_000)])
mean_output = draws.mean(0)
# [3]
print("training mean:", [round(v, 4) for v in mean_output.tolist()])
print(f"max |mean - h|: {(mean_output - h).abs().max():.4f}")
print("evaluation:", inverted_dropout(h, p=0.25, training=False).tolist())

training mean: [1.0025, -2.0057, 4.0064, 0.5024]
max |mean - h|: 0.0064
evaluation: [1.0, -2.0, 4.0, 0.5]



Dropout also has an approximate ensemble interpretation (Srivastava et al. (2014)). An ensemble is a set of models whose predictions are averaged, which usually reduces variance. Each dropout mask keeps a subset of the units and so selects a smaller subnetwork. A layer of \(k\) units has \(2^k\) possible masks, and all of these subnetworks share one set of weights. Training with a fresh random mask at every step trains this whole family at once, and evaluation with the full network stands in for averaging their predictions. The stand-in is approximate. Preserving the conditional mean of each masked activation does not make the full network’s prediction equal to the average prediction of the subnetworks, because nonlinear transformations \(\sigma\) generally do not commute with expectation:
\[
\E[\sigma(\vect{z})]
\ne \sigma(\E[\vect{z}]).
\]


Early stopping
Monitor validation loss during training. Early stopping ends training when validation performance stops improving, even if training loss continues to decrease, and keeps the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. The widening gap between the two curves is the overfitting of Chapter 1: the model keeps fitting the training set while getting worse on fresh data. Early stopping is therefore model selection along one training run. Each checkpoint is a candidate model, and the validation set chooses among them, the role Chapter 1 gave it. Figure 4.4 illustrates this choice, and Chapter 7 treats model selection in general.






Figure 4.4: Early stopping as model selection along one training trajectory. In this schematic, validation loss eventually increases while training loss continues to decrease. The checkpoint at the validation minimum is retained.









NoteCheck yourself



Write one parameter update, then answer the following questions.

Under what sampling assumptions is a minibatch gradient unbiased, and why does it vary between batches?
What information from earlier gradients is used by momentum and Adam?
Why is an \(L_2\) penalty under Adam different from uniform weight decay, and what does AdamW change?
Why does inverted dropout need no rescaling at evaluation time, and how does leaving dropout active change validation predictions?

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
4.11 Okay, so: the training loop
The pieces above fit into one training loop:

Instantiate the parameters \(\vect{w}^{(0)}\): PyTorch layers initialize their weights automatically when they are created (Chapter 5 analyzes why that initial scale governs trainability).
For each epoch: shuffle, split into minibatches of size \(B\).
For each batch: training-mode forward pass (including dropout, if used) \(\rightarrow\) loss (your noise model in disguise) \(\rightarrow\) backward pass for the gradients \(\rightarrow\) optimizer step (\(\eta\), momentum or Adam, weight decay).
Switch to evaluation mode for validation. Watch the curve, schedule the learning rate, and stop early when it turns.

Here is that recipe as a tested function, Listing 4.1. Later chapters import it and show only their model builder and their budget:



Declare one reusable interface for the model factory, data, and training budget.
Seed before constructing the model and optimizer.
Reshuffle the examples and visit every minibatch each epoch.
Predict, measure cross-entropy, backpropagate, and update.
Return the trained model as the experiment artifact.


"""Listing 4.1 — the supervised training loop, importable.

Chapter 4 derives this loop and prints it; Chapters 6 and 9 import it and
print only their deltas (the model builder and the budget). The loop is the
book's canonical minibatch recipe: seed, build, then repeat
predict -> measure -> step over reshuffled minibatches.
"""
from collections.abc import Callable

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn


# [1]
def fit_supervised(
    model_fn: Callable[[], nn.Module],
    X: torch.Tensor,
    y: torch.Tensor,
    *,
    epochs: int,
    batch: int = 64,
    lr: float = 1e-3,
    seed: int = 6050,
) -> nn.Module:
    """Train a fresh model on (X, y) with cross-entropy and Adam.

    Seeding precedes construction, so a given (model_fn, seed) pair always
    starts from the same tensors; each epoch reshuffles example order.
    """
    # [2]
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = model_fn()
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    # [3]
    for _ in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(X))
        for i in range(0, len(X), batch):
            idx = perm[i : i + batch]
            # [4]
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model(X[idx]), y[idx])
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
    # [5]
    return model

Two reading notes. Seeding precedes construction, so one (model_fn, seed) pair always trains from the same starting tensors, which a paired comparison requires. And the loss line is Case 1 of Section 4.6.1: at fixed parameters, a uniformly sampled batch average has the unbiasedness of Equation 4.4. Along a reshuffled training run the parameters depend on earlier batches, so the identity holds at each fixed parameter vector and says nothing about the run as a whole. The minibatch size therefore remains a dial for compute and noise.
One step in that loop remains to be derived: the backward pass for the gradients. Computing millions of partial derivatives for about twice the arithmetic of one forward pass is the subject of Chapter 5.

Sources and further reading

Tieleman and Hinton, “Lecture 6.5 — RMSProp,” COURSERA: Neural Networks for Machine Learning (2012): the original public provenance for RMSProp’s running average of squared gradients.
Gilbert Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data, §VI.4–VI.5, is a classical numerical-linear-algebra treatment: gradient descent, condition numbers, and momentum on quadratic bowls (§VI.4), and stochastic gradient descent’s semi-convergence, unbiased-gradient assumption, and convergence in expectation (§VI.5, especially pp. 361–365).
Robbins and Monro, “A Stochastic Approximation Method” (1951) is the classical starting point for replacing exact quantities with noisy observations in an iterative procedure.
Sutskever et al., “On the Importance of Initialization and Momentum in Deep Learning” (2013) shows how initialization and momentum interact with curvature in deep-network training.
Kingma and Ba, “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization” (2015) gives the algorithm, bias corrections, and motivation for adaptive moment estimates.
Loshchilov and Hutter, “Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization” (2019) explains why coupled \(L_2\) regularization and weight decay separate under adaptive optimizers.
Srivastava et al., “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (2014) introduces dropout and its model-averaging motivation.

title: 4  Training: Loss and Stochastic Gradient Descent
text:
At a fixed \(\vect{w}\), a subset of size \(B\) drawn without replacement is unbiased, and its variance is the with-replacement variance times the finite-population correction \((n-B)/(n-1)\), which reaches zero at \(B=n\). Across an epoch, however, reshuffled batches create path dependence between iterates, and dedicated random-reshuffling theory handles that sequence.↩︎
The per-parameter denominator is RMSProp. Adam adds bias-corrected first moments and names RMSProp directly.↩︎

title: 5  Backpropagation
text:
5.1 One neuron, one chain
Recall the gradient-descent update of Chapter 1: new parameters come from old parameters by stepping against the gradient, \(\vect{w}^{(t+1)} = \vect{w}^{(t)} - \eta\,\nabla_{\vect{w}}\loss\). For linear regression we could write that gradient down by hand. A modern network has millions, sometimes billions, of parameters composed through many layers. We could estimate each partial derivative by perturbing one parameter at a time and rerunning the network, a method called finite differences, but that needs at least one extra forward pass per parameter: millions of passes for a single gradient. Chapter 3 named the underlying difficulty, the credit assignment problem. A hidden unit has no target of its own, so we must work out how much each hidden weight contributed to the output error.
Backpropagation solves this problem exactly. It computes all the partial derivatives in one backward sweep whose cost is a small constant multiple of the forward graph’s operations. It is the multivariable chain rule, organized for computational reuse. We will derive it as a recursion on loss derivatives, implement it from scratch on a batch, and analyze its arithmetic and memory costs.
Start with the smallest possible case: one neuron on one training example. The previous activation \(a^{(l-1)}\) is multiplied by a weight \(w\) and shifted by a bias \(b\), giving the pre-activation \(z = w\,a^{(l-1)} + b\). The activation function produces \(a^{(l)} = \sigma(z)\), written \(a\) below, and \(a\) feeds a loss \(\loss\).
To see how much \(\loss\) changes when \(w\) changes slightly, follow the chain: a change in \(w\) changes \(z\), the change in \(z\) changes \(a\), and the change in \(a\) changes \(\loss\). The chain rule multiplies these local derivatives:
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial w}
= \frac{\partial \loss}{\partial a}\cdot
  \frac{\partial a}{\partial z}\cdot
  \frac{\partial z}{\partial w} .
\tag{5.1}\]
Figure 5.1: Computation as a graph. The forward pass (top, blue) computes each value and keeps what the backward pass will reuse. The backward pass (bottom, dark red) starts from \(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \mathcal{L} = 1\) and multiplies one local derivative per edge, right to left. Each box on the lower lane is the derivative of the loss with respect to the node above it. The one at \(z\) is the \(\delta\) of the next section.
Two properties shown in Figure 5.1 generalize to any network, however deep:
