title: 5  Backpropagation
section: 5.2 Propagating loss derivatives: the four layer equations
text:
5.2 Propagating loss derivatives: the four layer equations
For a full layer of neurons, the number of chain-rule paths grows quickly. The remedy is to introduce one derivative vector per layer and propagate it backward. At the output, the loss is an explicit function of the network’s last values. For a weight ten layers deep, the dependence runs through every layer in between. Backpropagation carries the loss derivative from the output, where it is explicit, back to each layer that needs it.






NoteThe loss derivative at a layer



Define, for each layer \(l\), the loss derivative
\[
\delta^{(l)} \;:=\; \frac{\partial \loss}{\partial \vect{z}^{(l)}} ,
\]
the gradient of the loss with respect to that layer’s pre-activations. Entry \(j\) measures how much unit \(j\) is to blame for the loss: if \(z^{(l)}_j\) moved by a small \(\varepsilon\), the loss would move by about \(\delta^{(l)}_j\,\varepsilon\). To reduce the loss, \(z^{(l)}_j\) should move against the sign of \(\delta^{(l)}_j\). Automatic differentiation calls such a quantity an adjoint: the derivative of the final output with respect to an intermediate value, computed backward from the output.


For fully connected layers with elementwise activation functions, backpropagation takes the following four forms. Here \(\odot\) denotes the elementwise (Hadamard) product.
1. Start at the output layer \(L\), where the loss derivative is explicit:
\[
\delta^{(L)} = \frac{\partial \loss}{\partial \vect{a}^{(L)}} \odot \sigma'(\vect{z}^{(L)}) .
\tag{5.2}\]
For the half-squared-error convention \(\loss=\tfrac12\|\vect{a}^{(L)}-\vect{y}\|^2\), \(\partial \loss / \partial \vect{a}^{(L)}\) is the prediction error \(\vect{a}^{(L)} - \vect{y}\). Other conventions contribute a known scale: mean squared error, for example, contributes \(2/D_{\text{out}}\) for \(D_{\text{out}}\) scalar outputs. In every case the output error is then multiplied by the activation derivative.
2. Propagate one layer back:
\[
\delta^{(l)} = \Bigl( (\matr{W}^{(l+1)})^\top \delta^{(l+1)} \Bigr) \odot \sigma'(\vect{z}^{(l)}) .
\tag{5.3}\]
The loss derivative travels backward through the same weights the signal traveled forward through. Unit \(j\) of layer \(l\) fed every unit \(i\) of layer \(l+1\) through the weight \(W^{(l+1)}_{ij}\), so it collects \(\sum_i W^{(l+1)}_{ij}\,\delta^{(l+1)}_i\), which is entry \(j\) of \((\matr{W}^{(l+1)})^\top\delta^{(l+1)}\): hence the transpose. The activation derivative \(\sigma'(\vect{z}^{(l)})\) then scales it. This recursion runs from the last layer to the first.



Fix the seed, draw weights for layer sizes 3, 4, 4, 1 and one input, and start an empty cache.
Cache the forward pass, then apply equations 1 and 2 from the output back.



import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
sizes = [3, 4, 4, 1]
Ws = [torch.randn(sizes[i + 1], sizes[i]) for i in range(3)]

x = torch.randn(3)                       # forward pass, cached
zs, a = [], x
# [2]
for W in Ws[:-1]:                        # hidden layers: sigmoid
    zs.append(W @ a)
    a = torch.sigmoid(zs[-1])
zs.append(Ws[-1] @ a)                    # identity output, as in our 2-layer build

delta = [None] * 3                       # backward pass: eqs. 1 and 2
sp = lambda z: torch.sigmoid(z) * (1 - torch.sigmoid(z))
delta[2] = zs[2] - 1.0                               # eq. 1 (identity output, y = 1)
delta[1] = (Ws[2].T @ delta[2]) * sp(zs[1])          # eq. 2
delta[0] = (Ws[1].T @ delta[1]) * sp(zs[0])          # eq. 2 again










Figure 5.2: Equation 5.3 as two operations, run right to left on a 3–4–4–1 network (random weights, one example): multiply by \(\matr{W}^\top\), which sends each loss derivative back to every unit that fed it, then multiply elementwise by the activation derivative \(\sigma'(z) \le 0.25\) (gray). The numbers are the executed values. Blue is negative and dark red positive on one shared scale, so the fading toward the input shows the activation derivatives at work. The outlined row has the smallest activation derivative: a large pulled-back value leaves it as a small loss derivative.





3. Convert loss derivatives into weight gradients:
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial \matr{W}^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} \, (\vect{a}^{(l-1)})^\top .
\tag{5.4}\]
4. And into bias gradients:
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial \vect{b}^{(l)}} = \delta^{(l)} .
\tag{5.5}\]
Check the shapes in Equation 5.4. With \(D_{\text{out}}\) neurons in layer \(l\) and \(D_{\text{in}}\) in layer \(l-1\), \(\delta^{(l)}\) is \((D_{\text{out}} \times 1)\), and \((\vect{a}^{(l-1)})^\top\) is \((1 \times D_{\text{in}})\). Their outer product is a \(D_{\text{out}} \times D_{\text{in}}\) matrix, matching the dimensions of \(\matr{W}^{(l)}\), and entry \((i,j)\) is the loss derivative of neuron \(i\) times the activation of neuron \(j\) that fed it, \(\partial \loss/\partial W^{(l)}_{ij} = \delta^{(l)}_i\,a^{(l-1)}_j\). A weight’s gradient is derivative out times signal in, and the matrix form maps directly onto the parallel matrix multiplies that GPUs are built for.



Form the weight-gradient outer product.



# [1]
d2 = delta[1]                              # layer-2 sensitivity  (4,)
a1 = torch.sigmoid(zs[0])                  # layer-1 activations  (4,)
G = torch.outer(d2, a1)                    # eq. 3










Figure 5.3: Equation 5.4 with the loss derivatives and activations from the network of Figure 5.2: a \((4 \times 1)\) derivative column times a \((1 \times 4)\) activation row gives the whole \((4 \times 4)\) gradient at once. The outlined cells trace the largest entry, \(\delta_i\,a_j\). Every other cell is built the same way. Loss derivatives and gradients share the signed blue-to-dark-red scale. The activations, all positive, are green.

title: 5  Backpropagation
text:
5.3 Manual implementation and autograd verification
We implement the four equations on a two-layer network using basic tensor operations, with no autograd involved, and then run PyTorch’s autograd on the same network. If the derivation and tensor shapes are correct, the two sets of gradients agree to machine precision.



Load the chapter dependencies and establish reproducible state.



import torch

# [1]
_ = torch.manual_seed(6050)


The code makes one change of layout: it processes \(n\) examples at once, stored as rows as in Chapter 1. Stack the activations into \(\matr{A}^{(l-1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times D_{\text{in}}}\) and the loss derivatives into \(\matr{\Delta}^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times D_{\text{out}}}\), row \(r\) holding example \(r\)’s \(\delta^{(l)}\). The single-example outer product of Equation 5.4 then becomes one matrix product that sums the per-example outer products,
\[
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial \matr{W}^{(l)}}
= (\matr{\Delta}^{(l)})^\top \matr{A}^{(l-1)}
= \sum_{r=1}^{n} \delta^{(l)}_r \,(\vect{a}^{(l-1)}_r)^\top ,
\]
and Equation 5.3, transposed row by row, becomes \(\matr{\Delta}^{(l)} = \bigl(\matr{\Delta}^{(l+1)}\matr{W}^{(l+1)}\bigr) \odot \sigma'(\matr{Z}^{(l)})\), with the pre-activations stacked into \(\matr{Z}^{(l)}\) in the same way. The mean’s \(1/n\) already sits inside \(\matr{\Delta}^{(2)}\), so the sum is the batch average.



Draw a batch of 32 inputs and targets and the two-layer weights.
Cache the forward pass, propagate the loss derivatives backward, and form the gradients.
Rebuild the network from requires_grad copies and let autograd differentiate it.
Print the largest gap between each hand-computed gradient and autograd’s.



# [1]
n, d, h = 32, 5, 8                            # batch, input dim, hidden dim
X = torch.randn(n, d)
y = torch.randn(n)

W1, b1 = torch.randn(h, d) * 0.3, torch.zeros(h)
W2, b2 = torch.randn(1, h) * 0.3, torch.zeros(1)

# [2]
# forward pass -- cache everything the backward pass will need
Z1 = X @ W1.T + b1                            # (n, h)
A1 = torch.sigmoid(Z1)                        # (n, h)
Z2 = A1 @ W2.T + b2                           # (n, 1)
L = ((Z2.squeeze() - y) ** 2).mean()

# backward pass -- the four equations (batch-averaged)
sig_prime = A1 * (1 - A1)                     # sigma'(z) = sigma(z)(1 - sigma(z))
delta2 = 2 * (Z2.squeeze() - y)[:, None] / n  # eq. 1 (identity output: no gate)
delta1 = (delta2 @ W2) * sig_prime            # eq. 2: back through W^T, then gated
grads = {                                     # eqs. 3 & 4: sensitivity out x signal in
    "W2": delta2.T @ A1, "b2": delta2.sum(0),
    "W1": delta1.T @ X,  "b1": delta1.sum(0),
}

# [3]
# same network, autograd's turn
params = {k: v.clone().requires_grad_(True) for k, v in
          {"W1": W1, "b1": b1, "W2": W2, "b2": b2}.items()}
A1_ = torch.sigmoid(X @ params["W1"].T + params["b1"])
L_ = (((A1_ @ params["W2"].T + params["b2"]).squeeze() - y) ** 2).mean()
L_.backward()

# [4]
for k in grads:
    gap = (grads[k] - params[k].grad).abs().max()
    print(f"{k}: max |ours - autograd| = {gap:.2e}")

W2: max |ours - autograd| = 0.00e+00
b2: max |ours - autograd| = 0.00e+00
W1: max |ours - autograd| = 3.73e-09
b1: max |ours - autograd| = 1.86e-09



The largest discrepancy is \(3.73\times10^{-9}\), consistent with float32 rounding. The four equations are what autograd computes: the framework builds the computation graph during the forward pass and then traverses it backward, caching and reusing intermediate results as we did.
The code also shows where the backward cost comes from. The forward pass computed the output layer with one matrix product, \(\matr{A}^{(1)}(\matr{W}^{(2)})^\top\). The backward pass needed two matrix products for it, one for each input of that product: \(\matr{\Delta}^{(2)}\matr{W}^{(2)}\) carries the loss derivative to the layer’s input, and \((\matr{\Delta}^{(2)})^\top\matr{A}^{(1)}\) forms the weight gradient. For an \(n\times k\) input and an \(m\times k\) weight, each of the three products costs \(2nmk\) floating-point operations, so a matrix-multiply layer’s backward pass costs about twice its forward pass and a training step about three forward passes. That is the small constant multiple stated at the start of the chapter. (The first layer needs no input gradient, because nothing upstream of the input \(\matr{X}\) is trained, and our code never forms one.)
Caching also costs memory. The backward pass read the hidden activations \(\matr{A}^{(1)}\) twice, once for the activation derivative \(\sigma'(\matr{Z}^{(1)})\) and once for the gradient of \(\matr{W}^{(2)}\). It also read the input \(\matr{X}\) for the gradient of \(\matr{W}^{(1)}\). Both therefore had to stay in memory after the forward pass. Here \(\matr{A}^{(1)}\) alone holds \(32 \times 8 = 256\) numbers, more than all \(57\) parameters of the network, and it grows with the batch size while the parameter count does not. A deep network keeps about one such block per layer until the backward pass has used it. This is why training a network takes more memory than running it, and why evaluation code runs under torch.no_grad(), where no graph is recorded and nothing is kept for a backward pass. Recomputing some activations during the backward pass instead of storing them, gradient checkpointing, trades extra arithmetic for memory (Chen et al., 2016).

title: 5  Backpropagation
section: 5.4 Order and accumulation: how autograd traverses graphs
text:
5.4 Order and accumulation: how autograd traverses graphs
The four layerwise equations derived above assume a sequential network, where each layer feeds a single successor. Real computational workflows form directed acyclic graphs (DAGs): a single intermediate value may branch into multiple downstream operations. Extending reverse-mode differentiation to arbitrary DAGs requires two rules:

Reverse topological ordering. A topological order lists the nodes so that each comes after every node it depends on. The backward sweep visits them in the reverse of that order, so every downstream consumer of an intermediate tensor has finished propagating its derivative before that tensor sends its own gradient upstream.
Gradient accumulation. When an intermediate variable branches into multiple operations, the multivariable chain rule makes its total derivative the sum of the derivatives along each path. Autograd engines therefore add each new contribution to the stored adjoint.

A small engine shows both rules. Each Value node records its parents and a local derivative rule; its grad field holds its adjoint \(\partial \loss/\partial v\), and the rule passes that adjoint on to the parents.
This teaching implementation is adapted from Andrej Karpathy’s micrograd, released under the MIT License. We use only the scalar reverse-mode pattern, as a readable model of these two rules; the upstream copyright and license notice are preserved in the repository’s third-party notices.



Implement scalar reverse-mode autodiff with a topological backward traversal.



# [1]
class Value:
    """A scalar that remembers its history -- a node in the computation graph."""

    def __init__(self, data: float, parents=(), backward_rule=lambda: None):
        self.data = data
        self.grad = 0.0
        self._parents = parents
        self._backward_rule = backward_rule

    def __add__(self, other: "Value | float") -> "Value":
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data + other.data, (self, other))
        def rule():                      # d(out)/d(self) = d(out)/d(other) = 1
            self.grad += out.grad
            other.grad += out.grad
        out._backward_rule = rule
        return out

    def __mul__(self, other: "Value | float") -> "Value":
        other = other if isinstance(other, Value) else Value(other)
        out = Value(self.data * other.data, (self, other))
        def rule():                      # product rule, one side at a time
            self.grad += other.data * out.grad
            other.grad += self.data * out.grad
        out._backward_rule = rule
        return out

    def sigmoid(self) -> "Value":
        s = 1 / (1 + 2.718281828459045 ** (-self.data))
        out = Value(s, (self,))
        def rule():                      # sigma' = s (1 - s), the gate
            self.grad += s * (1 - s) * out.grad
        out._backward_rule = rule
        return out

    def backward(self) -> None:
        order, seen = [], set()
        def topo(v):                     # creators land in order first
            if v not in seen:
                seen.add(v)
                for p in v._parents:
                    topo(p)
                order.append(v)
        topo(self)
        self.grad = 1.0                  # dL/dL = 1: seed the output adjoint
        for v in reversed(order):
            v._backward_rule()





Build one sigmoid neuron from Value nodes and its squared error against the target 0.3.
Call loss.backward() to fill every node’s grad.
Print the engine’s dL/dw beside the same derivative from the hand formula.



# [1]
w, x, b = Value(0.7), Value(2.0), Value(-0.5)
a = ((w * x) + b).sigmoid()             # one neuron, forward
loss = (a + (-0.3)) * (a + (-0.3))      # squared error vs target 0.3
# [2]
loss.backward()

# analytic check: dL/dw = 2(a - y) * sigma'(z) * x
z = 0.7 * 2.0 - 0.5
s = 1 / (1 + 2.718281828459045 ** (-z))
# [3]
print(f"micro-autograd: dL/dw = {w.grad:.6f}")
print(f"by hand:        dL/dw = {2 * (s - 0.3) * s * (1 - s) * 2.0:.6f}")

micro-autograd: dL/dw = 0.337801
by hand:        dL/dw = 0.337801



The check exercised both rules. The loss writes a twice, in both factors of (a + (-0.3)) * (a + (-0.3)), so a.grad is the sum of two contributions, and the sort guarantees that both arrive before a’s own rule passes the total on toward w. PyTorch’s autograd keeps the same two rules and changes the unit of work: its nodes hold tensors, and each local rule is a vector–Jacobian product, which maps the adjoint of an output to the adjoints of the inputs without ever forming a Jacobian. For the layer product \(\matr{Z} = \matr{A}\matr{W}^\top\), the rule is the pair from the batched code, \(\bar{\matr{A}} = \bar{\matr{Z}}\matr{W}\) and \(\bar{\matr{W}} = \bar{\matr{Z}}^\top\matr{A}\), where a bar marks an adjoint. The scalar engine models the bookkeeping, not the speed.



  
  Watch the mechanism: one value, two branches, one counter
  
    The chapter's squared error writes a twice, so its gradient comes back along two edges. Does the counter on a end up holding one arrival or the sum of both?
    The backward pass of the chapter's own autograd check, drawn from the branch down: one activation feeding two copies of the same subtraction, and the running total the engine keeps with +=.

      \( \loss = \class{bb-product}{u\,v}, \qquad u = v = \predictionpart{a} - \targetpart{0.3} \)\( \residualpart{\dfrac{\partial \loss}{\partial \predictionpart{a}}} = \class{bb-first}{\dfrac{\partial \loss}{\partial u}\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial \predictionpart{a}}} \class{bb-plus}{+} \class{bb-second}{\dfrac{\partial \loss}{\partial v}\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial \predictionpart{a}}} \)
      Two uses, two arrivals, one sum. That is where the factor of two comes from.

    The calculation is readable without playback. Opening this panel loads the optional controls.
    
      This is the backward pass of one already-written expression: nothing here is trained, no weight is updated, and the forward values are the chapter's own.
      Scope and caveats
        The picture starts below the neuron. The chapter's forward pass runs w, x and b through a sigmoid to reach a; that single chain is the one-chain excerpt, which names branch accumulation as the thing it leaves out. This panel picks the derivative up at a and puts the trunk back in only at the end, as one grey factor, so that the arithmetic lands on the gradient the chapter prints.
        The two subtraction nodes are drawn apart because the chapter's line evaluates (a + (-0.3)) twice and the engine therefore builds two nodes, each recording a as a parent. Written once and multiplied by itself, it would be a single node with the same parent recorded twice, and the accumulation would be identical: the product rule adds one contribution per recorded use, not one per line of source.
        The hollow bar under the meter is a counterfactual, not a second model: it marks where the counter would stop if the rules assigned with = instead of accumulating with +=, and the struck number beside it is what the chapter would then have printed. Every value shown is recomputed from the declared inputs with the chapter's own value of e, at four decimal places; the loss value itself is never drawn, because only its seed of one enters the backward pass. Green is the activation the chapter computes, purple the target it is compared against, wine the gradient travelling back, orange the learnable weight, grey the scenery and the trunk.
      
    
    Check yourself. Change one digit so the second subtraction takes 0.1 away instead of 0.3 — the same activation, two different targets. What does the counter on a read now, and is it still twice one branch?
      1.0219, and no. The product rule sends each branch the other branch's value, so the upper edge carries 0.6109 and the lower carries 0.4109, and the counter holds their sum. Doubling was never the rule; it was what equal branches happened to give. The trunk then prints 0.4200 instead of 0.3378.
    
    Transcript and keyboard help
      
        Predict. The activation a holds 0.7109. Two nodes below it each compute a minus the target 0.3, and both give 0.4109; one product node multiplies them. The counter on a is empty. The gradient is about to come back along two edges: will the counter hold one arrival or both?
        Seed the loss. The backward pass sets the loss's own gradient to 1, the line the chapter comments as seeding the output adjoint. The product rule is about to send each branch the other branch's value.
        The first branch arrives. A packet of 0.4109 leaves the product along the upper edge, passes through the upper subtraction unchanged, and is added into the counter on a, which reads 0.4109.
        Hold. The second packet is still waiting at the product node, carrying the same 0.4109. The counter still reads one arrival. Predict what it will read once the second lands.
        The second branch arrives. The packet travels the lower edge and is added into the same counter, which now reads 0.8219 — the sum, not the last value. This is the plus in the engine's plus-equals.
        What assignment would have cost. A hollow bar grows back out to 0.4109: the reading the counter would have kept if the rules had written a plain equals. The meter itself does not move; the real total stands.
        Down the trunk. The accumulated 0.8219 is multiplied by the sigmoid's own slope 0.2055 and by the input 2, and lands on 0.3378 — the gradient the chapter prints as 0.337801.
        Compare. Beside it, struck through, is 0.1689: what the same trunk would have produced from a single arrival. Two uses, two arrivals, one sum, and the factor of two in the derivative of a square.

title: 5  Backpropagation
section: 5.5 PyTorch autograd in practice: five rules
text:
5.5 PyTorch autograd in practice: five rules
Autograd uses the same reverse pass we built manually, and that pass explains its practical rules. The five rules below cover the common autograd errors, and Figure 5.4 draws four of them in PyTorch syntax.






Figure 5.4: Four autograd rules in PyTorch syntax. (a) After the backward pass, the leaf w holds its gradient, and the non-leaf y_hat used its gradient and released it. (b) A second backward pass adds into w.grad until optimizer.zero_grad() resets it. (c) Of four ways to write an update, only the in-place one with recording paused keeps w a trainable leaf. (d) A loss stored from a forward pass that is never backpropagated keeps its graph and cached activations alive. loss.item() and loss.detach() keep only the value.



Rule 1: by default, only leaf tensors retain gradients. A leaf is a tensor you created directly (your parameters). A non-leaf is the result of an operation (activations, losses). For a leaf that requires gradients and contributes to the loss, the backward pass accumulates its gradient in the attribute .grad, while intermediate gradients are used and released. Call .retain_grad() on a non-leaf before the backward pass only when you explicitly need its gradient for inspection.
Rule 2: gradients accumulate. Each backward pass adds into the gradient attribute. Zero the gradients before each step (optimizer.zero_grad()), or every update uses the sum of all past gradients.



Create a leaf parameter w and a non-leaf output y_hat computed from it.
Backpropagate twice without clearing the leaf gradient.
Print the leaf and non-leaf gradients, then call backward() on a rebuilt sum and reprint w.grad.



# [1]
w = torch.randn(3, requires_grad=True)      # leaf: our parameter
y_hat = (w * 2).sum()                       # non-leaf: result of an operation

# [2]
y_hat.backward()
# [3]
print(f"leaf grad:      {w.grad.tolist()}")            # populated
print(f"non-leaf grad:  {y_hat.grad}")                 # None -- rule 1

(w * 2).sum().backward()                    # backward again, WITHOUT zeroing
print(f"after 2nd pass: {w.grad.tolist()}")            # doubled -- rule 2

leaf grad:      [2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
non-leaf grad:  None
after 2nd pass: [4.0, 4.0, 4.0]



Rule 3: update parameters in place, with recording paused. Write the update as w -= lr * w.grad inside with torch.no_grad():. Both parts of this idiom matter: the in-place subtraction and the paused recording. Pausing the recording keeps the step itself off the graph. The in-place subtraction changes the values of the existing leaf, so w remains the same trainable tensor that the optimizer and the next backward pass refer to. Drop either part and the update breaks (Figure 5.4, panel c). The rebinding w = w - lr * w.grad creates a new non-leaf whose gradient is not populated on the next pass. An in-place update with recording on raises an error. A rebinding with recording paused yields a tensor that no longer requires gradients, so learning silently stops. Assigning a plain tensor to a registered module parameter fails loudly instead. The idiom:



Save the leaf parameter and choose a learning rate.
Pause graph recording and update the parameter in place.
Verify that the update changed the value without changing leaf status.



# [1]
before = w.detach().clone()
lr = 0.1

# [2]
with torch.no_grad():
    w -= lr * w.grad

# [3]
assert not torch.equal(w, before)
assert w.is_leaf


Rule 4: in-place operations can corrupt the backward pass. Methods ending in _ (add_, relu_) overwrite values that the backward pass may still need from the forward cache. After the required backward pass, parameter updates can use them with recording paused. Anywhere else, prefer creating a new tensor.
Rule 5: stored tensors can retain computation graphs. Every forward pass builds a fresh graph, and the backward pass frees the activations that graph cached. A tensor that is kept, such as the loss appended to a list for plotting, still holds a reference to the graph that produced it, and one kept from a forward pass that is never backpropagated (an evaluation loop that leaves recording on, for example) holds every cached activation as well. Store loss.item() (a plain float) or loss.detach() instead: the detached tensor has the same value and no reference to the graph.






WarningKeep updates outside the graph



The manual-update pattern used here is in place and unrecorded: w -= lr * w.grad inside with torch.no_grad():, then clear the leaf’s gradient (Rule 2) before the next backward pass. Rules 1 and 3 combine into a common raw-tensor bug: the rebinding w = w - lr * w.grad creates a new non-leaf, and its .grad comes back None on the next pass.

title: 5  Backpropagation
text:
5.6 Activation derivatives and depth
In Equation 5.3, the transposed weight matrix combines loss derivatives from the next layer, and the activation derivative scales each resulting component. A derivative near zero attenuates that component, and a derivative equal to one leaves it unchanged.
For the logistic sigmoid,
\[
\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) \leq \frac14 .
\]
The maximum occurs at \(z=0\). As the activation saturates toward either endpoint, its derivative approaches zero.



Evaluate the sigmoid and ReLU derivative gates.



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# [1]
z = torch.linspace(-6, 6, 300)
sig = torch.sigmoid(z)
sigmoid_gate = sig * (1 - sig)
relu_gate = (z > 0).float()










Figure 5.5: Activation derivatives on a common vertical scale. The sigmoid derivative never exceeds \(0.25\) and approaches zero under saturation. The ReLU derivative is zero for negative inputs and one for positive inputs.








  Watch the mechanism: active forward, quiet backward
  
    Can a neuron have a large output and still pass almost no backward sensitivity?
    Watch one activation component in both directions. Its face is its own activation curve: the operating point rides that curve, and the tangent drawn there is the multiplier a backward unit probe meets. The timeline moves z; you can drag it too.

        \( \sigma'(z)\leq\class{dg-quarter}{\tfrac14},\quad \operatorname{ReLU}'(z)=\class{dg-open}{1}\ (z>0) \)
        \( \prod_{j=1}^{k}\sigma'(z_j)\leq\class{dg-quarter}{(\tfrac14)^k} \)
      
      Ten best-case sigmoid gates: below one millionth, yet not zero. Weights and branching, omitted here, also scale the full gradient.
      
  
    
    
    
    Play

    The calculation is readable without playback. Opening this panel loads the optional controls.
    
      The unit probe measures a local sensitivity, not an observed loss gradient.
      Scope and caveats
        Filled area is proportional to that sensitivity; the hollow ring only locates a signal that may be too small to see. The component's face shows its activation function on that function's own vertical scale (sigmoid from 0 to 1, ReLU from 0 to 6), so a tangent's tilt compares slopes within one face, not across the two; the printed multiplier is the number. The z slider covers the chapter's plotted domain, from −6 to 6: every value at a dragged z is computed from the chapter's formulas, not printed in it. The ten-component path isolates best-case sigmoid derivative factors, not ten simulated forward activations. Its ruler is a logarithmic scale, a drawing device: multiplying by one quarter is one equal step of log10(¼), and the active-ReLU mark stays at 1 because each active factor is one. Weight matrices and branching are omitted from this ceiling, not assumed harmless: they also affect the complete backward recursion. Active ReLU contributes one locally; negative inputs contribute zero. At its nondifferentiable zero, PyTorch chooses zero for backpropagation, a convention and not a slope, so no tangent is drawn there. Nothing is trained or updated.
      
    
    Check yourself. At z = −6 the sigmoid's output is about 0.0025: a quiet neuron. What is its backward factor?
      About 0.0025 again: the sigmoid's slope at −6 equals its slope at +6, 0.002467. The slope is what matters, and the S is flat at both ends. Sensitivity peaks at z = 0, where the factor is exactly ¼.
    
    Transcript and keyboard help
      
        The picture is an activation component inside a network: the weighted sum supplies pre-activation z; the component emits a for the next layer. The component's face is its own activation curve between two dotted rails, the output's floor and ceiling, with no grid. At z=0 the operating point sits mid-curve and the sigmoid emits one half.
        Keep that forward value cached. A tangent appears at the operating point, tied by a dashed link to the multiplier on the backward lane, which reads "times slope". A normalized unit sensitivity then travels from the output side toward the input side. This probe isolates the activation derivative; it does not cross an uncomputed weight matrix. The slope stays withheld until the probe meets the multiplier.
        At the component the filled signal area becomes one quarter of its incoming area. The derivative at zero is exactly one quarter even though the manuscript's even-sized 300-point plotting grid does not sample zero. Then z rises toward six: the point rides up the curve, the output grows, the tangent tilts flat, and the multiplier returns to a question mark.
        At z=6 the sigmoid output is approximately 0.9975 and the tangent is nearly flat. Predict the backward multiplier before watching the probe return.
        The same unit probe is now multiplied by approximately 0.002467. The large forward output stays visible. A large activation does not imply a large local derivative: activity and sensitivity are different quantities. Dragging z to minus six shows the other side: output near zero and the same tiny slope, quiet forward and quiet backward.
        Substitute ReLU at the same positive input. Its face is a line with an explicit vertex at zero; its output is six and its slope is one, so the unit backward probe passes unchanged. For a negative input the slope is zero and nothing is delivered. At the kink no tangent is drawn: PyTorch's zero there is a convention, not a classical derivative. This is not a guarantee about surrounding weights.
        Return to the sigmoid witness and isolate only the sigmoid factors along a longer backward path. The numbered components count factors in reverse traversal order, not measured network layers. Each is given its largest possible multiplier, one quarter; the weight-matrix contributions are outside this calculation. Under the path a logarithmic ruler runs from 1 on the right past ten to the minus six on the left. Each crossing moves its marker one equal step left, because multiplying by a constant is an equal step on a log scale. A second mark, the active-ReLU path, stays at 1.
        Ten such factors give at most 1/1,048,576, approximately 9.54 times ten to the minus seven: ten equal steps, ending just past the ten-to-the-minus-six tick. The filled signal is still positive even when it becomes subpixel; its outline is only a location cue. This ceiling is not a bound on the complete gradient. The manuscript's separate experiment measures actual networks.
      
      Silent; paused initially; 1.5× playback. Focus the animation pane: Space or K plays/pauses, arrows seek between beats, Home/End jump, Escape pauses. The scrubber and speed menu also work by keyboard. The z slider is the one parameter control: the timeline moves it, and dragging it pauses playback and recomputes the whole picture from your z; its arrow keys change z by 0.1 and never seek the timeline. Play, a scrub or a beat key returns z to the timeline. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat's state instead of moving between them.
    
  



Products of these derivatives cause one of the central failure modes of deep networks. The chain rule multiplies the local Jacobians, the matrices of partial derivatives of each layer’s outputs with respect to its inputs. Along a sigmoid path, each activation derivative contributes a factor of at most \(0.25\), so the product of \(k\) such factors is at most \(0.25^k\). After ten factors the bound is below one in a million. The weight matrices and branching paths also scale the full Jacobian, so this bound covers the activation-derivative product alone. It still shows why repeated sigmoid derivatives strongly favor vanishing signals.
Now replace the sigmoid with ReLU. \(\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\) has derivative \(1\) for \(z > 0\) and \(0\) for \(z < 0\). At the kink \(z=0\), PyTorch uses derivative \(0\), and exact zeros can occur with zero biases or sparse activations. The derivative is therefore either one or zero. At an active unit the loss derivative passes through this factor unchanged. The surrounding weight matrices can still amplify or attenuate it, which is where the weight scale comes in.
We test the argument in two networks that differ only in the activation function. Both have 30 layers, one with sigmoid units and one with ReLU. Both get the same weights and input batch, every weight drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0,\, 2/D_{\text{in}})\) with \(D_{\text{in}} = 64\), a scale the next section explains. We record how much gradient reaches each layer. We compute the diagnostic in float64 so the norm itself does not underflow; then we ask the practical float32 question: would a learning-rate-\(0.1\) update actually change the first layer’s stored weights?



Define the reusable gradient_diagnostic helper.
Start an empty diagnostics dictionary and open the figure.
Implement the depth experiment.
Show the plot, then print each network’s first-layer max gradient and its nonzero and changed counts.



from torch import nn

# [1]
def gradient_diagnostic(
    activation: type[nn.Module], depth: int = 30, width: int = 64
) -> dict[str, object]:
    torch.manual_seed(6050)
    layers = []
    for _ in range(depth):
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, width), activation()]
    net = nn.Sequential(*layers, nn.Linear(width, 1)).double()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for layer in net:
            if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, std=(2 / layer.in_features) ** 0.5)
                nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)

    out = net(torch.randn(128, width, dtype=torch.float64)).mean()
    out.backward()
    linears = [layer for layer in net if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)][:-1]
    first = linears[0]
    grad32 = first.weight.grad.float()
    weight32 = first.weight.detach().float()
    changed = ((weight32 - 0.1 * grad32) != weight32).sum().item()
    return {
        "norms": [layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in linears],
        "first_max": first.weight.grad.abs().max().item(),
        "first_nonzero": grad32.count_nonzero().item(),
        "first_changed": changed,
        "first_size": grad32.numel(),
    }

# [2]
diagnostics = {}
plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
# [3]
for act, color in [(nn.Sigmoid, "#232D4B"), (nn.ReLU, "#E57200")]:
    diagnostics[act.__name__] = gradient_diagnostic(act)
    plt.semilogy(diagnostics[act.__name__]["norms"], "o-", ms=3,
                 color=color, label=act.__name__)
plt.xlabel("layer (0 = closest to input)")
plt.ylabel(r"$\|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial W^{(l)}\|$")
# [4]
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for name, result in diagnostics.items():
    print(f"{name:7s}: max|g0|={result['first_max']:.2e}; "
          f"nonzero={result['first_nonzero']}/{result['first_size']}; "
          f"changed={result['first_changed']}/{result['first_size']}")







Figure 5.6: Gradient reaching each layer of two matched 30-layer MLPs (float64 norm, log scale). With the same weights and inputs, repeated sigmoid derivatives leave a nonzero but unusably small first-layer signal. ReLU preserves enough signal for a float32 update to change every first-layer weight.





Sigmoid: max|g0|=9.47e-17; nonzero=4096/4096; changed=0/4096
ReLU   : max|g0|=2.54e-02; nonzero=4096/4096; changed=4096/4096



Read the slopes, then read the printed counts of nonzero gradient entries and changed weights. All 4,096 sigmoid first-layer entries remain nonzero after the float32 cast. They are so small, however, that subtracting \(0.1g\) changes none of the stored float32 weights. The ReLU network changes all 4,096. That distinction matters, and Appendix C names both failures: a displayed float32 norm can underflow while individual entries remain nonzero, and a nonzero entry can still produce an update that rounds away when subtracted from a larger stored weight.

title: 5  Backpropagation
text:
5.7 Initialization and signal scale
The weights also scale the signal at each layer, so their initial scale is a second factor we choose. If each layer multiplies the variance of the signal by more than one, activations explode after enough layers. If it multiplies the variance by less than one, they vanish. Forward activation scales and backward derivative scales are related but distinct, and keeping each roughly constant gives the two conditions below.
The variance scales predictably through the dot product. For \(z = \sum_{i=1}^{D_{\text{in}}} w_i x_i\) with independent, zero-mean inputs and weights, \(\var(z) = D_{\text{in}} \var(w) \var(x)\). Keeping \(\var(z) = \var(x)\) demands the first condition below. On the backward pass, each input unit collects a sum over the units it fed, so keeping the variance of the loss derivatives constant demands the second:
\[
\var(w) = \frac{1}{D_{\text{in}}} \quad \text{(forward)}, \qquad
\var(w) = \frac{1}{D_{\text{out}}} \quad \text{(backward)}.
\]
The two conditions disagree when \(D_{\text{in}} \ne D_{\text{out}}\). Glorot and Bengio (2010) compromised with \(\var(w) = 2/(D_{\text{in}} + D_{\text{out}})\), which lies between them. This recipe is called Xavier initialization, after Xavier Glorot. Both conditions assume an activation that keeps the variance. ReLU sets about half of its inputs to zero and so halves the mean square. He et al. (2015) therefore doubled the forward recipe to \(\var(w) = 2/D_{\text{in}}\), now called He initialization, after Kaiming He. A PyTorch linear layer follows neither recipe by default: it draws its weights uniformly with variance \(1/(3D_{\text{in}})\), a sixth of the He value, so a deep ReLU stack without normalization needs an explicit choice.



Define the reusable signal_std helper.
Fix the seed, define two naive weight scales (0.05, 0.12) and He scaling, and open the figure.
Signal energy vs depth.
Add a legend naming each initialization scheme and show the plot.



from collections.abc import Callable

# [1]
def signal_std(
    scale_fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor, int], torch.Tensor],
    depth: int = 40, width: int = 256
) -> list[float]:
    x = torch.randn(512, width)
    stds = []
    for _ in range(depth):
        W = scale_fn(torch.randn(width, width), width)
        x = torch.relu(x @ W)
        stds.append(x.std().item())
    return stds

# [2]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
schemes = {
    "naive  (std = 0.05)": lambda W, n: W * 0.05,
    "naive  (std = 0.12)": lambda W, n: W * 0.12,
    "He  (std = sqrt(2/n))": lambda W, n: W * (2 / n) ** 0.5,
}
plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
# [3]
for (name, fn), color in zip(schemes.items(), ["#5379AA", "#722F37", "#E57200"]):
    plt.semilogy(signal_std(fn), color=color, label=name)
plt.xlabel("layer"); plt.ylabel("std of activations")
# [4]
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 5.7: Activation standard deviation through 40 ReLU layers of width \(D = 256\). Each fixed weight scale multiplies the signal by a roughly constant factor per layer, a straight line on the log axis. The He-initialized trace stays near its starting scale in this run.






Over 40 layers, the two fixed scales, \(0.05\) and \(0.12\), move the signal by many orders of magnitude before training starts, while the He scale keeps it level. Initialization sets the starting scale of the weights, and the choice of activation determines the derivative factors. Together they determine whether the forward and backward signals keep their scale through depth at the start of training. Two later tools work on the same problem during training: normalization layers rescale intermediate computations, and skip (residual) connections add paths that bypass a block’s activation derivatives and weights alike. Normalization and residual connections appear in Chapter 10, and layer normalization becomes part of every Transformer block in Chapter 16.






NoteCheck yourself



Close the book for one minute and run the chain rule backward.

What does each layer cache on the forward pass, and what does that cost in memory?
Why does the loss derivative \(\delta\) pass through a transposed weight matrix?
How do activation derivatives and initialization together control gradient scale with depth?

title: 5  Backpropagation
section: 5.8 Okay, so: the chain rule, organized
text:
5.8 Okay, so: the chain rule, organized

The graph. Any network is a computation graph. The forward pass computes and caches, while the backward pass multiplies local derivatives in reverse and sums contributions from multiple paths.
The loss derivative. \(\delta^{(l)} = \partial \loss / \partial \vect{z}^{(l)}\) reduces the computation to four equations: start at the output (Equation 5.2), propagate through \(\matr{W}^\top\) and the activation derivative (Equation 5.3), then read off weight and bias gradients (Equation 5.4, Equation 5.5). On a batch, each forward matrix product costs two backward ones, so the sweep delivers every gradient for about twice the forward arithmetic, at the memory cost of the cached activations.
We verified it. Our hand-built equations match PyTorch’s autograd to \(10^{-8}\). The scalar engine illustrates reverse topological order and adjoint accumulation by addition.
Activation derivatives and depth. The sigmoid-derivative product along a path is bounded above by \(0.25^k\) after \(k\) activation-derivative factors. ReLU has an activation derivative of one on positive inputs. Initialization helps control activation and gradient scales at the start of training.

Backpropagation trains every model from here through Chapter 23. When a deep model fails to learn, the first questions concern the gradient: whether it reaches the early layers, what attenuates it, and what its scale is.

title: 5  Backpropagation
text:
Sources and further reading

Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, “Learning representations by back-propagating errors” (1986): the landmark short account of learning internal representations by reverse error propagation.
Baydin et al., “Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey” (2018): separates reverse-mode automatic differentiation from symbolic and numerical differentiation.
Glorot and Bengio, “Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks” (2010): the variance argument behind Xavier initialization.
He et al., “Delving Deep into Rectifiers” (2015): derives the rectifier-aware initialization used in the matched depth experiment.
CS231n, “Gradient Checks”: the centered-difference and relative-error safeguards used in Exercise 6.
Chen, Xu, Zhang, and Guestrin, “Training Deep Nets with Sublinear Memory Cost” (2016): stores a subset of activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading arithmetic for memory.
Shakeri, Deep Learning: Making It Trainable, Chapter 11, “The Gradient Has a Memory: Reverse Accumulation and Checkpointing” (2026): a treatment of reverse accumulation as a memory and numerical diagnostic, including fan-out accumulation, vector–Jacobian products, retained state, and checkpoint replay.

Common misconception: “absolute error below \(10^{-4}\) proves the gradient”: absolute error ignores the scale of the quantity being checked.
(Pencil.) Let \(\hat{\vect{y}} = \operatorname{softmax}(\vect{o})\) for logits \(\vect{o} \in \mathbb{R}^K\). Show that its Jacobian is \(\partial\hat{\vect{y}}/\partial\vect{o} = \operatorname{diag}(\hat{\vect{y}}) -
\hat{\vect{y}}\hat{\vect{y}}^\top\), and that for any upstream derivative \(\vect{u} = \partial \loss/\partial\hat{\vect{y}}\) the vector–Jacobian product is \(\partial \loss/\partial\vect{o} = \hat{\vect{y}} \odot \bigl(\vect{u} -
\langle\vect{u}, \hat{\vect{y}}\rangle\,\mathbf{1}\bigr)\), which costs \(O(K)\) where forming the Jacobian costs \(O(K^2)\). Choose \(\vect{u}\) for \(\loss = -\log \hat{y}_c\) and recover Equation 2.6. Choose it for squared error against a one-hot target and recover the row formula in Exercise 4 of Chapter 2. (Code.) Implement softmax_vjp(y_hat, u), check it against torch.autograd.grad in float64 for random logits and upstream vectors under a fixed seed, and time it against multiplying by the materialized Jacobian for \(K = 10^2, 10^3, 10^4\).

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
text:
6.1 The baseline fit: empirical risk and clean validation
We now have expressive models, likelihood-derived losses, an optimizer that scales, and an efficient way to compute gradients. Applied to Fashion-MNIST, this machinery classifies most held-out validation images correctly.
Yet a clean validation score estimates performance only under the distribution sampled by that validation set. It does not establish tolerance to transformations we have not tested. A small shift, for example, preserves the garment’s visual identity, so we expect a robust model to keep its prediction. A complete pixel scramble, by contrast, destroys the two-dimensional spatial arrangement. Requiring a model to keep its output under arbitrary scrambling is neither expected nor desirable. Task-relevant invariance is selective: an image model should tolerate small displacements that leave the object unchanged while remaining sensitive to the spatial structure that defines an object.
We compare these transformations under two protocols: evaluating an already trained model on transformed inputs, and retraining on transformed data. The first tests one fitted network. The second tests what the architecture and training recipe can learn, a property of the whole model family: the set of functions the architecture can compute. The comparison also motivates the locality and weight sharing developed in Part II.
We use a subset of Fashion-MNIST, a classic benchmark of \(28 \times 28\) grayscale images of clothing in ten classes. The model and training loop come from earlier chapters: we train an MLP from Chapter 3 exactly as in Chapter 4:
This MLP has no layer that behaves differently in training and evaluation, but keep the net.eval() line: it disables training-only behavior such as the dropout mechanism from Chapter 4 before evaluation.
The model makes useful predictions on held-out images from the same distribution as its fitting data. We fixed the split before any experiment, and the separate test set remains sealed until the end of the chapter. What the validation score does not establish is whether those predictions respond appropriately when the spatial arrangement changes.
Before probing the model, we separate three questions that are often collapsed into “the model worked.” Each question needs different evidence.

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
text:
Load and flatten the Fashion-MNIST subset, split off 200 validation images, and import fit_supervised.
Define the reusable helpers: train_mlp and accuracy.
Fit the Chapter 4 recipe on the fixed Fashion-MNIST development split.
Print the train and validation accuracy.



import torch
from torch import nn

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
development = torch.load("../../data/fashion-train.pt")
holdout = torch.load("../../data/fashion-test.pt")
X_dev = development["X"].float().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0  # (1200, 784)
y_dev, classes = development["y"], development["classes"]
X_test = holdout["X"].float().reshape(-1, 784) / 255.0     # (600, 784)
y_test = holdout["y"]

split = torch.randperm(len(X_dev), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050))
fit_idx, val_idx = split[:1000], split[1000:]
X_tr, y_tr = X_dev[fit_idx], y_dev[fit_idx]                 # (1000, 784), (1000,)
X_val, y_val = X_dev[val_idx], y_dev[val_idx]               # (200, 784), (200,)

from dlbook.supervised import fit_supervised   # Listing 4.1
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [2]
def train_mlp(
    X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor, hidden: int = 256,
    epochs: int = 40, seed: int = 6050
) -> nn.Module:
    # The delta from Listing 4.1 is one line: this chapter's model.
    return fit_supervised(
        lambda: nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(784, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, 10)
        ),
        X, y, epochs=epochs, seed=seed,
    )

def accuracy(net: nn.Module, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (net(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

# [3]
net = train_mlp(X_tr, y_tr)
# [4]
print(f"train accuracy: {accuracy(net, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}")
print(f"validation accuracy: {accuracy(net, X_val, y_val):.1%}")

train accuracy: 95.0%
validation accuracy: 76.0%









Table 6.1: Three claims that require three kinds of evidence. Low training error is evidence about one optimization run and, indirectly, about the available capacity. Generalization needs evidence of its own.










Question
Evidence that answers it
What that evidence does not settle




Representation: can the architecture, with some choice of weights, compute a useful rule?
An explicit construction, an approximation theorem, or one trained network that computes such a rule
Whether the optimizer will find that rule


Optimization: did this training procedure reach low empirical risk?
The loss trace, gradients, restarts, and a final training-set check
Behavior on fresh or shifted data


Generalization: does the fitted procedure work on the distribution we care about?
Independent evaluation data drawn from that declared distribution
Performance under an undeclared deployment shift

section: 6.2 Two experiments that challenge the baseline
text:
6.2 Two experiments that challenge the baseline

Experiment 1: shift every image two pixels
We keep the trained network fixed, shift each validation image two pixels to the right, and compare the accuracy on the shifted images with the clean accuracy. A shift of two pixels should preserve the class of a recognizable garment. Because shifting within a finite frame can also crop the image, we will check that effect separately. Before you run the cell, predict the accuracy after the shift.



Define the reusable shift_right helper.
Shift validation images while keeping the trained MLP fixed.



# [1]
def shift_right(X: torch.Tensor, px: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    img = X.reshape(-1, 28, 28)
    out = torch.zeros_like(img)
    if px > 0:
        out[:, :, px:] = img[:, :, :-px]
    else:
        out = img.clone()
    return out.reshape(-1, 784)

# [2]
for px in [0, 2]:
    print(f"shift {px}px: validation accuracy "
          f"{accuracy(net, shift_right(X_val, px), y_val):.1%}")

shift 0px: validation accuracy 76.0%
shift 2px: validation accuracy 46.5%



After the two-pixel shift, the accuracy falls to 46.5%.
Does the shift fail because it pushes garments off the canvas? Fashion-MNIST scales each garment’s longest edge to fill the frame (Xiao et al.), so wide items such as sandals, sneakers, and ankle boots reach the right border, and a two-pixel shift crops them. We measure the crop on its own by zeroing the same two columns without moving anything.



Measure how much ink the two cropped columns hold.
Zero those columns in place, leaving every garment where it was.
Print the two ink measurements and the validation accuracy with those columns zeroed.



# [1]
edge = X_val.reshape(-1, 28, 28)[:, :, -2:]        # the columns a 2px shift crops
touched = (edge.flatten(1) > 0).any(dim=1).float().mean().item()
ink_share = (edge.sum() / X_val.sum()).item()
# [2]
cropped = X_val.reshape(-1, 28, 28).clone()
cropped[:, :, -2:] = 0
# [3]
print(f"images with ink in the two cropped columns: {touched:.1%}")
print(f"share of all ink in those columns:          {ink_share:.1%}")
print(f"columns zeroed in place, nothing moved:     validation accuracy "
      f"{accuracy(net, cropped.reshape(-1, 784), y_val):.1%}")

images with ink in the two cropped columns: 35.0%
share of all ink in those columns:          1.2%
columns zeroed in place, nothing moved:     validation accuracy 74.0%



Removing those columns in place costs two percentage points, far less than the full shift. The crop therefore explains only a small part of the loss after displacement.
This is the distinction from Chapter 1: validation data drawn from the data-generating distribution \(P\) estimates performance under \(P\), and performance under a transformed distribution needs its own test. If \(T\) shifts an image while preserving its label, then
\[
R_{T_\#P}(\theta)
=
\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right],
\tag{6.1}\]
where \(T_\#P\) is the distribution obtained by transforming inputs drawn from \(P\) while retaining their labels. The MLP generalized moderately from its fitting sample to fresh clean examples from \(P\), but it was not robust under \(T_\#P\). Clean validation and shift robustness answer different questions: minimizing empirical risk on samples from \(P\) places no constraint on predictions under \(T_\#P\). Appendix E gathers the \(P\), \(T_\#P\), and deployment-distribution notation in one place.
As the validation images move right by 0 to 4 pixels, Figure 6.1 follows the same fixed network. We call the resulting drop in accuracy the shift cliff.



Measure validation accuracy at right shifts of 0 to 4 pixels and open the figure.
Plot accuracy vs. shift.



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# [1]
shifts = list(range(5))
accs = [accuracy(net, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
plt.figure(figsize=(5.6, 3.3))
# [2]
plt.plot(shifts, accs, "o-", color="#E57200", lw=2, ms=7)
plt.axhline(0.1, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.text(0.1, 0.115, "chance (10 classes)", color="#8A8A7A", fontsize=9)
plt.xlabel("shift (pixels right)"); plt.ylabel("validation accuracy")
plt.ylim(0, 0.9); plt.xticks(shifts)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 6.1: Validation accuracy of the clean-trained network under rightward shifts of the validation images. The network is not retrained, and the original labels are retained. The dotted line marks the ten-class chance level, and accuracy approaches it after four pixels of shift.








Experiment 2: permute the pixel coordinates
We choose one fixed random permutation of the 784 pixel positions and apply it to every image, fitting and validation alike, then retrain with the same recipe and seed. We keep the original labels attached to the examples. The scrambled arrays are no longer recognizable garments: the ordinary grid adjacency has been destroyed.
We have no reason to expect the clean-trained classifier to keep its decisions under a scramble, so we ask a different question: can a fresh model learn the original labels from this consistently re-encoded dataset? The permutation is invertible, so it changes where information is stored without removing it. Predict before retraining: does the altered arrangement cost this MLP five points, twenty, or almost nothing?



Set the seed to 0 and draw pixel_perm, a random reordering of the 784 pixel positions.
Retrain on one fixed permutation of the pixel coordinates.
Print validation accuracy for the original MLP and for the retrained MLP on shuffled images.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(0)
pixel_perm = torch.randperm(784)          # one fixed scrambling for all images

# [2]
net_shuffled = train_mlp(X_tr[:, pixel_perm], y_tr)
# [3]
print(f"original images:  validation accuracy {accuracy(net, X_val, y_val):.1%}")
print(f"shuffled pixels:  validation accuracy "
      f"{accuracy(net_shuffled, X_val[:, pixel_perm], y_val):.1%}")

original images:  validation accuracy 76.0%
shuffled pixels:  validation accuracy 77.0%



The two validation accuracies are close in this one seeded comparison. This shows that the training recipe can learn a useful classifier in the scrambled representation.
The two experiments used different protocols. Experiment 1 kept the clean-trained model and changed only the validation images. Experiment 2 transformed both the fitting and validation images and retrained. Complete the other two cells of that two-by-two design:



Evaluate the clean model on scrambled images, without retraining.
Retrain the same MLP on shifted images, then evaluate it on shifted images.
Print validation accuracy for the scrambled, trained-clean case and the shifted, retrained case.



# [1]
zero_shot_scramble = accuracy(net, X_val[:, pixel_perm], y_val)
# [2]
net_shifted = train_mlp(shift_right(X_tr, 2), y_tr)
retrained_shift = accuracy(net_shifted, shift_right(X_val, 2), y_val)
# [3]
print(f"scramble, trained clean:     validation accuracy {zero_shot_scramble:.1%}")
print(f"two-pixel shift, retrained:  validation accuracy {retrained_shift:.1%}")

scramble, trained clean:     validation accuracy 8.0%
two-pixel shift, retrained:  validation accuracy 76.5%









NoteDiagnostic protocol: a fixed model versus retraining



Validation accuracy for the four combinations of transformation and protocol. The baseline is the clean-trained model on untouched validation images (the baseline fit). All scores use the original labels, including those attached to the scrambled inputs.








Protocol
Two-pixel shift
Fixed pixel scramble




Fixed model: trained clean, evaluated transformed
46.5%

The two results in the first row have different interpretations. The shift result shows a failure of the desired tolerance to small position changes. The scramble result shows sensitivity to a much larger change in spatial organization, for which we did not require invariance.
The second row shows that retraining recovers similar accuracy in both transformed datasets under this recipe. For the fixed scramble, the next section gives an exact coordinate-permutation argument. A zero-filled shift also discards boundary pixels, so the argument does not cover it, and its retrained result is purely empirical.

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
text:
6.3 Inside the weights: full-frame templates
Why does retraining recover the accuracy on scrambled images? The first layer gives an exact answer. Write the fixed scramble as a permutation matrix \(\matr{\Pi}\), so a scrambled image is \(\matr{\Pi}\vect{x}\). For any first-layer matrix \(\matr{W}_1\), set \(\matr{W}_1' = \matr{W}_1\matr{\Pi}^\top\). Then
\[
\matr{W}_1'(\matr{\Pi}\vect{x})
= \matr{W}_1\matr{\Pi}^\top\matr{\Pi}\vect{x}
= \matr{W}_1\vect{x},
\tag{6.2}\]
because \(\matr{\Pi}^\top\matr{\Pi} = \matr{I}\). With the first-layer bias vector \(\vect{b}_1\) and later layers unchanged, the entire network produces the same output. Every function this MLP can compute in the original coordinates therefore has a matching set of weights in the scrambled coordinates.
The identity is a property of the model family. It changes the first-layer weights along with the inputs. One fitted network keeps its weights fixed, and for fixed weights \(\matr{W}_1\matr{\Pi}\vect{x}\) differs from \(\matr{W}_1\vect{x}\), which is why the clean-trained model fails on scrambled images. Training also treats the two coordinate systems alike. The initialization is exchangeable across input coordinates: permuting the coordinates leaves the distribution of the initial weights unchanged. Adam applies the same coordinate-wise rule, so the training procedures correspond in distribution under a fixed permutation (Exercise 1). Resetting the seed does not itself permute the initial weights, so the two particular runs need not have identical accuracies.
The dense parameterization therefore gives no built-in preference to the original pixel adjacency over another ordering. It can still learn spatial regularities from data, but it builds in neither locality nor translation invariance.
We can inspect that parameterization directly. Each row \(\vect{w}_j^\top\) of \(\matr{W}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{256\times784}\) assigns a separate coefficient to every input pixel. As in Chapter 1, it is a template scored by the inner product \(\langle\vect{w}_j,\vect{x}\rangle\). Reshaping the row into a 28×28 image shows its coordinate weights.



Select the largest-norm first-layer templates.



# [1]
W1 = net[0].weight.detach()               # (256, 784)
order = W1.norm(dim=1).argsort(descending=True)[:16]
scale = float(W1[order].abs().max())










Figure 6.2: Sixteen first-layer weight rows with the largest norms, reshaped into images. The labeled scale runs from negative weights at the blue end through pale zero to positive weights at the red end. Each map shows a separate coefficient for every input pixel. Its appearance alone does not show what the full network recognizes or how robustly it does so.





We should not expect these maps to resolve into edges, contours, or parts that a person would name, and reading them is subjective. A picture of the weights cannot tell us whether the network will tolerate a spatial change or fail under it. Only a transformation test can. What the maps do display is the full-frame parameterization: each hidden unit scores the image with an unconstrained template that spans the whole canvas, with an independent coefficient at every pixel coordinate. The layer contains no compact local detector that is reused at other positions.
For the pre-activation \(z_j(\vect{x})=\vect{w}_j^\top\vect{x}+b_j\), a transformation \(T\) changes the score by
\[
z_j(T(\vect{x}))-z_j(\vect{x})
=\vect{w}_j^\top\bigl(T(\vect{x})-\vect{x}\bigr).
\]
The transformations of interest are label-preserving: small shifts of the garment within the frame, or a symmetry such as the left–right reflection of a shirt, after which the garment remains recognizable and its class is unchanged. A shift moves each intensity to a neighboring coordinate, where a different coefficient multiplies it. The dense parameterization does not tie the two coefficients together, and only training determines how similar they are. For a shift of \(s\) columns to the right, the intensity in the \(s\) rightmost columns leaves the frame and changes the score as zeroing those columns in place would, the crop that Experiment 1 measured on its own. Every other pixel \(p\) moves to the position \(p+s\), \(s\) columns to its right, and these pixels contribute the rest of the difference, \(\sum_p (w_{j,p+s}-w_{j,p})\,x_p\), with the sum taken over them. The score change is therefore set by how each coefficient compares with its neighbor \(s\) columns away, a relation the dense layer leaves untied.
Asking each unit’s score to stay fixed would be the wrong remedy. Ignoring the pixels lost at the border, requiring the displacement term to vanish for arbitrary images would force equal neighboring coefficients: a template constant along every row and blind to horizontal arrangement. Instead, we want a detector’s response to move with the input. What the dense layer lacks is a unit tied to the shifted copy of \(\vect{w}_j\), so that the response could move with the garment, as the response of a shared local detector does. A change in one hidden score does not by itself settle the classifier’s decision either: the ReLU and the output layer combine all 256 hidden scores, whose changes can cancel or accumulate. Tolerance must therefore be measured at the output, as in Experiment 1.
During training, the gradient for row \(j\) is a weighted sum of the input images, \(\sum_i\delta_{ij}\,\vect{x}_i\), from the batched form of Equation 5.4, where \(\delta_{ij}\) is the loss derivative of hidden unit \(j\) on image \(i\). Adam rescales the coordinates separately, but neither that update nor the parameterization enforces a compact template or shared coefficients across positions. Expressive power alone does not supply the particular invariances we want. We next examine how clean performance changes with capacity.

section: 6.4 Diagnosing the failure: capacity versus geometry
text:
6.4 Diagnosing the failure: capacity versus geometry
Is the model too flexible, or is the data too sparse for 784 dimensions?

Capacity: testing the classical U-curve
The classical picture, the schematic in Chapter 1, predicts that as capacity grows, validation error first falls and then rises as the model overfits. A width sweep at two dataset sizes tests that prediction on real data:



Choose the hidden widths to sweep, from 2 up to 256 units.
Measure validation error across widths and fitting-set sizes.



# [1]
widths = [2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256]
# [2]
width_errors = {
    n: [1 - accuracy(train_mlp(X_tr[:n], y_tr[:n], hidden=h, epochs=60),
                       X_val, y_val)
        for h in widths]
    for n in (300, 1000)
}










Figure 6.3: Testing the classical U-curve: validation error vs. hidden width at two fitting-set sizes. Error falls steeply as capacity grows, then flattens. In this one seeded sweep, n=300 shows a small late upturn while n=1000 does not.





The left side of the schematic appears in both curves: networks with too little capacity underfit badly. The right side barely appears: a slight upturn at \(n = 300\) and a flat plateau at \(n = 1000\). The classical picture predicts a sustained rise in validation error once the width passes its best value, and neither curve shows one. As Chapter 1 warned, the U-shaped curve is a useful schematic that real training need not follow: the optimizer, the sample size, and the structure of the data can all shape the curve. A single seeded Adam sweep describes its own regime, so it cannot separate their effects, estimate a scaling law, or establish a \(1/n\) variance law.
The sweep measures clean validation performance. A network’s response to a shift needs its own measurement at each width.


Geometry: the curse of dimensionality
The width sweep leaves the shift failure unexplained, so we turn from the model to its input, the raw pixel vectors. How informative is the distance between two such vectors? Our images use 784 numbers. A small color image (\(32 \times 32 \times 3\)) uses 3,072, a \(224 \times 224 \times 3\) input uses 150,528, and a one-megapixel color photo uses three million. Covering every combination of pixel values is out of reach: a grid with 9 values per coordinate has \(9^2\) points in two dimensions and \(9^d\) in \(d\) dimensions, about \(10^{748}\) at \(d = 784\).
High dimension also erodes the contrast between near and far points:



Fix the seed, list dimensions from 2 to 5000, and start an empty ratios list.
Measure the nearest-to-farthest distance ratio by dimension.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
dims = [2, 10, 100, 784, 5000]
ratios = []
# [2]
for d in dims:
    P = torch.rand(300, d)
    D = torch.cdist(P, P)
    ratios.append(((D + torch.eye(300) * 1e9).min(1).values / D.max(1).values).mean())










Figure 6.4: Distance concentration for 300 points sampled uniformly from a unit cube: the average ratio of nearest-neighbor to farthest-neighbor distance, by ambient dimension. At d=784 the ratio reaches 0.89. The uniform cube is a controlled geometry example, and natural images do not fill it uniformly.








  
  Watch the mechanism: where "nearest neighbour" stops meaning anything

crumbs: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
text:
6.5 Inductive bias: constraints as knowledge
Recall inductive bias from Chapter 1: the assumptions and preferences that distinguish fitted solutions beyond their agreement with the training sample. Here we have prior knowledge about image structure and about which position changes should preserve the label. Two principles suggest how to use it:

Locality. Nearby pixels jointly form edges, textures, and parts. Local connectivity gives these relationships a structural role that the dense parameterization does not assign them.
Translation structure. A local detector’s response should move with the feature (equivariance), while a classifier’s final prediction should tolerate or ignore small changes in position (invariance). The shift experiment tests this desired tolerance at the classifier’s output.


Data augmentation: specifying label-preserving transformations
The shift cliff suggests another route. If moving a garment a little should not change its class, let \(T\) be a random label-preserving transformation drawn from a declared distribution \(\mathcal{A}\). The population objective becomes
\[
R_{\mathcal A}(\theta)
=
\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\E_{T\sim\mathcal{A}}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right].
\tag{6.3}\]
This is data augmentation. Beyond enlarging the dataset, it is a data-side inductive bias: the transformation distribution states which changes we believe should preserve the target. By sampling shifts from \(-3\) to \(+3\) pixels, we declare that location within that window does not matter for the label. This is an assumption about the task, and it covers shifts only. Retraining on one fixed scramble does something different: it changes the encoding of the whole dataset. The empirical augmented objective used in training replaces the outer expectation with the sample average. Drawing one fresh \(T\) when an example enters a batch then gives a Monte Carlo estimate of the inner expectation: a random sample stands in for the average over all transformations. Exercise 2 asks you to include those shifts in the training batches and measure both how augmentation changes the shift-response curve of Figure 6.1 and what it costs on clean images. Appendix E summarizes the corresponding estimators and distributions.
Augmentation encourages translation tolerance by training on shifted examples, while the dense network still gives each position its own coefficients. Weight sharing ties those coefficients directly. Exercise 2 measures the effect of augmentation with the current MLP, and Part II develops the architectural alternative.
We can now place three familiar levers side by side:

Architecture-side bias changes which functions are available or easy to learn. Local connectivity and shared convolutional filters are the route Part II will take.
Objective- or training-side bias changes which fitted solution is preferred. Weight penalties, dropout, and early stopping from Chapter 4 are examples. The minibatch noise discussed there may also bias which solution training reaches.
Data-side bias changes the examples the model is fitted to. Augmentation encodes a chosen family of label-preserving transformations.

These routes can work together, and each has its own limits. Training on a finite set of shifted copies encourages consistent predictions, and the network may still respond differently to shifts it never saw. An architectural constraint can make a symmetry exact in a layer, but it may exclude useful functions. A penalty prefers some solutions without specifying which input changes should preserve a label. And augmentation needs a label-preserving transformation: flipping a garment may be harmless, while flipping a digit or a directional sign may change the answer.
For Part II we begin with the architecture-side route: build locality and translation structure into the network itself as constraints. We constrain each template to a small local patch instead of the whole frame. Then we share that template across every position, so the local detection rule uses the same parameters throughout the image. These constraints supply locality and sharing, and the full classifier’s shift tolerance will still need to be measured. The parameter count falls too: our MLP has 203,530 parameters, while the LeNet model in Chapter 9 will have 61,706, less than a third as many.






TipWhy a constraint can add knowledge



Local connectivity and weight sharing constrain a corresponding dense network with the same layer sizes. Through the bias–variance lens of Chapter 1 (statistical bias of the average fit, a different notion from inductive bias), we accept assumptions about image structure to reduce the space of solutions considered. When those assumptions are appropriate, the restriction can improve data efficiency. The choice remains task-dependent: we want tolerance to small position changes while the model still responds to the arrangement of the pixels. With sufficient data and a suitable training recipe, architectures with weaker spatial constraints can also perform well, as Vision Transformers illustrate in Chapter 19.

Sliding a local template across the image and scoring each position by an inner product is a classical operation, decades older than deep learning. Part II opens by building this operation by hand and then poses the following question:
What if the template were learnable?

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
section: 6.8 Okay, so: build in the structure the task needs
text:
6.8 Okay, so: build in the structure the task needs

Clean accuracy and shift robustness are different claims. The MLP predicts well on clean held-out images but loses accuracy after a small, label-preserving displacement.
Invariance must match the task. A complete scramble changes the spatial organization and need not preserve a clean-trained model’s decision. Retraining on that fixed permutation tests whether the recipe can learn in a different encoding.
The model family has a coordinate symmetry. The reparameterization in Equation 6.2 explains why a dense architecture gives no built-in preference to the original pixel ordering. The weight maps display its coordinate-specific coefficients, and their appearance alone establishes neither robustness nor its cause.
Capacity and ambient dimension do not settle the diagnosis. The width sweep describes one clean-data regime, and the uniform-cube example illustrates distance concentration under its own distribution. The shift experiment exposes a mismatch between pixel distance and the tolerance the task requires.
Inductive bias specifies useful structure. It can enter through architecture, objectives, training procedures, or data. Part II develops locality and weight sharing, and augmentation is a complementary way to specify which transformations should preserve the label.
crumbs: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias

title: 6  Generalization, Distribution Shift, and Inductive Bias
text:
Deeper dive






NoteFurther discussion: memorization, confidence, and double descent





Networks can memorize random labels. Zhang et al. reported 100% training accuracy on randomly labeled CIFAR-10 and 95.20% on randomly labeled ImageNet under their finite training budget. Capacity is abundant enough that fitting noise is easy (Exercise 4 reproduces the phenomenon on our subset). Capacity alone therefore does not explain generalization. The data, the optimizer, and the architecture must enter the account.
Confident far from the data. A trained ReLU network is piecewise affine: its input space splits into polyhedral regions, and on each one the logits \(o_k=\tilde{\vect{w}}_k^\top\vect{x}+\tilde b_k\), with effective slope \(\tilde{\vect{w}}_k\) and offset \(\tilde b_k\) on that region, are affine in \(\vect{x}\). Along a ray that remains in one such region, if one logit has a strictly larger slope than the others, its softmax probability approaches 1 as the distance increases. Hein, Andriushchenko, and Bitterwolf analyze this behavior for ReLU classifiers. High softmax confidence therefore need not indicate that an input resembles the training data. This is a separate question from the label-preserving shift test.
The bias–variance picture, updated. Test error can sometimes descend again beyond the interpolation threshold, where the model first becomes able to interpolate the training sample: “double descent.” The width sweep above does not establish that pattern. It illustrates why a classical U-shaped curve should not be assumed in every training regime.
Further reading

Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, Vinyals, “Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization” (ICLR 2017), the primary source for the random-label experiment.
Neal, “On the Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Textbooks Need an Update” (2019), the source of the view that the U-shaped curve is not universal.
Belkin et al., “Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off” (PNAS 2019), a primary account of double descent.
Hein, Andriushchenko, and Bitterwolf, “Why ReLU networks yield high-confidence predictions far away from the training data and how to mitigate the problem” (CVPR 2019), the theorem behind confident predictions far from the data.
