title: 9  CNNs: Making the Filters Learnable
text:
9.5 Receptive fields grow with depth
Stacking has one more consequence. Every kernel here is tiny and local, \(5 \times 5\), yet recognizing a garment requires combining evidence across the image. Depth enlarges the local receptive fields, and in our LeNet the dense head then combines them across the frame.
The receptive field of a unit is the patch of the input image that can change its value. A unit of the first feature map reads a \(5 \times 5\) patch of the image, so its receptive field is \(5 \times 5\). A unit one layer up reads a \(5 \times 5\) patch of the first feature maps. Each value in that patch already depends on its own \(5 \times 5\) patch of the image, and neighboring patches are offset from one another, so together they cover a larger patch of the image.
Pooling makes the field grow faster. After a \(2\times2\) pool with stride 2, neighboring values of the pooled map come from image positions two pixels apart, so a window on the pooled map spans twice as much of the image. For the LeNet built in the next section, the field grows in four stages:

conv1: each unit reads \(5 \times 5\) pixels, a field of \(5 \times 5\).
The first pool: each unit combines a \(2 \times 2\) block of conv1 units, one pixel apart, so its field grows by one pixel to \(6 \times 6\).
conv2: each unit reads a \(5 \times 5\) window of pooled units, which sit two pixels apart, so the window adds \(4 \times 2 = 8\) pixels to the field: \(14 \times 14\).
The second pool: a \(2 \times 2\) block of conv2 units, two pixels apart, adds two more pixels: \(16 \times 16\).

The final field covers more than half the frame in each direction, built from \(5 \times 5\) kernels alone.








Figure 9.3: Receptive fields by depth. Each box is the patch of the input that one unit depends on after a stage, drawn concentric for comparison. On the coat, the nested fields cross the visible sleeves, torso, and boundary. One unit depends on a 5×5 patch after conv1, 6×6 after the first pool, 14×14 after conv2, and 16×16 after the final pool. Local wiring yields increasingly large fields, and the dense head then combines all 25 overlapping final fields at once.





This is the compositional hierarchy of Chapter 3, now encouraged by the architecture. MLP layers also compose features. Convolution adds local connectivity and spatial sharing to that composition, and growing receptive fields let later layers compose earlier responses over larger regions. Learned channels often progress from edge-like patterns to textures and parts, but the architecture does not force those human labels. The CNN enlarges its receptive fields gradually, through depth, and its dense head completes the combination across the frame.

text:
9.6 The LeNet architecture
Our network is a variant of LeNet, Yann LeCun’s digit-reading network, and it follows a familiar CNN pattern: convolve, shrink, deepen, repeat, then classify. Spatial size falls (28 \(\rightarrow\) 14 \(\rightarrow\) 5) while feature depth grows (1 \(\rightarrow\) 6 \(\rightarrow\) 16): the network trades “where” for “what” stage by stage, until a small dense head maps the final \(16 \times
5 \times 5\) summary to class scores.



  Watch the mechanism: LeNet's tensor, one layer at a time
  
    The text says the maps shrink 28 → 14 → 5. The second convolution has no padding: what size does it hand to the second pool?

LeNet.



# [1]
class LeNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 5, padding=2)  # (N,1,28,28)->(N,6,28,28)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5)            # (N,6,14,14)->(N,16,10,10)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16 * 5 * 5, 120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, 10)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), 2)   # -> (N, 6, 14, 14)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)   # -> (N, 16, 5, 5)
        x = x.flatten(1)                             # -> (N, 400)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        return self.fc3(x)                           # logits, (N, 10)


Every line is a tool we already own: Equation 9.1 twice, Equation 9.2 behind the choice of padding=2, pooling twice, then the MLP of Chapter 3 as the decision head. The convolutional layers form the backbone, and fc1 through fc3 replace the single linear head of Chapter 2 with a small MLP. Following the advice of Chapter 2, the model returns raw logits and lets F.cross_entropy handle the probabilities.






NoteLeNet, then and now



The LeNet family (LeCun and colleagues, 1989–1998) began by reading handwritten ZIP codes for the US Postal Service, and its mature form, LeNet-5, went on to read a substantial share of America’s bank checks. Our variant keeps the classic skeleton but changes its internals: ReLU where the original used sigmoid-family activations (Chapter 3, Chapter 5), max pooling where it used subsampling based on averaging, Adam as the optimizer. Our later CNNs add one more modern stabilizer, batch normalization, which we meet properly in Chapter 10.


Before training, we count the parameters: weight sharing in Chapter 8 should save many, and Chapter 6’s MLP is the yardstick:



Define the reusable make_mlp helper.
Instantiate a fresh LeNet and a fresh MLP from make_mlp.
Parameter audit, LeNet vs. Chapter 6’s MLP.

def make_mlp() -> nn.Sequential:
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(),
                         nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))

# [2]
lenet, mlp = LeNet(), make_mlp()
# [3]

    print(f"{name:14s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):16s} {p.numel():>7,}")

print(f"MLP:   {n_mlp:,} parameters")

conv2.bias     (16,)                 16

LeNet: 61,706 parameters (2,572 of them convolutional)

These parameter counts can be read two ways. Against the MLP of Chapter 6, rebuilt here as make_mlp (the network of that chapter with an nn.Flatten() in front: 784 inputs, 256 hidden ReLU units and 10 outputs), LeNet carries 61,706 parameters to the MLP’s 203,530 (less than a third) while performing far richer spatial computation. This is the saving that the matrix view of Chapter 8 showed. Within LeNet, the two convolutional layers, which compute the spatial features, hold 2,572 parameters (about 4%), and the dense head holds the rest. We reduce that imbalance in Chapter 10, where modern architectures go deeper in convolution and lighter in the head.
We train both models once, with one seed, under one shared optimization recipe: same fitting split, optimizer, minibatch size, number of epochs, and therefore number of parameter updates. The comparison fixes the training schedule. It matches neither the parameter count nor the floating-point operations, which differ because a convolutional layer and a dense layer do different computation per update.



Define the reusable helpers: train_model and accuracy.
Run one recipe, two architectures.
Print train and validation accuracy for the MLP and for LeNet.



from dlbook.supervised import fit_supervised   # Listing 4.1

# [1]
def train_model(
    model_fn, X_fit: torch.Tensor = X_tr, y_fit: torch.Tensor = y_tr,
    epochs: int = 150, batch: int = 128, seed: int = 6050
) -> nn.Module:
    # Listing 4.1 verbatim; this chapter's deltas are the budget (150
    # epochs, batch 128) and, below, the models that get trained.
    return fit_supervised(
        model_fn, X_fit, y_fit, epochs=epochs, batch=batch, seed=seed
    )

@torch.no_grad()
def accuracy(model: nn.Module, X: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    model.eval()
    return (model(X).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

# [2]
mlp = train_model(make_mlp)
lenet = train_model(LeNet)
# [3]
for name, model in [("MLP  ", mlp), ("LeNet", lenet)]:
    print(f"{name}  train {accuracy(model, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}   "
          f"validation {accuracy(model, X_val, y_val):.1%}")

MLP    train 100.0%   validation 75.5%
LeNet  train 99.5%   validation 74.5%



Read the clean-validation column: the MLP scores 75.5% and LeNet 74.5% in this single seeded run. That one-point gap comes from a single seed and validation split, so it cannot rank the architectures by their expected accuracy across fresh seeds and data draws. Both models reach near-perfect accuracy on their fitting images. Our small-data regime makes a narrower point: LeNet reaches comparable clean accuracy with less than a third of the parameters. The shift experiment now compares the two models on shifted garments.

title: 9  CNNs: Making the Filters Learnable
text:
9.7 LeNet under the two-pixel shift
We now give LeNet the shift test of Chapter 6: both trained networks stay fixed, the validation images are shifted right by 0 to 4 pixels, and LeNet’s accuracy is compared with the MLP’s. There, a two-pixel shift took our MLP from 76.0% to 46.5% accuracy. Retrained here on LeNet’s schedule, the two models start from the comparable clean accuracies reported above. The question is whether the convolutional structure makes the classifier more tolerant of the shift.



Define the reusable shift_right helper.
Compute acc_mlp and acc_cnn, validation accuracy under right shifts of 0 to 4 pixels.
Plot accuracy vs. shift, both models.



# [1]
def shift_right(X: torch.Tensor, px: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.zeros_like(X)
    if px == 0:
        return X.clone()
    out[..., px:] = X[..., :-px]
    return out

# [2]
shifts = list(range(5))
acc_mlp = [accuracy(mlp, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
acc_cnn = [accuracy(lenet, shift_right(X_val, s), y_val) for s in shifts]
# [3]
for s in shifts:
    print(f"shift {s}px:   MLP {acc_mlp[s]:.1%}   LeNet {acc_cnn[s]:.1%}")

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 3.2))
plt.plot(shifts, acc_mlp, "o-", color="#E57200", lw=2, ms=7, label="MLP (Ch. 6)")
plt.plot(shifts, acc_cnn, "s-", color="#232D4B", lw=2, ms=7, label="LeNet")
plt.axhline(0.1, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.xlabel("shift (pixels right)"); plt.ylabel("validation accuracy")
plt.ylim(0, 0.9); plt.xticks(shifts); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

shift 0px:   MLP 75.5%   LeNet 74.5%
shift 1px:   MLP 64.0%   LeNet 66.0%
shift 2px:   MLP 42.0%   LeNet 57.5%
shift 3px:   MLP 27.0%   LeNet 42.0%
shift 4px:   MLP 18.5%   LeNet 23.0%








Figure 9.4: Validation accuracy under right shifts. Both architectures use the same optimizer schedule, though not matched compute. At two pixels the MLP falls from 75.5% to 42.0%, while LeNet falls from 74.5% to 57.5%. The dotted line is chance.






LeNet stays above the MLP at every nonzero shift, and the gap is largest at two and three pixels. At one pixel the two are close, 66.0% for LeNet and 64.0% for the MLP. At two pixels the MLP loses 33.5 points and LeNet 17.0. At three pixels LeNet scores 42.0% against 27.0%, and at four, 23.0% against 18.5%. These numbers come from one validation split and one seed, and the contrast within this run is large.
The comparison changes the complete architecture, so it does not isolate the contributions of locality, weight sharing, pooling or the classifier head. Several operations can still introduce shift sensitivity: cropping and padding affect the responses at the border, pooling depends on window alignment, and the dense head gives each spatial position, retained after flattening, its own weights. Chapter 10 replaces that position-sensitive head with global pooling.
In Chapter 6, the MLP’s first-layer weights were full-frame templates with broad, diffuse patterns. Figure 9.5 shows the six \(5 \times 5\) kernels of LeNet’s first layer and, under each, its feature map after the ReLU on the coat of Figure 9.3, a validation image.

Figure 9.5: What LeNet’s first layer learned. Top: six first-layer 5×5 kernels (red positive, blue negative). Bottom: their feature maps on the coat of Figure 9.3, a validation image whose sleeves and torso make spatial responses easy to compare. The maps respond differently, but several kernels remain diffuse and should not be over-interpreted.





The six local kernels produce distinct response maps on the same image. Some show directional structure. Others remain noisy enough that naming them as detectors would claim more than this one run supports. Nobody designed them: they result from optimizer steps on the classification loss, with gradients flowing backward through Equation 9.1.

No choice in this chapter depended on them.

title: 9  CNNs: Making the Filters Learnable
section: 9.9 Okay, so: the kernel became learnable
text:
9.9 Okay, so: the kernel became learnable

One change: the kernel’s numbers became parameters. Gradient descent can recover a hand-crafted detector from data (the kernel-recovery experiment) and, in a real CNN, learn kernels whose coefficients were not specified in advance, supervised only by the task loss at the far end.
Channels turn one detector into many: output channels stack the feature maps of several kernels, and input channels let each next-layer kernel combine all maps at once (Equation 9.1).
Padding and stride are the shape budget: \(n_{\text{out}} = \lfloor (n + 2p -
k)/s \rfloor + 1\) (Equation 9.2). Padding lets networks go deep without shrinking to nothing, and stride shrinks on purpose.
Pooling summarizes each window by one number: max pooling keeps the largest activation and discards its exact position within the window. Any resulting shift tolerance depends on the activations, window alignment, and later layers.
Receptive fields grow with depth: \(5 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 14 \rightarrow
16\) in our LeNet. Stacked local layers cover more of the frame at each stage. Like the MLP layers of Chapter 3, they compose features, now with local connectivity and spatial sharing.
The verdict: on the reused test set, one seed puts clean accuracy at 82.2% for the MLP and 82.5% for LeNet, a gap too small to rank them. Under the predeclared two-pixel shift, the same models score 41.8% and 62.3%. Under this training recipe, LeNet achieves higher accuracy on the shifted images with fewer parameters. The comparison is between two complete models, so it isolates no single architectural constraint.

Most of LeNet’s parameters remain in its dense head, and its accuracy still declines under image shifts. The next chapter examines smaller classifier heads, deeper convolutional networks, and the training choices needed to compare them.

title: 10  Modern CNNs and Transfer Learning
text:
10.1 Why \(5 \times 5\)? Stack small kernels instead
Chapter 9 built a modern version of LeNet, one of the first practical convolutional networks, and tested its response to image shifts. The model reaches 82.5% clean test accuracy with 61,706 parameters, but 96% of those parameters belong to its dense head, and a two-pixel shift lowers its test accuracy to 62.3%. The architectures that followed, mostly between 2012 and 2017, kept LeNet’s ingredients (local kernels, channels, pooling) and arranged them better. We take them in an order in which each design fixes a problem that the previous one exposes, and we examine how kernel size, channel mixing, normalization, and residual connections change the cost and trainability of a convolutional network, and then which features can be reused on another task.
The networks of those years are many. Four design questions organize their mechanisms:
Each question has a representative answer: VGG for the first, ResNet for the second, the \(1\times1\) convolutions and global pooling of NiN for the third, and the habit of building in blocks for the fourth. We test each answer on our own data, and then test what transfers when we reuse a pretrained backbone.
Read each row from left to right: first the operators inside the block, then how often the block repeats, then the head.
Both trainers follow Listing 4.1, with one change: the inner loop (train_existing) accepts a model and optimizer that already exist, because we will train models we did not just construct: fresh heads on frozen trunks, and selectively thawed layers at their own learning rates.
The 600 held-out images are the book’s fixed benchmark of Chapter 6; the code keeps the familiar X_te name for them.
The recipe has two small novelties, both because these networks contain batch normalization: model.train() before each step and model.eval() before each evaluation. Batch normalization uses different statistics in each mode.
VGG (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014) answers with a design move: build larger receptive fields by stacking \(3 \times 3\) kernels until the field is as wide as needed. Recall from Chapter 9 that stacking grows the receptive field. Two stacked \(3 \times 3\) convolutions give the second layer a \(5 \times 5\) window on the input, the same receptive field as one \(5 \times 5\) kernel. But the parameter counts differ for a layer with \(C\) channels in and \(C\) out:
\[
\underbrace{25\,C^2}_{\text{one } 5\times5}
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
\underbrace{2 \times 9\,C^2 = 18\,C^2}_{\text{two } 3\times3\text{s}},
\]
a 28% saving. The stacked pair also fires a ReLU twice where the big kernel fires once. The pair has the same receptive field and fewer parameters. Three \(3\times3\)s reach a \(7\times7\) field for \(27C^2\) against \(49C^2\): the saving grows with depth.
The \(18C^2 < 25C^2\) arithmetic assumes the channel width stays \(C\) through the stack. When a layer grows channels (as LeNet’s \(6 \rightarrow 16\) did), splitting it into two growing \(3\times3\)s can cost more parameters than the single layer. VGG’s design sidesteps this by keeping width constant inside each block and changing it only between blocks, which is the shape our code takes. (Exercise 1 asks for the break-even point.)

text:
10.2 Batch normalization
Before we stack deeper, we need the tool Chapter 9 deferred. To show the problem it addresses, we measure how the scale of activations changes as a signal crosses twelve freshly initialized \(3\times3\) conv layers:



Define the reusable stack12 helper.
Fix a seed, take 256 garments as x, build plain_stack and bn_stack, and list their conv layers.
Activation scale through 12 conv layers, with and without BN.
Pass x through both stacks and print the activation std after every other conv layer.



# [1]
def stack12(with_bn: bool, ch: int = 16) -> nn.Sequential:
    layers = [nn.Conv2d(1, ch, 3, padding=1)]
    for _ in range(11):
        if with_bn:
            layers.append(nn.BatchNorm2d(ch))
        layers += [nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1)]
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)

# [2]
torch.manual_seed(0)
x = X_tr[:256]
plain_stack = stack12(False)
bn_stack = stack12(True)
plain_convs = [m for m in plain_stack if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d)]
bn_convs = [m for m in bn_stack if isinstance(m, nn.Conv2d)]
# [3]
for source, target in zip(plain_convs, bn_convs):
    target.load_state_dict(source.state_dict())       # identical convolution weights

# [4]
for tag, network in [("without BN", plain_stack), ("with BN   ", bn_stack)]:
    h, stds = x, []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for layer in network:
            h = layer(h)
            if isinstance(layer, nn.Conv2d):
                stds.append(h.std().item())
    print(f"{tag} layer stds: " + "  ".join(f"{s:.3f}" for s in stds[::2]))

without BN layer stds: 0.344  0.059  0.043  0.046  0.049  0.061
with BN    layer stds: 0.344  0.404  0.395  0.385  0.432  0.384



Without normalization the signal’s spread collapses by an order of magnitude within a few layers and never recovers. Forward activation scales and backward gradients are different quantities, but the stack’s weights and nonlinearities shape both. Poorly scaled activations are therefore a warning to inspect the gradient flow directly, as we do below.
Batch normalization (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) re-standardizes at every layer. For each channel of an NCHW tensor, BatchNorm2d computes the mean and variance across the current minibatch and both spatial axes (\(N\), \(H\), and \(W\)), normalizes the activations, then applies a learned scale and shift through two parameters:
\[
\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_{\text{batch}}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{batch}} + \epsilon}},
\qquad
y = \gamma\,\hat{x} + \beta .
\tag{10.1}\]
Here \(\epsilon\) is a small constant that keeps the denominator nonzero. The output is not constrained to remain at zero mean and unit variance: \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) control its scale and shift, while each layer starts from standardized activations. In the printout above, the BN row holds a near-constant spread at every printed depth: the signal reaches each layer at a usable scale from the first step. The standard placement we adopt is conv \(\rightarrow\) BN \(\rightarrow\) ReLU, with bias=False on the convolution, since \(\beta\) already provides the shift.

WarningBN uses different statistics in training and evaluation



At training time BN normalizes by the current batch’s statistics. At evaluation time, the models here use stored running averages collected during training, including when they process one image at a time. model.train() and model.eval() switch between the two. Forgetting the switch is a common BN error: a prediction made in train mode depends on the other images in the batch, and a network trained in eval mode never updates its running statistics. Our train_model recipe flips the switch in both directions; look for it. It follows that BN needs real batches to estimate statistics, so it gets unreliable at tiny batch sizes.








NoteNormalize across what?



Batch statistics are one choice among several. When we build transformers (Chapter 16), batches of variable-length sequences will make per-batch statistics awkward, and the same standardize-then-rescale idea will reappear computed per token instead: layer normalization, which applies Equation 10.1 along a different axis.

title: 10  Modern CNNs and Transfer Learning
section: 10.3 Building with blocks: a small VGG
text:
10.3 Building with blocks: a small VGG
Now combine the small stacked kernels of the first section with reusable blocks. Define the atom (conv, BN, ReLU) once. A block stacks atoms and pools, and a network stacks blocks. This is the point about VGG versus its hand-tuned predecessors: one block is designed once and repeated.



Define the reusable helpers: atom and VGGSmall.
VGGSmall: two blocks of stacked 3×3 atoms.
Print total and head parameter counts for VGGSmall, the head’s share, and test accuracy.



# [1]
def atom(c_in: int, c_out: int) -> list[nn.Module]:
    return [nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU()]

class VGGSmall(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            *atom(1, 16), *atom(16, 16), nn.MaxPool2d(2),    # -> (16, 14, 14)
            *atom(16, 32), *atom(32, 32), nn.MaxPool2d(2),   # -> (32, 7, 7)
        )
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(),
                                  nn.Linear(32 * 7 * 7, 128), nn.ReLU(),
                                  nn.Linear(128, 10))
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.features(x))

# [2]
vgg = train_model(VGGSmall, epochs=60)
n_head = count(vgg.head)
# [3]
print(f"VGGSmall: {count(vgg):,} parameters ({n_head:,} in the head, "
      f"{n_head / count(vgg):.0%})")
print(f"test accuracy {accuracy(vgg, X_te, y_te):.1%}")

VGGSmall: 218,586 parameters (202,122 in the head, 92%)
test accuracy 86.7%



This VGG-style model illustrates both a gain and a remaining bottleneck. It reaches 86.7%, four points above LeNet in this run, though changing depth, width, normalization, kernel size, parameter count, and training duration together prevents isolating which ingredient drove the improvement. At the same time, it carries 218,586 parameters, three and a half times LeNet’s total, and the dense head on the flattened grid still accounts for 92% of them. Keeping the convolutional kernels small did not keep the network small. That raises the question of the classifier head: how can we reduce its parameters?

section: 10.4 \(1 \times 1\) convolutions and a smaller classifier head
text:
10.4 \(1 \times 1\) convolutions and a smaller classifier head
Most parameters sit in nn.Linear(1568, 128). We will replace that flattened head with global averaging. First, a convolution whose kernel is \(1 \times 1\) mixes channels before pooling without combining neighboring spatial positions.
The window of a \(1 \times 1\) kernel is a single pixel. Across channels, however, it computes Equation 9.1: at each position, take the \(C_{\text{in}}\) channel values and form \(C_{\text{out}}\) weighted combinations plus bias. At each spatial position, the same learned affine map transforms the channel vector. A following ReLU makes this a nonlinear transformation of the features at that position. The spatial grid is unchanged, while \(C_{\text{out}}\) determines the new channel width. The kernel uses \(C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}\) weights, against the \(k^2C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}\) weights of a \(k\times k\) spatial kernel.

      The channel values and weights drawn here are illustrative: the chapter's network learns its own weights, and only the shapes and the counts are NINSmall's.
      Scope and caveats
        The shapes are NINSmall's. Its first block, nin_block(1, 16), turns a 28 × 28 garment into 16 maps with a 3 × 3 convolution, batch normalization and ReLU, then runs nn.Conv2d(16, 16, 1) and a ReLU twice. The chapter trains those weights and prints none of them, so the two columns, the weights and the biases here are made up, in halves between −1 and 2, and every output is computed from them exactly.
        The identity is exact, not a metaphor. nn.Conv2d(C_in, C_out, 1) holds a weight tensor of shape Cout × Cin × 1 × 1, and at every pixel it computes what nn.Linear(C_in, C_out) computes on that pixel's channel vector: one set of weights, shared by all 784 pixels. Its bill, Cout × Cin + Cout, never mentions the map's height or width.
        Chapter 9's hand-built corner kernel summed both edge channels over a 5 × 5 window. A 1 × 1 layer keeps that cross-talk between channels and drops the neighbourhood; finding spatial patterns stays with the 3 × 3 before it. The same count is where the Inception bottleneck later in this chapter gets its savings: a 1 × 1 squeezes the channels before an expensive 5 × 5 reads them.
        In the weight grid a filled square is a positive weight and a hollow one a negative weight, its area proportional to the size; an open ring is an output of exactly zero after the ReLU. The skewer and the dial are neutral ink: how many output channels to make is a design choice, not a learned parameter.
      
    
    Check yourself. A sequence carries 256 numbers at every time step. How many parameters does nn.Conv1d(256, 32, kernel_size=1) hold, and what does it do at each step?
      8,224: a 32 × 256 weight matrix and 32 biases, whatever the length of the sequence. At every time step it applies the same nn.Linear(256, 32) to that step's 256 numbers. It is the Inception box's 256 channels squeezed to 32, run along time instead of across an image, and it is how Chapter 16's position-wise feedforward network treats every token.
    
    Transcript and keyboard help
      
        One pixel, one channel. A 1 by 1 kernel sits on a single pixel of a 28 by 28 map. With one channel, all it can do is scale that pixel and add a bias: nearly a no-op.
        Sixteen deep. The map has 16 channels, so under the pixel lies a column of 16 numbers, one per channel. The column is lifted out and laid flat.
        Predict. Sixteen numbers in, sixteen out. How many weights does the layer need, and does every pixel get weights of its own?
        One pixel, one linear layer. The weights appear: a grid W of 16 rows and 16 columns, and 16 biases. Each row mixes all 16 channel values into one output, a ReLU turns the negative ones into zero, and the 16 outputs are written into the output at the same pixel.
        Another pixel. The skewer moves along the row. A different column passes through the very same W and is written at its own pixel. The layer holds 16 times 16 plus 16, 272 parameters, and every pixel shares them.
        Every pixel. The skewer visits all 784 pixels with the same W. The output is 16 by 28 by 28: height and width pass through untouched.
        Depth is a choice. The number of output channels sets how many rows W has: 4 channels squeeze the depth for 68 parameters, 32 expand it for 544. The map stays 28 by 28.
        A 1 by 1 convolution is one linear layer across channels, run with the same weights at every pixel. The dial tries another output depth.
      
      Silent; paused initially; 1.5× playback. Focus the animation pane: Space or K plays/pauses, arrows seek between beats, Home/End jump, Escape pauses. The scrubber and speed menu also work by keyboard. The output-channel dial pauses playback and redraws the whole picture for the depth you choose; playing or scrubbing returns to the timeline. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat's finished state instead of moving between them.
    
  


The Network-in-Network design (Lin et al., 2013) combines this tool with a global-averaging head. A NiN block is one \(3\times3\) (some spatial mixing) followed by two \(1\times1\)s (per-pixel channel mixing). And the classifier becomes:

Let the last block produce a stack of feature maps.
Global average pooling (GAP): average each map over all positions: 64 maps in, 64 numbers out. No parameters at all.
One small linear layer to the logits.




Define the reusable helpers: nin_block and NINSmall.
Fix a seed, build NINSmall, and give it an Adam optimizer nin_opt at learning rate 1e-3.
NINSmall: architecture and first 75 epochs.



# [1]
def nin_block(c_in: int, c_out: int) -> list[nn.Module]:
    return [nn.Conv2d(c_in, c_out, 3, padding=1, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(c_out), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(c_out, c_out, 1), nn.ReLU()]

class NINSmall(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            *nin_block(1, 16), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            *nin_block(16, 32), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            *nin_block(32, 64),
        )
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(),
                                  nn.Linear(64, 10))
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.features(x))

# [2]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
nin = NINSmall()
nin_opt = torch.optim.Adam(nin.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
# [3]
nin = train_existing(nin, nin_opt, epochs=75)





NINSmall: continue the same optimizer through epoch 150.
Print the total and head parameter counts of NINSmall and its test accuracy.



# [1]
nin = train_existing(nin, nin_opt, epochs=75)
# [2]
print(f"NINSmall: {count(nin):,} parameters "
      f"(head: {count(nin.head):,})")
print(f"test accuracy {accuracy(nin, X_te, y_te):.1%}")

NINSmall: 35,034 parameters (head: 650)
test accuracy 76.2%



NINSmall has 35,034 parameters, six times fewer than VGGSmall, and a 650-parameter head. The accuracy is 76.2%, and we examine that dip after returning to image shifts. Chapter 9 showed that LeNet’s shift tolerance is incomplete. A flatten head assigns separate weights to separate spatial positions. GAP removes that position-specific parameterization by averaging each feature map before classification. This gives a reason to test shift tolerance, although comparing LeNet with NINSmall does not isolate the effect of the head. The shift test of Chapter 9 runs a third time:



Define the reusable helpers: LeNet and shift_right.
Shift curves, flatten head vs GAP head.
Print per-shift test accuracy for LeNet and NINSmall; plot both curves with a dotted line at 0.1.



# [1]
class LeNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, 5, padding=2)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, 5)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(400, 120)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(120, 84)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(84, 10)
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), 2)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)
        x = x.flatten(1)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        return self.fc3(x)

# [2]
lenet = train_model(LeNet, epochs=150)          # Chapter 9's model, same recipe

def shift_right(X: torch.Tensor, px: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    if px == 0:
        return X.clone()
    out = torch.zeros_like(X)
    out[..., px:] = X[..., :-px]
    return out

shifts = list(range(5))
acc_lenet = [accuracy(lenet, shift_right(X_te, s), y_te) for s in shifts]
acc_nin = [accuracy(nin, shift_right(X_te, s), y_te) for s in shifts]
# [3]
for s in shifts:
    print(f"shift {s}px:   LeNet {acc_lenet[s]:.1%}   NIN+GAP {acc_nin[s]:.1%}")

plt.figure(figsize=(5.5, 3.2))
plt.plot(
    shifts, acc_lenet, "s-", color="#232D4B", lw=2, ms=7,
    label="LeNet (flatten head)",
)
plt.plot(
    shifts, acc_nin, "^-", color="#E57200", lw=2, ms=7,
    label="NINSmall (GAP head)",
)
plt.axhline(0.1, ls=":", color="#B8B8A8")
plt.xlabel("shift (pixels right)"); plt.ylabel("test accuracy")
plt.ylim(0, 0.9); plt.xticks(shifts); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

shift 0px:   LeNet 82.5%   NIN+GAP 76.2%
shift 1px:   LeNet 74.8%   NIN+GAP 70.3%
shift 2px:   LeNet 62.3%   NIN+GAP 69.3%
shift 3px:   LeNet 45.3%   NIN+GAP 67.5%
shift 4px:   LeNet 26.8%   NIN+GAP 66.5%








Figure 10.2: The shift experiment of Chapter 9, run a third time. LeNet’s accuracy still falls below 30% by four pixels of shift, while NINSmall, with its global-average-pooling head, declines gently. The two networks also differ in their trunks, so the curves do not isolate the effect of GAP. GAP removes position-specific weights from the head, but padding, stride, pooling, and content clipped at the image edge keep the complete network from being exactly shift-invariant.






LeNet’s curve falls from 82% to 27%, while NINSmall’s is a gentle slope from 76% to 67%. Position-specific weights are gone from NINSmall’s head, and the result is consistent with the flatten-head diagnosis. It is not a matched-head ablation: the trunks differ too. The complete CNN is only approximately shift-tolerant. Boundaries, strides, and pooling can still change its features.
On clean, centered test garments NINSmall scores six points below LeNet. That result is consistent with the warning in Chapter 9: on centered data, position can carry information, and a GAP head cannot assign separate weights to separate locations. But GAP is not the only changed ingredient, so this run does not prove it caused the gap. At our scale the comparison exposes a hypothesis worth testing with a matched-head ablation: shift tolerance may cost positional information.






NoteAnother reusable block: Inception



GoogLeNet’s Inception block (2014) answers “which kernel size?” with “all of them”: parallel \(1\times1\), \(3\times3\), \(5\times5\), and pooling branches, concatenated. Its cost is kept low by the \(1\times1\) bottleneck, which compresses channels before the expensive spatial kernels. Take one \(5\times5\) branch that maps 256 input channels to 128 output channels. Applied directly, it holds \(5^2 \times 256 \times 128 \approx 819\)k parameters. With a \(1\times1\) squeeze to 32 channels first, it holds \(256 \times 32 + 5^2 \times 32 \times 128 \approx 111\)k, an 86% reduction in weights, with the same input and output channel counts and the same nominal spatial receptive field. We will not build Inception here. The part that transfers to other designs is its principle of compressing channels before the expensive spatial kernels. Exercise 2 works through the arithmetic.

title: 10  Modern CNNs and Transfer Learning
text:
10.5 Training deeper networks
VGG’s design favors depth. We stack twenty of our two-conv blocks (with BN, per the recipe, on a \(14\times14\) grid so the experiment fits a laptop) and compare the result against the identical stack with one change: residual connections.
Predict before running. Two networks have identical parameter counts and twenty blocks each. One is plain, one residual. How do the two networks differ in their fit to the training set under the same budget?



Define the reusable helpers: Block and DeepNet.
Train the plain 20-block network.
Print the plain network’s train and test accuracy.



# [1]
class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ch: int, residual: bool):
        super().__init__()
        self.c1 = nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.b1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(ch)
        self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.b2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(ch)
        self.residual = residual
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        y = self.b2(self.c2(F.relu(self.b1(self.c1(x)))))
        return F.relu(y + x) if self.residual else F.relu(y)

class DeepNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, nblocks: int, residual: bool, ch: int = 12):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Conv2d(1, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2)                       # 28 -> 14 early
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(*[Block(ch, residual)
                                      for _ in range(nblocks)])
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(),
                                  nn.Linear(ch, 10))
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.blocks(self.pool(F.relu(self.stem(x)))))

# [2]
plain = train_model(lambda: DeepNet(20, residual=False), epochs=30)
# [3]
print(f"plain-20     train {accuracy(plain, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}   "
      f"test {accuracy(plain, X_te, y_te):.1%}")

plain-20     train 60.8%   test 51.0%






Train the matched residual 20-block network.
Print the residual network’s train and test accuracy.



# [1]
resid = train_model(lambda: DeepNet(20, residual=True), epochs=30)
# [2]
print(f"residual-20  train {accuracy(resid, X_tr, y_tr):.1%}   "
      f"test {accuracy(resid, X_te, y_te):.1%}")

residual-20  train 100.0%   test 77.8%



Look at the training column first. The plain 40-conv-layer network did not fit the 1,200 images it trains on within the 30-epoch training budget: 61% train accuracy, while its residual twin memorizes them and generalizes twenty-seven points better. This is an optimization failure in the same family as the degradation problem that He et al. reported in 2015: their 56-layer plain network fitted its training set worse than their 20-layer one. The result is surprising, because the deeper network contains the shallower one. If its 36 extra layers computed the identity map, it would fit exactly as well, so a fit at least as good as the shallow network’s exists. Gradient descent fails to find one, because even the identity map is hard to learn through a stack of convolutions and ReLUs. Both of our networks use BatchNorm, so their activations start well scaled, and the plain network’s failure has another cause. Our experiment isolates the effect of the residual connection at one depth. A strict demonstration that adding depth degrades a plain network would also require a shallower plain control.
A residual connection adds the block input to the learned branch before applying the final ReLU. Writing \(u=x+F(x)\) for this pre-activation sum, the implemented block returns \(\operatorname{ReLU}(u)\). Figure 10.3 shows both operations. The sum \(x + F(x)\) needs \(x\) and \(F(x)\) of the same shape. Our blocks keep 12 channels and the grid size, so Block needs only the identity route. When a block changes the number of channels, or halves the grid with a stride, ResNets commonly put a \(1\times1\) convolution on the shortcut, with stride 2 like the branch’s first convolution, to match the shapes (He et al.). This projection shortcut costs \(C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}\) weights: the \(1\times1\) convolution of NiN reappears as a shape adapter. With the identity route, differentiating through the sum gives
\[
u = F(x) + x
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\partial \loss}{\partial x}
= \frac{\partial \loss}{\partial u}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + I\right).
\tag{10.2}\]








Figure 10.3: A residual block in the original ResNet form, which Block implements. The identity stream carries \(x\) straight to the sum. The learned branch adds a correction \(F(x)\), so \(u=x+F(x)\), and a ReLU follows. The sum has no weights, so the shortcut is a direct route for activations and gradients wherever \(u\) is positive. Pre-activation ResNets move that ReLU into the branch and leave the route clean.








  
  Watch the mechanism: the shortcut adds a lane; it does not guarantee a gradient
  
    A block's learned branch has local slope −0.9, and the shortcut adds the identity. How much of a gradient of 1 arriving at the sum H(x) reaches the block's input: all of it, 1.9, or 0.1?
    The residual block, run backward in one dimension: follow one gradient as it splits at the sum and returns to x along both routes.
    
      
        
          The shortcut adds a lane, not a guarantee
          
          xH(x)Fslope −0.9identity lanelearned branch1 along the lane−0.9 through F0.1 reaches x
          
          
          xH(x)Fslope −0.9identity lanelearned branch1 along the lane−0.9 through F0.1 reaches x
          
        
      
      
        
          
          
          −101
        
        slope −0.90
      
      \( \displaystyle \residualpart{\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}} = \residualpart{\frac{\partial L}{\partial H}}\left(\class{il-branch}{\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}} + \class{il-lane}{I}\right) \)
      The shortcut guarantees a route, not a gradient: the learned branch can still cancel it.
      
  
    
    
    
    Play
  
  Playback position
  0:00 / 0:40
  0.5×1×1.5×2×
  
    
    
    Fullscreen
  



    
    
    The calculation is readable without playback. Opening this panel loads the optional controls.
    
      One number stands in for each Jacobian here; with matrices the learned term can also rotate the identity term, which a single dimension cannot show.
      Scope and caveats
        The block and its numbers are a declared toy in one dimension, where the identity I is 1 and the learned branch's Jacobian is a single number, its local slope: 0.5, then 0, then −0.9 on the timeline, with the dial running from −1 to 1. The chapter measures gradients at the stem of whole networks and prints no Jacobian of its own.
        The chapter's block applies a ReLU after the sum and returns ReLU(H(x)), where H(x) = x + F(x) is the sum itself; the chapter's ∂L/∂H already includes that ReLU's derivative. This picture leaves the ReLU out, as if it were active (H(x) positive, slope 1), so the gradient at the output is the gradient at the sum. Where H(x) is negative, the ReLU passes no gradient to either route.
        A stack multiplies these per-block factors, each 1 plus its own slope, so many blocks keep a gradient near its size only while their learned slopes stay small. The chapter's measurement, residual gradients within one order of magnitude across its depths, is of whole networks, not of any one factor drawn here.
        Each copy of the gradient is an arrow whose length is its value on one shared scale and whose direction is its sign: a positive copy points along its route toward x, a negative one points back toward the output, and an open ring is a copy of exactly 0. Wine is the gradient and its copies, orange the learned branch's weights (the outline of F), ink the identity lane, the sum, the slope and the dial, and blue the input x and the output H(x).
        The chapter's figure and this panel both draw the identity lane in ink; orange stays with the learned weights. The slope is the branch's local derivative, not a weight, so its dial wears ink as well.
      
    
    Check yourself. Two residual blocks in a row have learned slopes 0.5 and then −0.5. What reaches the first block's input from a gradient of 1 at the output, and what would the same blocks pass without shortcuts?
      0.75. Each block multiplies what arrives by 1 plus its own slope: 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75. Without shortcuts each block passes only its slope: 0.5 × (−0.5) = −0.25, a quarter of the gradient with its sign flipped.
    
    Transcript and keyboard help
      
        One residual block, laid left to right. The input x feeds two routes: the learned branch F, whose local slope is 0.5, and the identity lane, which arcs over F. The two meet at the sum, and the sum is the output H of x.
        A gradient of 1 arrives at the output H of x and reaches the sum, where it splits into two copies of 1: one waits at the entrance of the identity lane, the other at the entrance of F.
        Both copies travel back to x. The lane's copy arrives unchanged, still 1; the copy that crosses F is multiplied by its slope and shrinks to 0.5. Under x the two are laid head to tail on a short scale, and together they measure 1.5.
        The slope glides to 0: F is doing nothing, F = 0. Its copy shrinks to an open ring, and exactly the 1 that the lane carries is left at x.
        Predict. The learned slope is now −0.9, and a gradient of 1 sits at the output again. How much of it reaches x: all of it, 1.9, or 0.1?
        The gradient splits again. The copy that crosses F flips to point back toward the output and shrinks to −0.9. Laid head to tail with the lane's 1, it cancels most of it, and only 0.1 is left under x.
        The slope sweeps from −0.9 up to 0.5, then down to −1, where it rests. What x receives is always the lane's 1 plus the slope: 1.5 at slope 0.5, 0 at slope −1.
        The slope returns to −0.9. The shortcut guarantees the gradient a route, not a size: the learned branch can still amplify it or cancel most of it. The slope dial tries any other slope.
      
      Silent; paused initially; 1.5× playback. Focus the animation pane: Space or K plays/pauses, arrows seek between beats, Home/End jump, Escape pauses. The scrubber and speed menu also work by keyboard. The slope dial pauses playback and redraws the whole picture for the slope you choose; playing or scrubbing returns to the timeline. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat's finished state instead of moving between them.
    
  



Here \(\loss\) is the training loss, \(I\) is the identity, and \(\partial \loss/\partial u\) already includes the derivative of the final ReLU. The identity term provides an additive gradient contribution that is not multiplied by the learned branch’s weights. The full gradient still depends on the ReLU’s derivative and the branch Jacobian, which can amplify, attenuate, or partly cancel that contribution. The block only needs to learn the residual, a correction to the identity map. A zero correction is represented by \(F = 0\).
We next measure how the stem gradient changes with depth at initialization. We extend the depth experiment of Chapter 5 from dense layers to conv stacks:



Define the reusable helpers: PlainNoBN and stem_grad.
Run stem_grad on plain no-BN, plain + BN, and residual + BN nets at 4, 12, and 24 blocks.
Gradient at the stem vs. depth, three designs.



# [1]
class PlainNoBN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, nconvs: int, ch: int = 12):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem = nn.Conv2d(1, ch, 3, padding=1)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2)
        self.layers = nn.Sequential(*[m for _ in range(nconvs)
                                      for m in (nn.Conv2d(ch, ch, 3, padding=1),
                                                nn.ReLU())])
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(),
                                  nn.Linear(ch, 10))
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.layers(self.pool(F.relu(self.stem(x)))))

def stem_grad(
    make_net: Callable[[], nn.Module],
) -> tuple[float, float, int, int]:
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = make_net()
    F.cross_entropy(net(X_tr[:128]), y_tr[:128]).backward()
    grad = net.stem.weight.grad
    return (grad.double().norm().item(), grad.abs().max().item(),
            torch.count_nonzero(grad).item(), grad.numel())

# [2]
depths = [4, 12, 24]                                  # blocks (2 convs each)
diagnostics = {
    "plain, no BN": [stem_grad(lambda d=d: PlainNoBN(2 * d)) for d in depths],
    "plain + BN": [stem_grad(lambda d=d: DeepNet(d, False)) for d in depths],
    "residual + BN": [stem_grad(lambda d=d: DeepNet(d, True)) for d in depths],
}
curves = {name: [row[0] for row in rows]
          for name, rows in diagnostics.items()}
# [3]
for name, ys in curves.items():
    print(f"{name:14s}: " + "   ".join(f"{v:.1e}" for v in ys))
norm64, maxabs, nonzero, total = diagnostics["plain, no BN"][-1]
print(
    f"48-layer no-BN check: max |component| {maxabs:.1e}; "
    f"nonzero {nonzero}/{total}; float64 norm {norm64:.1e}"
)

plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.4))
for (name, ys), color in zip(curves.items(),
                             ["#B8B8A8", "#E57200", "#232D4B"]):
    xs = [2 * d for d in depths]
    plt.semilogy(xs, ys, "o-", ms=5, color=color, label=name)
plt.xlabel("conv layers")
plt.ylabel(r"$\|\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial W^{(\mathrm{stem})}\|$")
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

plain, no BN  : 9.0e-06   3.3e-13   2.2e-23
plain + BN    : 7.6e-02   5.0e-01   8.3e+01
residual + BN : 1.6e-01   4.9e-01   5.0e-01
48-layer no-BN check: max |component| 5.2e-24; nonzero 108/108; float64 norm 2.2e-23








Figure 10.4: Gradient magnitude reaching the stem (first layer) at initialization, versus depth, for three designs. In the 48-layer no-BN stack, the norm computed in float64 is 2.2e-23. A float32 norm calculation reports zero because squaring these nonzero components underflows. In this initialization check, the plain BN stack’s stem gradient grows with depth, while the residual stack’s stays within one order of magnitude across these depths.






The final no-BN row also exposes a numerical trap: its components remain nonzero, but squaring them in float32 can underflow before the norm is summed. The range, resolution, and accumulator roles behind that distinction are gathered in Appendix C.






NoteArchitecture bridge (optional): DenseNet concatenates the history



A residual connection combines an incoming representation with a learned correction by addition: \(x_{\ell+1}=x_\ell+F_\ell(x_\ell)\), and the block above applies a ReLU after that sum. A DenseNet block makes a different connectivity choice. If \(x_j\) denotes layer \(j\)’s output feature map, layer \(\ell\) receives the channel-wise concatenation \([x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{\ell-1}]\) and contributes a small new group of feature maps for later layers. Earlier features therefore remain directly available instead of being recreated, while the channel axis grows. Transition layers compress channels and downsample between dense blocks. The defining operation, in the tensor vocabulary of Appendix B, is concatenation along the feature-channel axis, a different operation from residual addition.








TipResidual streams beyond CNNs



Residual connections reach well beyond CNNs, and they became a central design device in many deep architectures. When we assemble a transformer in Chapter 16, every attention layer and every feedforward layer will be wrapped as \(x + F(x)\), and the freshly met layer normalization will sit beside each skip. The picture to carry forward is a residual stream with direct additive routes through the network, each block reading from it and writing a correction back. Those routes improve conditioning without making the stream immune to learned-branch interactions. Attention will be one kind of correction. You now own both parts of that skeleton.

section: 10.6 Four architectures on the full data
text:
10.6 Four architectures on the full data
The small-data studies isolated mechanisms. To compare architectures, we use the full task: we split all 60,000 Fashion-MNIST training images once into 50,000 for fitting and 10,000 for validation, and we open the official 10,000-image test set only after selecting the checkpoint on the validation split. We ran LeNet, NiN, VGG, and a nine-block residual network for three end-to-end seeds each, all under one training recipe. These are full-data variants, wider than the networks built above: a LeNet with 16 and 32 channels (202,738 parameters); a NiN of three blocks with 48, 64 and 96 channels (76,698); a VGG of three blocks of two convolutions with 32, 64 and 128 channels and a global-average-pooling head (288,170); and a residual network of nine blocks with 32, 64 and 128 channels (1,084,010).



Load the 12 pinned full-data run records.
Summarize test accuracy and parameter count by architecture.



# [1]
import json
from pathlib import Path

scorecard_root = Path("../../experiments/rivanna/results/scorecard")
scorecard_records = [
    json.loads(path.read_text()) for path in sorted(scorecard_root.glob("*.json"))
]
scorecard_order = ["lenet", "nin", "vgg", "resnet"]
scorecard_colors = ["#B8B8A8", "#232D4B", "#E57200", "#5379AA"]

# [2]
scorecard = {}
for model_name in scorecard_order:
    rows = [row for row in scorecard_records if row["model"] == model_name]
    accuracies = torch.tensor([row["test_accuracy"] for row in rows])
    scorecard[model_name] = {
        "parameters": rows[0]["parameter_count"],
        "mean": accuracies.mean().item(),
        "sd": accuracies.std(unbiased=True).item(),
    }










Figure 10.5: Full-data Part II accuracy against parameters. Points show mean official-test accuracy and bars one sample standard deviation across three seeds. LeNet reaches 92.52%, NiN 92.78%, VGG 93.73%, and the residual network 94.20%. NiN is the most parameter-efficient point, VGG attains higher accuracy with a larger parameter count, and residual blocks reach the strongest endpoint in this declared training regime. Parameter count measures storage and says little about training compute, and the four points rank these architectures only under this recipe.





The full-data training recipe changes the comparison from the 1,200-image mechanism studies. NiN no longer scores below LeNet in clean accuracy, and all four architectures exceed 92%. The residual network has the highest mean accuracy under this declared recipe, but the plot still has one horizontal axis too few: parameters measure storage, and the plot shows neither optimizer steps, activation memory, nor total training work.

title: 10  Modern CNNs and Transfer Learning
section: 10.7 Transfer learning: mechanics and a shoe experiment
text:
10.7 Transfer learning: mechanics and a shoe experiment
Everything so far trains from scratch. Common practice often does not: most image features are shared (edges, textures, parts transfer across tasks), so we train one strong backbone once, on a large dataset, and reuse it for many tasks. We consider two adaptation settings:

Linear probe: freeze the pretrained trunk entirely (requires_grad = False), extract its features, train only a new linear head on your labels. The frozen backbone also runs in evaluation mode, so BatchNorm uses its stored statistics.
Partial fine-tuning: additionally unfreeze the last block or two, training them, usually at a much smaller learning rate than the fresh head, to limit changes to the pretrained representation.

Under a linear probe, the frozen trunk turns each image \(x\) into a vector of features \(h(x)\), a representation (or embedding) of the image, and the probe tests whether the target labels can be read from that vector by a linear model. Whatever the trunk learned in pretraining reaches the new task only through \(h(x)\). Chapter 11, the interlude that follows, builds such representations without labels, by training a network to compress its input and reconstruct it.
Our test case is a shoe task: classify the three shoe classes (sandal, sneaker, ankle boot) from ten labeled examples each. The 30-image regime is where transfer is expected to help most: a small labeled set may be insufficient to learn useful features, which makes pretrained features a plausible advantage. We compare three contenders:

From scratch, our VGG-style trunk trains on the 30 images alone.
Our own pretrained trunk is the same trunk pretrained on the seven non-shoe classes (863 images), then frozen under a linear probe.
An ImageNet-pretrained backbone is SqueezeNet 1.1 trained on ImageNet (1.2 million photographs, 1,000 classes), loaded from weights committed with this book, frozen, and read by a linear probe on its 512-dimensional features. (We upsample the Fashion images to \(96 \times 96\) and repeat them across three channels to fit its expectations. That awkwardness is part of the experiment.)

Rank the three contenders before you run them, and state whether you expect the ImageNet probe to improve on training from scratch.



Pick out the shoe test images, relabeled 0 to 2, and the non-shoe training images, relabeled 0 to 6.
Define the Trunk network.
Implement the shoe task, our own trunk, and the frozen probes.
Print own-trunk source-task accuracy; load and freeze ImageNet SqueezeNet, wrapped as squeeze_features.
Define the reusable helpers: own_features and linear_probe.



from torchvision.models import squeezenet1_1

# [1]
shoe = torch.tensor([5, 7, 9])
new_label = {5: 0, 7: 1, 9: 2}
is_shoe_tr = (y_tr[:, None] == shoe).any(1)
is_shoe_te = (y_te[:, None] == shoe).any(1)
X_shoe_te = X_te[is_shoe_te]
y_shoe_te = torch.tensor([new_label[int(c)] for c in y_te[is_shoe_te]])

# our own trunk: pretrain on the 7 non-shoe classes
src = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8]
remap = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(src)}
X_src = X_tr[~is_shoe_tr]
y_src = torch.tensor([remap[int(c)] for c in y_tr[~is_shoe_tr]])

# [2]
class Trunk(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_classes: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            *atom(1, 16), *atom(16, 16), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            *atom(16, 32), *atom(32, 32), nn.MaxPool2d(2), *atom(32, 64))
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1), nn.Flatten(),
                                  nn.Linear(64, n_classes))
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        return self.head(self.features(x))

# [3]
own_trunk = train_model(lambda: Trunk(7), epochs=100, data=(X_src, y_src))
X_src_te = X_te[~is_shoe_te]
y_src_te = torch.tensor([remap[int(c)] for c in y_te[~is_shoe_te]])
# [4]
print(f"own trunk, source task (7 classes): "
      f"{accuracy(own_trunk, X_src_te, y_src_te):.1%}")

# the real thing: ImageNet SqueezeNet, from committed weights (no download)
sq = squeezenet1_1(weights=None)
sq.load_state_dict(torch.load("../../data/squeezenet1_1-imagenet.pt"))
sq.eval()
for p in sq.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False

IMNET_MEAN = torch.tensor([0.485, 0.456, 0.406]).view(1, 3, 1, 1)
IMNET_STD = torch.tensor([0.229, 0.224, 0.225]).view(1, 3, 1, 1)

@torch.no_grad()
def squeeze_features(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:  # (N,1,28,28) -> (N,512)
    x = X.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1)
    x = F.interpolate(x, size=96, mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)
    f = sq.features((x - IMNET_MEAN) / IMNET_STD)
    return F.adaptive_avg_pool2d(f, 1).flatten(1)

# [5]
@torch.no_grad()
def own_features(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:      # (N,1,28,28) -> (N,64)
    return F.adaptive_avg_pool2d(own_trunk.features(X), 1).flatten(1)

def linear_probe(Z_tr: torch.Tensor, y_f: torch.Tensor,
                 Z_te: torch.Tensor, seed: int) -> float:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    head = nn.Linear(Z_tr.shape[1], 3)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(head.parameters(), lr=1e-2,
                           weight_decay=1e-3)   # built-in L2 penalty (ch. 1's ridge)
    for _ in range(400):
        loss = F.cross_entropy(head(Z_tr), y_f)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return (head(Z_te).argmax(1) == y_shoe_te).float().mean().item()

own trunk, source task (7 classes): 79.7%






Set K = 10, the labeled images per shoe class, and start an empty rows list.
Scratch vs. own trunk vs. ImageNet trunk, three seeds.
Print scratch, own-trunk probe, and ImageNet probe accuracy per seed, then the seed means.



# [1]
K = 10
rows = []
# [2]
for seed in [0, 1, 6050]:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    idx = torch.cat([(y_tr == c).nonzero().squeeze(1)
                     [torch.randperm(int((y_tr == c).sum()))[:K]] for c in shoe])
    X_few = X_tr[idx]
    y_few = torch.tensor([new_label[int(c)] for c in y_tr[idx]])

    scratch = train_model(lambda: Trunk(3), epochs=100, seed=seed,
                          data=(X_few, y_few))
    rows.append((accuracy(scratch, X_shoe_te, y_shoe_te),
                 linear_probe(own_features(X_few), y_few,
                              own_features(X_shoe_te), seed),
                 linear_probe(squeeze_features(X_few), y_few,
                              squeeze_features(X_shoe_te), seed)))

# [3]
print("seed     scratch   own-trunk probe   ImageNet probe")
for seed, r in zip([0, 1, 6050], rows):
    print(f"{seed:4d}     {r[0]:.1%}       {r[1]:.1%}           {r[2]:.1%}")
mean = [sum(c) / 3 for c in zip(*rows)]
print(f"mean     {mean[0]:.1%}       {mean[1]:.1%}           {mean[2]:.1%}")

seed     scratch   own-trunk probe   ImageNet probe
   0     86.4%       68.9%           88.1%
   1     85.3%       65.5%           85.9%
6050     88.1%       77.4%           87.6%
mean     86.6%       70.6%           87.2%



These results do not support the expected advantage of transfer learning in this setting. The scratch model, trained on thirty images, and the ImageNet probe have similar mean accuracy across these three seeds: the means differ by less than a point. And our own pretrained trunk, competent on its source task per the printout above, performs worse than the scratch baseline under this probe-training recipe. There are three possible explanations:

A trunk transfers only the features its pretraining produced. Our own trunk was pretrained on 863 shirts, bags, and trousers. Nothing in that curriculum required foot-shaped detectors, so its 64 features may map sandals, sneakers, and boots to nearly the same point. The accuracies in the printout cannot show this, and a look at the features themselves would test it. In this sense, pretraining is a curriculum.
Domain and resolution gaps reduce what transfers. SqueezeNet’s filters were trained on 224-pixel color photographs, and we feed it 28-pixel grayscale images resized to 96 pixels. Its early layers respond to detail that these images do not contain. (The matching recipe, resize and normalize to match the pretraining pipeline, is consequential. We apply it subject to the limitations of the available data.)
A strong scratch baseline can leave less room for transfer to improve the result. Three shoe silhouettes at \(28 \times 28\) form a small problem: thirty images suffice for a strong scratch baseline, so there is little room for imported knowledge to help. The full ten-class task below is different: 50,000 fitting labels, 224-pixel inputs, and a ResNet-18-sized feature extractor.


Transfer on the full ten-class task
The full task separates three questions: what ImageNet features can do without changing, what the last residual stage can learn when allowed to adapt, and what the architecture learns from scratch with all 50,000 fitting labels.



Load the nine pinned ResNet-18 transfer records.
Summarize official-test accuracy by training regime.



# [1]
transfer_root = Path("../../experiments/rivanna/results/transfer")
transfer_records = [
    json.loads(path.read_text()) for path in sorted(transfer_root.glob("*.json"))
]
transfer_order = ["probe", "finetune", "scratch"]

# [2]
transfer_summary = {}
for regime in transfer_order:
    values = torch.tensor([
        row["test_accuracy"] for row in transfer_records if row["regime"] == regime
    ])
    transfer_summary[regime] = {
        "values": values,
        "mean": values.mean().item(),
        "sd": values.std(unbiased=True).item(),
    }










Figure 10.6: ImageNet transfer on full Fashion-MNIST at 224 pixels. Across three seeds, the frozen linear probe reaches 88.79% ± 0.08% official-test accuracy, last-block fine-tuning 93.92% ± 0.12%, and scratch 94.14% ± 0.08%. Fine-tuning raises the frozen-probe result by more than five percentage points, and scratch finishes slightly higher under this training recipe. Bars are means, dots are seeds, and error bars are one sample standard deviation.





These results compare the specified training procedures and do not establish a general ranking between transfer and scratch training. Pretraining alters the initial representation, whereas the target data and adaptation procedure determine how useful that starting point becomes.






TipWhen to reach for a pretrained backbone



Scarce labels, a feature-hungry target task, and pretraining data that plausibly covers the target’s features at a matched scale make transfer worth testing. Consider how many target labels are available, how closely the source and target images match, and how much adaptation the budget permits. Compare a frozen probe, partial fine-tuning, and a scratch baseline under an explicit selection procedure. These comparisons test whether the pretrained representation is useful for the target task. Knowing which regime you are in is the skill. The mechanics (requires_grad, learning-rate splits) are the easy part.


Returning to the 30-image shoe task, we now implement partial fine-tuning: SqueezeNet’s last block and a fresh head train at different learning rates, fast for the head and slow for the pretrained layers.



Define the reusable prep helper.
Sample K images per shoe class and apply prep, then load ImageNet SqueezeNet and add a 3-class head.
Fine-tuning: unfreeze the last block, two learning rates.
Score the fine-tuned trunk and head on the shoe test images and print the accuracy.



# [1]
def prep(X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    x = X.repeat(1, 3, 1, 1)
    x = F.interpolate(x, size=96, mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)
    return (x - IMNET_MEAN) / IMNET_STD

# [2]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
idx = torch.cat([(y_tr == c).nonzero().squeeze(1)
                 [torch.randperm(int((y_tr == c).sum()))[:K]] for c in shoe])
X_few, y_few = prep(X_tr[idx]), torch.tensor([new_label[int(c)]
                                              for c in y_tr[idx]])

ft = squeezenet1_1(weights=None)
ft.load_state_dict(torch.load("../../data/squeezenet1_1-imagenet.pt"))
head = nn.Linear(512, 3)
# [3]
for p in ft.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False
for p in ft.features[-1].parameters():         # last Fire block only
    p.requires_grad = True

opt = torch.optim.Adam([
    {"params": head.parameters(), "lr": 1e-3},       # fresh head: normal
    {"params": ft.features[-1].parameters(), "lr": 1e-4},  # trunk: gentle
], weight_decay=1e-3)

ft.train()
for _ in range(60):
    z = F.adaptive_avg_pool2d(ft.features(X_few), 1).flatten(1)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(head(z), y_few)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
ft.eval()
# [4]
with torch.no_grad():
    z = F.adaptive_avg_pool2d(ft.features(prep(X_shoe_te)), 1).flatten(1)
    print(f"fine-tuned (last block + head): "
          f"{(head(z).argmax(1) == y_shoe_te).float().mean():.1%}")

fine-tuned (last block + head): 88.7%



Fine-tuning scores slightly above the frozen probe on this seed and close to scratch. This is consistent with the regime analysis above: adaptation helps at the margin, but on this seed it does not give a clear advantage over scratch.
The pattern still matters: this loop, scaled to real backbones and feature-hungry tasks, is how most applied deep learning systems are built. The recipe “pretrain big, adapt cheaply” reaches beyond vision. It is the recipe for language too, and BERT (Chapter 18) runs it at scale.






NoteCheck yourself



Close the book for one minute and reconstruct the architecture and transfer choices.

Why can several small kernels replace one large kernel?
What changes between a frozen probe, partial fine-tuning, and training from scratch?
Which evidence here is a mechanism study, and which comes from the pinned full-data runs?

title: 10  Modern CNNs and Transfer Learning
section: 10.8 Okay, so: modern CNNs combine architectural and training advances
text:
10.8 Okay, so: modern CNNs combine architectural and training advances

Small kernels, stacked: two \(3\times3\)s cover the receptive field of one \(5\times5\), for \(18C^2\) against \(25C^2\), with two ReLUs instead of one, provided width holds constant through the stack. Design in blocks, repeat the block.
BatchNorm re-standardizes every channel over the batch and spatial axes, then applies a learnable scale and shift (\(\gamma, \beta\)) before the activation, with bias=False on the convolution. Training and evaluation use different statistics, so the mode must be set explicitly. Its per-token cousin, LayerNorm, appears in Chapter 16. Readers who want normalization treated as a choice of invariance, finite-sample state, and derivative path will find that treatment in Deep Learning: Making It Trainable (Shakeri, 2026), Chapter 15, “Normalization Chooses an Invariance”.
\(1\times1\) convolutions run the linear model of Chapter 1 across channels at every pixel. With global average pooling they replace the flatten head: parameters collapse (218k \(\rightarrow\) 35k) and the head has no position-specific weights. On our small dataset, NINSmall lost less accuracy under shift than LeNet but scored below it on centered images. The trunks also differ, so neither difference isolates GAP. Boundaries and downsampling still prevent exact invariance.
Residual connections made a deep stack trainable: our plain 40-layer net did not fit its own training set within the 30-epoch training budget. The residual connection \(u = F(x) + x\) adds an identity term to the Jacobian, and the same-depth twin trains to 100%. Transformer stacks will reuse this residual pattern around each attention and feedforward sublayer.
Transfer learning = freeze + probe, or gently fine-tune. Our experiment found similar mean accuracy for scratch and the ImageNet probe across three seeds at 28-pixel scale. Possible explanations include a pretraining curriculum that lacks the target’s features, domain and resolution gaps, and a small target task that leaves little room for imported features. The pinned full-scale runs report \(88.79\% \pm 0.08\%\) for the frozen probe, \(93.92\% \pm 0.12\%\) for fine-tuning, and \(94.14\% \pm 0.08\%\) for scratch with ResNet-18. Under these procedures, partial fine-tuning raises the frozen-probe result by more than five points, and scratch finishes slightly above fine-tuning. Diagnosing the regime is the skill.

Sources and further reading

Xiao, Rasul, and Vollgraf, Fashion-MNIST: a Novel Image Dataset for Benchmarking Machine Learning Algorithms: the target benchmark for the architecture and transfer studies.
Deng et al., ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database: the source benchmark behind the pretrained visual features used here.
Iandola et al., SqueezeNet: AlexNet-level accuracy with 50x fewer parameters and <0.5MB model size: the compact pretrained architecture used in the chapter’s first transfer experiment.
Simonyan and Zisserman, Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition: the small-kernel, repeated-block argument behind VGG.
Szegedy et al., Going Deeper with Convolutions: GoogLeNet’s Inception block, parallel branches of several kernel sizes joined by channel concatenation.
Lin, Chen, and Yan, Network In Network: introduces the \(1\times1\) channel mixer and global-average-pooling classifier.
Ioffe and Szegedy, Batch Normalization: the original normalization method, its train/evaluation distinction, and the backward pass through the batch statistics that Exercise 7 audits.
He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition: the degradation experiment and residual-block solution.
He et al., Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks: pre-activation residual blocks, which place BatchNorm and ReLU before each convolution in the learned branch and drop the ReLU after the sum, so the sum passes straight through.
Huang et al., Densely Connected Convolutional Networks: dense connectivity through feature-map concatenation and transition layers.
Yosinski et al., How Transferable Are Features in Deep Neural Networks?: a careful empirical account of when transferred features remain useful.
Hardt and Recht, Patterns, Predictions, and Actions: Datasets: a framework for treating a benchmark as a measured artifact rather than an unquestionable oracle.
Northcutt, Athalye, and Mueller, Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks: a large-scale audit of suspected benchmark-label errors and their effect on model comparison.
Shakeri, Deep Learning: Making It Trainable (2026), Chapter 15, “Normalization Chooses an Invariance”: normalization treated as a choice of invariance, finite-sample state, and derivative path.
