title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
11.1 Compress, then reconstruct
Most networks of Part II learned their filters from labels, by minimizing a classification loss. This interlude learns features without labels, by compression. A network maps each input to a short code and then rebuilds the input from that code alone. One motivation is the hypothesis that high-dimensional observations, such as images, concentrate near a much lower-dimensional set, often called a manifold. For an input with \(d\) coordinates, a compact code \(\vect{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k\) with \(k \ll d\) may capture that structure, and reconstruction lets us test what the code preserves. Such a code can also feed the fixed-size readout heads and classifiers of earlier chapters.
This interlude introduces the encoder–decoder architecture through unsupervised reconstruction, where the input itself supplies the target. We begin with principal component analysis (PCA), which finds the best flat subspace for squared reconstruction error in closed form. We rewrite PCA as a tied linear network optimized by gradient descent, then add depth and activations so that the reconstruction map can follow curved structure. A convolutional autoencoder then connects the compression principle to the spatial features of Part II.
The chapter ends with two limits of a fixed code. A code computed in one pass cannot be updated as a sequence arrives one element at a time (Figure 11.1), which Part III addresses. And a code says nothing about how to generate new data, which Chapter 22 addresses.
If an input has \(d\) coordinates, can a network preserve its important structure using only \(k<d\) numbers?
An autoencoder contains two maps. For one input \(\vect{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\), the encoder produces a code \(\vect{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}\) and the decoder reconstructs the input:
\[
\vect{z}=f_\phi(\vect{x}),
\qquad
\hat{\vect{x}}=g_\theta(\vect{z}).
\]
The narrow code is the bottleneck. For \(n\) examples stored as rows of \(\matr{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\), a squared reconstruction objective is
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AE}}(\phi,\theta)
=\frac{1}{nd}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\norm{\vect{x}_i-g_\theta(f_\phi(\vect{x}_i))}_2^2.
\]
The target needs no labels (the input supplies it), but the objective is still specific: preserve enough information to reconstruct the input. This is commonly called self-supervised because each input supplies its own target. It also belongs to unsupervised representation learning. The squared error is one choice of autoencoder loss among several. As Figure 1.8 showed, a loss is a noise model for the target. If each coordinate of \(\vect{x}\) is the decoder output plus independent Gaussian noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), the negative log-likelihood of the input is
\[
-\log p(\vect{x}\mid\vect{z})
=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\norm{\vect{x}-g_\theta(\vect{z})}_2^2+\text{const},
\]
so maximum likelihood gives the squared error. For binary coordinates, a Bernoulli model with a sigmoid output gives the binary cross-entropy (Equation 2.2) instead. Applied to gray levels in \([0,1]\), the same formula is a common surrogate, and it is no longer an exact likelihood.
The narrow code constrains what the encoder can pass to the decoder. If \(k\) is small and the maps have controlled capacity, the code may represent shared regularities more compactly than sample-specific variation.
crumbs: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
WarningA bottleneck does not guarantee generalization



A real-valued low-dimensional code can still carry a surprising amount of information, and a high-capacity network can memorize a finite training set. Check held-out reconstruction, latent behavior, and the decoder between observed codes. “The bottleneck learned meaning” is an empirical claim, and \(k<d\) alone does not imply it.
crumbs: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
11.2 Make PCA learnable
Appendix A computes PCA from a centered singular value decomposition. What if we replace the SVD with trainable weights and a reconstruction loss? The answer begins with the precise statement PCA is a linear autoencoder. Let the training rows be centered, so their mean is zero. Let the columns of \(\matr{V}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\) be the first \(k\) principal directions, the directions along which the centered data vary most. They have unit length and are orthogonal to one another, so they are orthonormal:
\[
\matr{V}_k^\top\matr{V}_k=\matr{I}_k.
\]
Entry \((i, j)\) of \(\matr{V}_k^\top\matr{V}_k\) is the dot product of columns \(i\) and \(j\), which is 1 when \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise.
PCA encodes and decodes by
\[
\vect{z}=\matr{V}_k^\top\vect{x},
\qquad
\hat{\vect{x}}
=\matr{V}_k\vect{z}
=\matr{V}_k\matr{V}_k^\top\vect{x}.
\]
The product \(\matr{P}_k=\matr{V}_k\matr{V}_k^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is the orthogonal projector onto the principal \(k\)-dimensional subspace. By the Eckart–Young–Mirsky result stated in Appendix A, applied to the centered data, this projector minimizes squared reconstruction error among all linear reconstruction maps of rank at most \(k\). Now replace the SVD with gradient descent. A tied linear autoencoder uses one trainable matrix \(\matr{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}\) in both directions:
\[
\vect{z}=\matr{W}^\top\vect{x},
\qquad
\hat{\vect{x}}=\matr{W}\matr{W}^\top\vect{x}.
\]
With centered data, squared loss, and an undercomplete linear map, a global optimum of this autoencoder can recover the same principal reconstruction subspace. That is the accurate content of “PCA is a linear autoencoder”. It does not promise that every optimizer run succeeds, or that the learned weights equal a particular PCA basis.






NoteSame subspace, not the same coordinates



For any orthogonal \(\matr{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\),
\[
(\matr{V}_k\matr{Q})(\matr{V}_k\matr{Q})^\top
=\matr{V}_k\matr{V}_k^\top.
\]
The latent axes may rotate or reflect, and the reconstruction projector stays fixed. For an untied encoder and decoder, any invertible latent change of basis can cancel between the two maps. Compare reconstruction products, projectors, or principal angles. Raw latent coordinates can differ between equally good solutions.








NoteFramework previews: SVD and \(\tanh\)



The experiment uses torch.linalg.svd only to compute PCA’s closed-form reference after the projection has been derived above; Appendix A explains that decomposition, its shapes, and its centering requirement. It also uses \(\tanh\), the smooth pointwise map \(\tanh(u)\in(-1,1)\), as the nonlinear activation inside the curved autoencoder. Chapter 3 already supplied the activation-layer idea. Here \(\tanh\) is simply a nonlinear map; its bounded range and derivative will matter only when repeated state updates make them a design constraint.

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
11.3 Nonlinear autoencoders
PCA gives the best flat rank-\(k\) reconstruction. What if the encoder and decoder were learnable nonlinear maps that could bend with the data?
Take a controlled curve with a known one-dimensional coordinate. For \(t\in[-1,1]\), define
\[
\vect{x}(t)
=\left(t,\;1.5\left(t^2-\frac{1}{3}\right)\right)^\top.
\]
The simpler curve \((t, t^2)\) would serve as well. The offset \(\tfrac13\) makes the second coordinate average to zero over the interval, and the factor 1.5 gives that coordinate a variance of 0.2, below the first coordinate’s \(\tfrac13\). PCA’s best line is then the horizontal axis, and it discards exactly the second coordinate’s variance, so its reconstruction error comes out at a round 0.1 per coordinate.
We assign the alternating grid points to the training and held-out sets. We give PCA, a tied linear autoencoder, and a nonlinear \(2\rightarrow24\rightarrow1\rightarrow24\rightarrow2\) autoencoder the same one-dimensional bottleneck. The comparison is about representational shape: the nonlinear model has far more parameters, so the study says nothing about parameter efficiency. Before you run it, predict which map can follow the bend with one number per point, and whether PCA and the tied linear autoencoder will find the same line.



Define the reusable helpers: planted_curve and principal_projection.
Define the reusable helpers: CurveAutoencoder and fit_curve.
Create empty lists curve_rows and curve_models to collect each seed’s metrics and model.
Rematch PCA and linear and nonlinear autoencoders on a planted curve.
Print per-seed MSEs, projector gap, and latent correlation, then their mean and SD.



# [1]
def planted_curve(t: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    return torch.stack((t, 1.5 * (t.square() - 1.0 / 3.0)), dim=1)


def principal_projection(train_x: Tensor) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
    mean = train_x.mean(dim=0)
    _, _, vh = torch.linalg.svd(train_x - mean, full_matrices=False)
    return mean, vh[:1].T


# [2]
class CurveAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 24), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(24, 1))
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 24), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(24, 2))

    def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
        z = self.encoder(x)
        return self.decoder(z), z


def fit_curve(seed: int) -> tuple[float, float, float, float, float, CurveAutoencoder]:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    t_all = torch.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 513)
    train_t, test_t = t_all[::2], t_all[1::2]
    train_x, test_x = planted_curve(train_t), planted_curve(test_t)
    mean, basis = principal_projection(train_x)

    pca_reconstruction = (test_x - mean) @ basis @ basis.T + mean
    pca_mse = F.mse_loss(pca_reconstruction, test_x).item()

    tied_weight = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(2, 1) * 0.2)
    tied_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([tied_weight], lr=0.03)
    centered_train = train_x - mean
    for _ in range(1800):
        tied_reconstruction = centered_train @ tied_weight @ tied_weight.T
        tied_loss = F.mse_loss(tied_reconstruction, centered_train)
        tied_optimizer.zero_grad()
        tied_loss.backward()
        tied_optimizer.step()

    tied_test = (test_x - mean) @ tied_weight @ tied_weight.T + mean
    tied_mse = F.mse_loss(tied_test, test_x).item()
    projector_gap = torch.linalg.norm(
        tied_weight @ tied_weight.T - basis @ basis.T
    ).item()

    model = CurveAutoencoder()
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.012)
    for step in range(4000):
        reconstruction, _ = model(train_x)
        loss = F.mse_loss(reconstruction, train_x)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        if step == 2500:
            for group in optimizer.param_groups:
                group["lr"] = 0.003

    with torch.no_grad():
        nonlinear_reconstruction, z = model(test_x)
        nonlinear_mse = F.mse_loss(nonlinear_reconstruction, test_x).item()
        centered_z = z[:, 0] - z[:, 0].mean()
        centered_t = test_t - test_t.mean()
        latent_correlation = (
            centered_z @ centered_t
            / torch.sqrt((centered_z @ centered_z) * (centered_t @ centered_t))
        ).abs().item()
    return pca_mse, tied_mse, projector_gap, nonlinear_mse, latent_correlation, model


# [3]
curve_rows = []
curve_models = []
# [4]
for curve_seed in range(6050, 6055):
    *curve_metrics, curve_model = fit_curve(curve_seed)
    curve_rows.append(curve_metrics)
    curve_models.append(curve_model)

curve_table = torch.tensor(curve_rows)
t_plot = torch.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 257)
x_plot = planted_curve(t_plot)
plot_mean, plot_basis = principal_projection(planted_curve(torch.linspace(-1, 1, 257)))
pca_plot = (x_plot - plot_mean) @ plot_basis @ plot_basis.T + plot_mean
with torch.no_grad():
    nonlinear_plot, z_plot = curve_models[0](x_plot)

# [5]
print("seed  PCA MSE    tied MSE   projector gap  nonlinear MSE  |corr(z,t)|")
for seed, row in zip(range(6050, 6055), curve_rows):
    print(seed, *(f"{value:.9f}" for value in row))
print("mean", *(f"{value:.9f}" for value in curve_table.mean(dim=0).tolist()))
print("SD  ", *(f"{value:.9f}" for value in curve_table.std(dim=0).tolist()))

Figure 11.2: A one-dimensional bottleneck behaves differently when its maps may bend. Rank-one PCA and the tied linear autoencoder recover the same projector here; the nonlinear autoencoder follows the planted curve and nearly unrolls its coordinate. This capacity-mismatched study shows a mechanism and claims no general advantage for nonlinear autoencoders.



The linear maps recover the principal projection. The nonlinear decoder follows the curve between the alternating training points, and its one-number code is almost monotone in the coordinate that generated the data. The study tests interpolation within the sampled interval and leaves extrapolation beyond it untested (Exercise 2). Nonlinearity alone does not guarantee that the code is meaningful, stable outside the observed region, or unique.
Learning a lower-dimensional coordinate system for data concentrated near a curved set is one form of manifold learning. The phrase names the goal, and a bottleneck need not recover a true manifold or its preferred coordinates.

text:
11.4 A code is not yet a distribution
The nonlinear autoencoder can reconstruct held-out points on this curve. Can we now generate by drawing an arbitrary random \(z\) and passing it through the decoder?
Nothing in the reconstruction objective tells us which distribution to draw from. Reconstruction trains the decoder on codes produced by the encoder. Between those codes (and especially outside their range), many decoder functions can fit the same targets. A small algebraic example builds two such decoders. Suppose the observed codes are \(z\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and one decoder is \(g_1(z)=z^2\). A second decoder can add any multiple of a function that vanishes at all three codes:
\[
g_2(z)=z^2+0.8z(z^2-1).
\]
The reconstructions agree on every observed code, yet disagree elsewhere.

WarningReconstruction does not specify a sampler



A deterministic autoencoder maps \(\vect{x} \mapsto \vect{z} \mapsto \hat{\vect{x}}\). It trains the decoder only on the codes that observed training examples produce. Reconstruction at the observed codes does not uniquely determine the decoder’s behavior between them or outside their empirical range.
Ordinary reconstruction training supplies no prior distribution over the latent space and no principled recipe for drawing a random starting vector. If we draw \(\vect{z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\vect{0}, \matr{I})\) and feed it to a deterministic decoder, the output can be a blur or an implausible mixture of training examples.
To turn a representation into a generative model, we must give the latent space a probability law. In Part V (Chapter 22) we build variational autoencoders (VAEs): networks whose encoder outputs a distribution, whose training penalizes its divergence from a known prior with the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and whose reparameterization trick makes the sampling step differentiable. For now, keep the distinction: a code is not yet a distribution.


One useful intermediate move is same architecture, different training. A denoising autoencoder corrupts an input to \(\widetilde{\vect{x}}\) and asks the network to recover the clean \(\vect{x}\):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DAE}}
=\E_{\vect{x}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\,
\widetilde{\vect{x}}\sim q(\widetilde{\vect{x}}\mid\vect{x})}
\left[
\norm{\vect{x}-g_\theta(f_\phi(\widetilde{\vect{x}}))}_2^2
\right].
\]
Training with clean inputs and clean targets teaches reconstruction. Training with noisy inputs and clean targets teaches denoising: under squared loss, the output moves toward the average of the clean inputs that could have produced the noisy one. The architecture is the same in both cases, and only the training pairs differ. Pairing inputs from one domain with targets from another, such as a sentence and its translation, teaches translation. Changing which inputs are paired with which targets changes what the code must preserve.

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
11.5 Convolutional autoencoders
A fully connected autoencoder flattens the image and has no built-in preference for nearby pixels. A convolutional autoencoder has one. Its encoder uses learned local filters and stride to reduce spatial resolution, and its decoder expands the code back into an image. More generally, the encoder and decoder can each be any differentiable architecture suited to the data, convolutional here and recurrent in Part III.
Here is the shape at each stage. The example is small enough to train on a CPU:








Stage
Shape for one example
Role




image
\(1\times28\times28\)
\(784\) observed pixel values


stride-2 convolution
\(8\times14\times14\)
local features, half resolution


stride-2 convolution
\(16\times7\times7\)
broader local features


learned code
\(16\)
a \(49{:}1\) value-count bottleneck


linear expansion
\(16\times7\times7\)
seed the spatial decoder


transposed convolutions
\(8\times14\times14\rightarrow1\times28\times28\)
reconstruct resolution



The expanding operator is called a transposed convolution because it is the transpose, or adjoint, of the linear map implemented by a convolution. If \(\mathcal{C}_{\matr{K}}\) denotes convolution with fixed weights \(\matr{K}\), then
\[
\left\langle \mathcal{C}_{\matr{K}}(\vect{x}),\vect{y}\right\rangle
=
\left\langle \vect{x},\mathcal{C}_{\matr{K}}^{\top}(\vect{y})\right\rangle.
\]
The matrix view of Figure 8.3 makes this concrete. There, a one-dimensional cross-correlation with three weights is a \(4 \times 6\) matrix that maps six inputs to four outputs. Its transpose is a \(6 \times 4\) matrix that maps four values back to six positions. Each column of the transpose holds the same three weights, so it spreads one value over three neighboring positions, and the contributions that land on the same position add. Convolution combines a local input patch into one output value, and its transpose distributes each value across the corresponding patch. That equation defines an adjoint, which differs from an inverse. Stride may discard information, and learned filters need not be invertible. A transposed convolution gives the decoder a learnable map with the right shapes, and it does not undo the encoder.
We can now make “same architecture, different training” measurable. Both models below use the architecture above. One receives clean images and reconstructs clean images. The other receives Gaussian-corrupted images, but we score its reconstructions against the clean targets. We split the development file into 900 fitting and 300 validation examples, and we evaluate on the committed 600-example shared benchmark only after validation has selected each checkpoint. We repeat training with five seeds. Labels never enter the experiment. Before the scores print, predict which arm reconstructs clean test images better and which copes better with the corrupted inputs.



Load the Fashion-MNIST subset, split off 900 fit images, and add seeded noise to validation and test copies.
Define the reusable helpers: ConvolutionalAutoencoder, reconstruction_mse, and fit_convolutional_autoencoder.
Compare clean and denoising input–target contracts with the same convolutional autoencoder.
Check the transposed-convolution adjoint, then print each arm’s mean and SD MSEs and the corrupted-input MSE.



# [1]
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float32)
fashion_development = torch.load("../../data/fashion-train.pt")
fashion_holdout = torch.load("../../data/fashion-test.pt")
development_images = fashion_development["X"].float().unsqueeze(1) / 255.0
holdout_images = fashion_holdout["X"].float().unsqueeze(1) / 255.0

split = torch.randperm(
    len(development_images), generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050)
)
fit_indices, validation_indices = split[:900], split[900:]
fit_images = development_images[fit_indices]
validation_images = development_images[validation_indices]

noise_sd = 0.35
validation_noise = torch.randn(
    validation_images.shape, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(70_050)
)
holdout_noise = torch.randn(
    holdout_images.shape, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(70_051)
)
noisy_validation = (validation_images + noise_sd * validation_noise).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
noisy_holdout = (holdout_images + noise_sd * holdout_noise).clamp(0.0, 1.0)


# [2]
class ConvolutionalAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, latent_dim: int = 16) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder_map = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 8, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(8, 16, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        self.to_code = nn.Linear(16 * 7 * 7, latent_dim)
        self.from_code = nn.Linear(latent_dim, 16 * 7 * 7)
        self.decoder_map = nn.Sequential(
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 8, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(8, 1, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.Sigmoid(),
        )

    def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> tuple[Tensor, Tensor]:
        z = self.to_code(self.encoder_map(x).flatten(1))
        features = F.relu(self.from_code(z)).reshape(-1, 16, 7, 7)
        return self.decoder_map(features), z


@torch.no_grad()
def reconstruction_mse(
    model: nn.Module, inputs: Tensor, targets: Tensor
) -> float:
    model.eval()
    reconstruction, _ = model(inputs)
    return F.mse_loss(reconstruction, targets).item()


def fit_convolutional_autoencoder(
    seed: int, denoising: bool, epochs: int = 30
) -> tuple[float, float, float, ConvolutionalAutoencoder]:
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    model = ConvolutionalAutoencoder()
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.003)
    order_generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 100_000)
    noise_generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 200_000)
    best_validation = float("inf")
    best_state = deepcopy(model.state_dict())

    for _ in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(fit_images), generator=order_generator)
        for indices in order.split(100):
            targets = fit_images[indices]
            if denoising:
                noise = torch.randn(targets.shape, generator=noise_generator)
                inputs = (targets + noise_sd * noise).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
            else:
                inputs = targets
            reconstruction, _ = model(inputs)
            loss = F.mse_loss(reconstruction, targets)
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

        validation_inputs = noisy_validation if denoising else validation_images
        validation_loss = reconstruction_mse(
            model, validation_inputs, validation_images
        )
        if validation_loss < best_validation:
            best_validation = validation_loss
            best_state = deepcopy(model.state_dict())

    model.load_state_dict(best_state)
    clean_mse = reconstruction_mse(model, holdout_images, holdout_images)
    noisy_mse = reconstruction_mse(model, noisy_holdout, holdout_images)
    return best_validation, clean_mse, noisy_mse, model


conv_rows: dict[bool, Tensor] = {}
conv_models: dict[bool, list[ConvolutionalAutoencoder]] = {}
# [3]
for denoising in (False, True):
    fitted = [
        fit_convolutional_autoencoder(seed, denoising)
        for seed in range(6050, 6055)
    ]
    conv_rows[denoising] = torch.tensor([row[:3] for row in fitted])
    conv_models[denoising] = [row[3] for row in fitted]

plain_model = conv_models[False][0]
denoising_model = conv_models[True][0]
example_indices = [7, 22]
with torch.no_grad():
    plain_noisy_reconstruction, _ = plain_model(noisy_holdout[example_indices])
    denoised_reconstruction, _ = denoising_model(noisy_holdout[example_indices])

# [4]
# A separate operator check: transposed convolution is the convolution's adjoint.
probe_x = torch.randn(2, 1, 13, 13, dtype=torch.float64)
probe_weight = torch.randn(3, 1, 3, 3, dtype=torch.float64)
probe_y = torch.randn(2, 3, 7, 7, dtype=torch.float64)
conv_x = F.conv2d(probe_x, probe_weight, stride=2, padding=1)
transpose_y = F.conv_transpose2d(
    probe_y, probe_weight, stride=2, padding=1
)
left_inner_product = (conv_x * probe_y).sum()
right_inner_product = (probe_x * transpose_y).sum()
adjoint_relative_gap = (
    (left_inner_product - right_inner_product).abs()
    / torch.maximum(left_inner_product.abs(), right_inner_product.abs())
)

print("arm       validation   clean test  noisy-input test")
for denoising, label in [(False, "plain"), (True, "denoising")]:
    table = conv_rows[denoising]
    print(label, "mean", *(f"{value:.6f}" for value in table.mean(0).tolist()))
    print(label, "SD  ", *(f"{value:.6f}" for value in table.std(0).tolist()))
print("corrupted-input test MSE", f"{F.mse_loss(noisy_holdout, holdout_images):.6f}")
print("transposed-convolution adjoint relative gap", f"{adjoint_relative_gap:.2e}")

arm       validation   clean test  noisy-input test
plain mean 0.022851 0.020701 0.033263
plain SD   0.000719 0.000565 0.003642
denoising mean 0.026020 0.026294 0.023810
denoising SD   0.000858 0.001445 0.000775
corrupted-input test MSE 0.068601
transposed-convolution adjoint relative gap 1.15e-16


















Figure 11.4: Although both arms share the same convolutional architecture, their input–target contracts differ: compared with the clean-trained arm, the denoising arm has higher error on clean inputs and lower error on inputs with the specified corruption.



Each arm excels on the input distribution it was trained to reconstruct: the denoising arm achieves lower error on corrupted test images, whereas the clean-trained arm is more accurate on uncorrupted ones. Changing the input corruption changes the mapping that a fixed architecture learns to approximate.

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
text:
11.6 From fixed-size inputs to sequences
An encoder compresses an input into a compact latent vector \(\vect{z}\), and a decoder reconstructs, denoises or transforms it. Why not solve sequence tasks, such as machine translation, by encoding an entire sentence into one \(k\)-dimensional vector and decoding it into another language? Figure 11.1 sets the two regimes side by side.
For short, bounded sequences, this one-shot compression can serve as a crude baseline (Exercise 6 builds one). But it does not match how sequential data arrives:

No incremental update. Every token of the input must be available before the one-shot encoder can run. The architecture cannot process tokens incrementally as sequence data arrives.
Static capacity against growing evidence. The code has the same width \(k\) whether it compresses a three-word phrase or a thousand-word contract.
No direct access to discarded detail. Word order, subordinate clauses and every intermediate detail must pass through the same static handoff. Once the encoder discards a detail to fit its bottleneck, the decoder cannot look back to retrieve it.

Padding or truncating inputs to a maximum length gives no incremental update rule either. What we need is a time-homogeneous state update, one rule applied at every step:
\[
\vect{h}_t = f_\theta(\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t).
\]
The model applies the same parameterized update rule as each token arrives, maintaining a running memory vector \(\vect{h}_t\) that evolves with the evidence. The state still has a fixed width, so recurrence does not remove every bottleneck, but it supplies the processing rule that a one-shot encoder lacks. That rule is the foundation of recurrent neural networks, the subject of Part III (Chapter 12).






NoteTwo different limitations



“A fixed-input encoder is not a variable-length process” asks how memory should update as evidence arrives. “A code is not yet a distribution” asks how a genuinely new sample could begin. The two problems are distinct: they ask different questions and require different machinery.








NoteCheck yourself



Answer these questions without looking back.

Under which restrictions does a linear autoencoder recover the principal subspace?
What changes when the encoder and decoder become nonlinear?
Why does successful reconstruction not define a sampling distribution or a variable-length update rule?

title: 11  Interlude: Autoencoders: Making PCA Learnable
section: 11.7 Okay, so: compression can be learned, but it has limits
text:
11.7 Okay, so: compression can be learned, but it has limits

An autoencoder learns an input–code–reconstruction contract. The target determines what information the code is rewarded for preserving.
PCA is the linear case under stated conditions. Center the data, use an undercomplete linear map and squared loss, and compare subspaces or projectors, because the latent coordinates are arbitrary.
Gradient descent can fit the same projection. Add depth and nonlinearity and the reconstruction map can follow curved structure. It gains capacity, with no guarantee that the code is meaningful.
Convolution preserves the spatial prior. Transposed convolution is the adjoint shape-changing operator used by the decoder, and it does not invert the encoder.
Same architecture, different contracts, different behavior. Clean reconstruction, denoising, and translation pair inputs and targets in distinct ways.
A static code leaves two questions open. How can a representation be updated as inputs arrive, and how can a model generate a new sample? Part III develops recurrent updates, and Chapter 22 develops probability models and sampling procedures.

Exercises

(Pencil.) Untie the linear maps. Replace \(\matr{W}\matr{W}^{\top}\) with an encoder \(\matr{W}_e\) and decoder \(\matr{W}_d\). Construct an invertible change of latent coordinates that changes both matrices but leaves their product unchanged.
(Audit.) Audit the bend. Extend the planted curve’s test interval beyond the range used for training. Compare interpolation with extrapolation and state which claim the original interleaving split earned.
(Code.) Change the corruption. Train the convolutional autoencoder with masking noise instead of Gaussian noise. Evaluate both corruptions without retuning and explain why “denoising ability” is not one scalar property.
(Pencil.) Prove the adjoint check. Write a one-channel convolution as an explicit matrix for a tiny input. Verify that applying its matrix transpose matches a transposed convolution with the corresponding stride and padding.
(Audit.) Stress the one-shot code. Design two sequence families that share the same final tokens but require remembering increasingly old information. Predict how a one-shot encoder and a recurrent state will fail differently as length grows.
(Code.) Running translator, v0. This exercise starts a project that later chapters extend one version at a time, from a one-shot code to pretrained models. Choose one sentence-pair corpus and keep it throughout: the English–French pairs of the Tatoeba collection and Multi30K’s English–German image descriptions are common starting points. Fix a split, a text normalization, a vocabulary with padding, unknown-word, and end-of-sentence tokens, and an evaluation you will reuse unchanged: validation loss per target token and token accuracy now, and BLEU once the exercises of Chapter 13 have you build it. Then replace the flattening with the mean of the source embeddings. (Audit.) For both encoders, measure the fraction of sentences truncated, token accuracy by source length, and whether a sentence and its reordering receive the same code. Keep the numbers: the next chapter tests its designs against these failures.

title: Sequences: Learning the Summary
text:
Skip to main content




While earlier parts relied on fixed-size coordinate grids or static bottlenecks, sequential data requires an incremental computation that updates its internal representation as each new element arrives. Here we maintain a fixed-width state vector and learn a parameterized transition rule to update it across time. The same transition parameters are applied at every step, extending weight sharing from spatial coordinates to the temporal dimension. A longer sequence requires more applications of the rule rather than additional parameters. This recurrence also deepens the backward computation: repeated Jacobian products across many steps can cause gradients to vanish or explode. Gated architectures counter vanishing gradients through additive state paths and learned retention gates. We will examine how these gating mechanisms and their parameter initialization affect whether a network can retain and learn from evidence that arrived dozens of steps earlier.
A recurrent encoder and decoder can then connect sequences of different lengths, as in machine translation. The rules for training such a pair and decoding from it carry over to the sequence decoders of Parts IV and V: the decoder reads the observed target shifted by one token, the loss is built from token-level log-likelihoods, masks specify which positions the loss grades and which a network may read, and outputs are found by search or drawn by sampling. In the baseline architecture developed here, all source information reaches the decoder exclusively through the encoder’s final state. Although the recurrent transition rule accommodates variable lengths, that one fixed-size summary remains an information bottleneck for long sequences. Part IV removes that bottleneck by introducing attention, giving the decoder direct, selective access to the encoder states at every position.

title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
12.1 From fixed windows to recurrent models
The autoencoders of Chapter 11 encode an input of one fixed size in a single pass. When a sequence grows by one element, they have no operation that updates the code already computed. In this chapter we learn such an operation: a rule that combines a fixed-width summary of the elements seen so far with the next element to give the new summary.
Text, audio, and sensor measurements are sequences: ordered lists of elements whose length varies from one example to the next. When the elements are symbols from a fixed set, such as the characters or words of a text, each element is called a token. For the streaming models developed in this chapter, we use six design goals to compare possible architectures:
The interlude’s one-shot autoencoder fails any length and streaming outright: it needs a maximum length, and it cannot finish before the last element arrives. Recurrence asks us to make the carried summary learnable: rather than compressing once, the model learns how to revise its memory after each new element.
A window. We predict the next element \(\vect{x}_{t+1}\) from the last \(k\), \(\vect{x}_{t-k+1}, \dots, \vect{x}_t\), by sliding a width-\(k\) window along the sequence and feeding each snapshot to an MLP. This is autoregression. Applying the same MLP at every window position reuses the locality and weight sharing of one-dimensional convolution, with the time axis in place of a spatial axis. Windows are useful (they power real forecasting systems), but their context length is fixed at \(k\): anything older than the last \(k\) elements lies outside the window and cannot affect the prediction. No fixed \(k\) covers every dependency, as in the sentence “The company whose first-day price we recorded back in January finally …”. The window thus fails reach, and widening it adds parameters.
A function per timestep. Next we let the model change over time: we learn \(f_1\) for step one, \(f_2\) for step two, and so on, and each passes a summary forward, \(\vect{h}_t = f_t(\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t)\). The parameter count now grows with sequence length: a length-500 essay needs 500 learned functions, and no function exists for a position beyond the longest sequence seen in training. The functions at positions 17 and 18 have separate parameters, so a pattern learned at one position must be learned again at the other. It fails any length and length-independent parameters at once.
Images posed the same problem in space: a separate template for every image position was wasteful and brittle, and convolution replaced the templates with one kernel shared across space. The same remedy applies here: share the function across time,
\[
\vect{h}_t = f(\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t),
\tag{12.1}\]
one learned rule \(f\), applied at every step, carrying a running summary \(\vect{h}_t\), the hidden state, from each step to the next. This is the third weight sharing: across examples, across space, and now across time. The rule’s output can still depend on position and context through the accumulated state. The rule is time-homogeneous: the same at every step. That is a property of the model, and the data distribution may still change along the sequence. On paper, one shared \(f\) meets every goal except trainable reach, a question about gradients taken up in the rest of this chapter.

title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
NoteThe hidden state and the Markov property



\(\vect{h}_t\), the state of the dynamical system that Equation 12.1 defines, is a fixed-size vector computed by the transition map \(f\) from everything seen so far. Feeding it back in gives the computation a property with a classical name, the Markov property: \(\vect{h}_{t-1}\) and \(\vect{x}_t\) together determine the model’s next update, and earlier inputs affect that update only through \(\vect{h}_{t-1}\). This interface permits streaming (process elements as they arrive), any sequence length (the loop runs once per element), and, later in this chapter, training on contiguous chunks. It is a property of the model’s computation. Whether \(\vect{h}_{t-1}\) keeps everything about the past that the best prediction needs is a separate question.

title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
12.2 A network with a loop
The simplest choice of \(f\) is a one-layer network with the state concatenated in: a linear map of \((\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t)\), squashed by a \(\tanh\):
\[
\vect{h}_t \;=\; \tanh\!\left(\matr{W}_{hh}\,\vect{h}_{t-1} + \matr{W}_{xh}\,\vect{x}_t + \vect{b}_h\right),
\qquad
\vect{s}_t \;=\; \matr{W}_{hs}\,\vect{h}_t + \vect{b}_s ,
\tag{12.2}\]
the vanilla recurrent neural network. The network has three weight matrices, reused at every step whether the sequence has five elements or five thousand. The readout \(\vect{s}_t\) holds the logits, one score per class, and you can collect one at every step (predicting each next character, labeling each word) or only at the end (classifying the whole sequence). Both designs appear below.
We build the loop by hand and verify it against the framework. The two results agree to within rounding error.



Run a seeded nn.RNN on 4 random 12-step sequences, then take its weights, summed bias, and a zero start state.
Implement the recurrence, written as the loop it is.
Print the largest absolute difference between manual and the nn.RNN output out_ref.



import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)
D, H, T, B = 8, 16, 12, 4                       # features, hidden, time, batch
rnn = nn.RNN(D, H, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(B, T, D)
out_ref, _ = rnn(x)

W_xh, W_hh = rnn.weight_ih_l0, rnn.weight_hh_l0
b = rnn.bias_ih_l0 + rnn.bias_hh_l0
h = torch.zeros(B, H)                            # h_0 = 0, the standard start
outs = []
# [2]
for t in range(T):                               # the loop IS the architecture
    h = torch.tanh(x[:, t] @ W_xh.T + h @ W_hh.T + b)
    outs.append(h)
manual = torch.stack(outs, 1)
# [3]
print(f"manual loop vs. nn.RNN: max |diff| = {(manual - out_ref).abs().max():.1e}")

manual loop vs. nn.RNN: max |diff| = 1.2e-07



An MLP takes input of shape (batch, features). With batch_first=True, as in the cell above, nn.RNN takes (batch, time, features). The time axis sits between the batch axis and the feature axis, and the loop runs over it carrying h along.
Sentences in one minibatch rarely share a length, so shorter ones are padded at the end to the longest one’s length, and the loop must not let padding rewrite the memory. A mask \(m_t\in\{0,1\}\) per sequence (1 for a real element, 0 for padding) keeps the old state on padded steps:
\[
\vect{h}_t = m_t\, f(\vect{h}_{t-1},\vect{x}_t) + (1-m_t)\,\vect{h}_{t-1}.
\tag{12.3}\]
Each sequence then ends holding the state of its own last real element, the state it would hold if run alone.
Unroll the loop in time and the RNN is an ordinary feedforward network that happens to be \(T\) layers deep with every layer’s weights tied.








Figure 12.1: Two drawings of the same machine. Left: one cell whose hidden state loops back into itself. Right: the loop unrolled: a chain of copies of the same cell, each consuming one input and passing the state along. Read vertically it is an ordinary feedforward network; read horizontally it is a network as deep as the sequence is long, with every layer’s weights tied.

title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
12.3 Gradients through time
The unrolled network is a deep network with tied weights, so backpropagation applies unchanged. Training on a sequence runs the loop forward, collects losses \(L_t\) at the readouts and sums them into \(L\), then backpropagates through the unrolled network, a procedure called backpropagation through time (BPTT). A gradient that lands on \(\vect{h}_T\) must travel back through every application of Equation 12.2 to reach an early input. Define \(\matr{D}_t = \mathrm{diag}\!\left(\tanh'(\cdot)\right)\) at step \(t\). The forward Jacobian for one hop is \(\matr{D}_t\matr{W}_{hh}\), so the full Jacobian is
\[
\frac{\partial \vect{h}_T}{\partial \vect{h}_1}
= (\matr{D}_T\matr{W}_{hh})\cdots
  (\matr{D}_2\matr{W}_{hh}),
\qquad
\vect{g}_{t-1}=\matr{W}_{hh}^{\!\top}\matr{D}_t\vect{g}_t
+\frac{\partial L_{t-1}}{\partial\vect{h}_{t-1}} .
\tag{12.4}\]
The Jacobian is a product of \(T-1\) factors that share \(\matr{W}_{hh}\), while the activation-derivative matrices \(\matr{D}_t\) vary along the sequence. The second expression runs the chain rule backward. It uses \(\vect{g}_t=\partial L/\partial\vect{h}_t\), the derivative of the total loss with respect to the state at step \(t\) (its adjoint, in the language of Chapter 5). The recursion starts at the last state with \(\vect{g}_T=\partial L_T/\partial\vect{h}_T\). Each step back then does three things: the activation derivative \(\matr{D}_t\) scales the incoming gradient, \(\matr{W}_{hh}^{\top}\) carries it to the previous state, and the loss \(L_{t-1}\) adds its own gradient there. The recursion ends at \(\vect{g}_0=\matr{W}_{hh}^{\!\top}\matr{D}_1\vect{g}_1\), because no loss is attached to \(\vect{h}_0\).
A deep network’s gradient has the same form, a product of per-layer Jacobians. If the factors shrink the signal, the product decays exponentially, and if they amplify it, the product explodes exponentially. In an RNN every factor contains the same \(\matr{W}_{hh}\) and a \(\tanh'\) that is at most 1. To preserve gradients over many steps, the cumulative Jacobian product must remain well scaled along the relevant directions, and near-unit gains at the individual steps are one way to achieve this. That balance is fragile, and it is easily lost. Initialization can at least start there. An orthogonal \(\matr{W}_{hh}\) has every singular value equal to one, so wherever the pre-activations sit near zero, where \(\tanh'\approx 1\), each hop preserves the gradient’s norm. Training then moves \(\matr{W}_{hh}\), and \(\tanh'\) drops below one as the pre-activations grow, so orthogonality helps only at the start of training (Exercise 2).
In an RNN, depth is counted in time steps: a paragraph of text, read one word per step, is a network about a hundred layers deep. We illustrate the effect of this depth in Figure 12.2, which plots, for a freshly initialized vanilla RNN, the norm of the gradient that reaches the first input against the sequence length \(T\). The first input is \(T-1\) recurrent transitions from the final state.



Define the reusable grad_at_first_input helper.
Build a seeded vanilla nn.RNN and compute g_rnn at lags 1, 5, 10, 20, 40, and 60.
Gradient reaching the first input vs. lag.



# [1]
def grad_at_first_input(rec: nn.Module, lags: list[int],
                        vocab: int = 4) -> list[float]:
    norms = []
    for T in lags:
        generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(100 + T)
        x = torch.randn(8, T, vocab, generator=generator, requires_grad=True)
        o, _ = rec(x)
        o[:, -1].sum().backward()
        norms.append(x.grad[:, 0].norm().item())    # gradient at input #1
    return norms

# [2]
lags = [1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60]
torch.manual_seed(0)
vanilla = nn.RNN(4, 32, batch_first=True)
g_rnn = grad_at_first_input(vanilla, lags)
# [3]
print("lag:      " + "   ".join(f"{l:>7d}" for l in lags))
print("|grad|:   " + "   ".join(f"{g:.1e}" for g in g_rnn))

plt.figure(figsize=(6.2, 3.2))
plt.semilogy(lags, g_rnn, "o-", color="#E57200", ms=5, label="vanilla RNN")
plt.xlabel("lag $T$ between output and first input")
plt.ylabel(r"$\|\partial L / \partial \mathbf{x}_1\|$")
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

lag:            1         5        10        20        40        60
|grad|:   2.9e+00   6.8e-01   2.6e-02   7.2e-05   3.4e-10   1.1e-15








Figure 12.2: Norm of the gradient \(\partial L/\partial\vect{x}_1\) that reaches the first input of a freshly initialized vanilla RNN, against the sequence length \(T\). The first input is \(T-1\) recurrent transitions from the final state. Here \(L\) is the sum of the entries of the last state \(\vect{h}_T\) over the batch and the hidden units. The norm falls by about fifteen orders of magnitude from \(T=1\) to \(T=60\).






At \(T=60\) the gradient reaching the first input is about \(10^{-15}\): at initialization, whatever happened at the start supplies almost no usable learning signal. Learning the dependency is still possible, but it is fragile. The mirror-image failure is explosion: one large spike in the product of Equation 12.4 can make an update destabilize training.






WarningGradient clipping limits explosion and leaves vanishing alone



In practice, explosion is handled with gradient clipping: if the gradient’s norm exceeds a threshold, it is rescaled down to the threshold before the step (nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_, which appears in every training loop below). This keeps a spike from destabilizing training, at the cost of damping legitimately large steps. It has no effect on vanishing gradients, so clipping alone cannot lengthen the memory a recurrent network learns.



Training with a finite horizon
Full BPTT requires memory and compute for the entire sequence at each training update. The standard fix relies on the Markov property of the forward pass: the carried state and the next input together determine the next state. In truncated BPTT, we cut the sequence into contiguous chunks, carry the recurrent state forward, and detach it at each boundary. The values cross the boundary, but the gradient graph does not. This bounds memory while preserving running context. For a cut after step \(t\), the next state is \[
\vect{h}_{t+1} = f\bigl(\operatorname{detach}(\vect{h}_t),\, \vect{x}_{t+1}\bigr),
\] where \(\operatorname{detach}\) returns the value of \(\vect{h}_t\) unchanged and passes no gradient back through it.
Where to cut is itself a choice: every \(K\) steps (a fixed horizon) or at random points. With a fixed horizon, the carried state still delivers the distant past to the forward pass, but the gradient trains only the dependencies whose two ends fall inside one chunk of \(K\) steps. A dependency that reaches \(\ell\) steps back links the loss at step \(t\) to the input at step \(t-\ell\). The loss at the \(j\)th step of a chunk reaches back \(j-1\) steps: immediately after a boundary (\(j=1\)) it reaches only its own input, and at the end of the chunk (\(j=K\)) it reaches back \(K-1\) steps. Only the losses at chunk steps \(\ell+1,\dots,K\), that is, \(K-\ell\) of the chunk’s \(K\) losses, therefore reach an input \(\ell\) steps back: such a dependency gets gradient from a fraction \(1-\ell/K\) of the losses, and from none once \(\ell \ge K\). With \(K=3\) and a cut after step 3, for example, the loss \(L_6\) uses the value that entered at \(\vect{x}_2\), four steps back. Since \(4 \ge K\), no gradient from \(L_6\) reaches step 2. The carried state may still contain longer-range information, but no gradient from a loss in a later chunk reaches the computations before the cut, so a fixed horizon biases training toward short-range structure.
Random cuts alone do not remove the bias, because long-range terms are still the ones most often cut. Dividing each surviving gradient term by the probability that the cuts spared it does remove it: a term kept with probability \(p\) and scaled by \(1/p\) contributes its full value on average, so the estimate of the full gradient is unbiased (Tallec & Ollivier, 2017). The unbiased estimate has two costs. First, a long-range term survives a random cut only rarely, and when it does it is multiplied by a large factor \(1/p\). These occasional large terms make the gradient estimate noisy: its variance grows. Second, a random cut can leave a long chunk, and backpropagation must keep the activations of every step in a chunk until the backward pass (the caching of Chapter 5). The memory needed therefore changes from one update to the next and must be budgeted for the longest chunk. A fixed horizon keeps the activations of the same \(K\) steps in every update and adds no reweighting variance. Most training therefore keeps the fixed horizon, at the price of its bias.
The character-level language model later in this chapter uses a simpler recipe that needs no cuts at all. It trains on random 100-character windows of text and starts each window from a zero state. This is fixed-window training. No state is carried between windows, so it differs from truncated BPTT, and it is cheap enough for a small demonstration. In production character models, contiguous chunks of roughly 20–50 steps with carried-and-detached state are common. In either recipe, clipping handles spikes, and no gradient crosses the horizon.

title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
12.4 Engineering a memory: the LSTM
In the vanilla RNN, the carried state passes through a weight matrix and a \(\tanh\) at every step, and its gradient through the repeated product of Equation 12.4. We can start with the additive update of residual networks and add multiplicative gates that control what the carried state keeps. We build the memory in four steps:

Add to the memory. In the vanilla RNN, the state is multiplied by \(\matr{W}_{hh}\) and squashed at every step, and those repeated multiplications shrink the gradient. Instead, we update a carried cell state \(\vect{c}_t\) by adding to it: \(\vect{c}_t = \vect{c}_{t-1} + \vect{\Delta}_t\). Along this path \(\partial\vect{c}_t/\partial\vect{c}_{t-1}\) is the identity, so the gradient passes back unchanged, as through the residual connection \(u = x + F(x)\) of Chapter 10. The three gates below decide how much of the state is kept, written and read.
Erase with a forget gate. Some stored content should expire. A forget gate \(\vect{f}_t \in (0,1)\) multiplies \(\vect{c}_{t-1}\) elementwise, so a value near 0 erases that coordinate and a value near 1 keeps it.
Write with an input gate. New information enters through an input gate \(\vect{i}_t\) that scales a candidate \(\tilde{\vect{c}}_t\), and their elementwise product is the update \(\vect{\Delta}_t\).
Read with an output gate. Expose only what the current step needs, through an output gate \(\vect{o}_t\) that scales \(\tanh(\vect{c}_t)\) into the hidden state \(\vect{h}_t\).

Each gate is a small learned layer squashed by a sigmoid (a number in \((0,1)\) read as what fraction passes). The candidate content passes through \(\tanh\), which keeps each coordinate between \(-1\) and \(1\). Assembled, this is the Long Short-Term Memory cell (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; the forget gate \(\vect{f}_t\) was added by Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins, 2000):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vect{f}_t &= \sigma\!\left(\matr{W}_f\,[\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_f\right)
&\quad
\vect{i}_t &= \sigma\!\left(\matr{W}_i\,[\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_i\right)
\\
\tilde{\vect{c}}_t &= \tanh\!\left(\matr{W}_c\,[\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_c\right)
&\quad
\vect{o}_t &= \sigma\!\left(\matr{W}_o\,[\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_o\right)
\\[2pt]
\vect{c}_t &= \vect{f}_t \odot \vect{c}_{t-1} \;+\; \vect{i}_t \odot \tilde{\vect{c}}_t
&\quad
\vect{h}_t &= \vect{o}_t \odot \tanh(\vect{c}_t).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.5}\]








Figure 12.3: The LSTM cell. All four learned layers read the same input \([h_{t-1}, x_t]\), drawn along the bottom. Along the top, the cell-state update path multiplies the old cell state elementwise by the forget gate \(f_t\) and adds the candidate content \(\tilde{c}_t\) scaled by the input gate \(i_t\); the output gate \(o_t\) controls what becomes visible as \(h_t\).

      Scope and caveats
        Real gates are vectors, differ per unit and per step, and are produced by the sigmoid layers of the LSTM update equations from [h_{t−1}, x_t], which this panel does not evaluate. The chapter does measure gates once, later: its forget-gate diagnostic reports mean activations of about 0.76 for the task-solving model and about 0.56 for the default-initialized one, over eighty steps on sixty-four probe sequences. Those are measurements of two trained models, not the openings shown here, and they appear nowhere on the picture. Nothing here is trained and no gradient is drawn: the direct cell-state product of forget gates, the positive forget-gate bias, and the recall experiment are the chapter's next argument, and the GRU is out of scope.
      
    
    Check yourself. Keep the picture's cell at 1.00 and now open the output gate fully. What is h?
      h = 1 × tanh(1.00) ≈ 0.762, and the cell still holds 1.00. Reading passes the memory through tanh and the output gate; it does not spend it.
    
    Transcript and keyboard help
      
        The cell-state path runs left to right. The previous cell state stands on it at the inlet, 1.00 high. Before playing on: if the output gate is shut, is what the cell state carries lost?
        Three gates appear, each drawn as a port with a vane: forget on the cell-state path, input on the branch that carries the candidate 0.50, output on the branch that leaves through tanh. Forget stands wide open at 1.00, input and output shut at 0.00, so the carried value crosses the forget gate untouched and parks mid-path at 1.00.
        The forget gate closes halfway, to 0.50. The carried bar downstream of it halves in place: 1.00 becomes 0.50. Nothing else moved.
        The input gate opens to 1.00. The candidate 0.50 travels up the branch into the sum, and the carried bar crosses the sum and grows to 1.00 at the outlet: 0.50 of old content plus 0.50 of new.
        The output gate opens halfway, to 0.50. The branch through tanh lights and the hidden state rises to 0.38, half of tanh(1.00).
        The output gate shuts to 0.00. The hidden state falls to 0.00, with a dashed mark left where it stood. The cell state's bar does not move: the cell state is still 1.00. Closing the output gate hides the memory; it does not erase it.
        The two states are named: the cell state 1.00, long-term memory carried along the cell-state path, and the hidden state 0.00, the working memory the rest of the network sees.
        A tag records that the three gates are not knobs: the weight matrices behind them are learned.
      
      Silent; paused initially; 1.5× playback. Focus the animation pane: Space or K plays/pauses, arrows seek between beats, Home/End jump, Escape pauses. The scrubber and speed menu also work by keyboard. Reduced-motion mode holds each beat’s state: every gate stands at its beat’s opening, the carried bar stands at its beat’s station, and nothing is between two values.
    
  


Two states now travel: the cell state \(\vect{c}_t\) (long-term memory, carried along the cell-state path) and the hidden state \(\vect{h}_t\) (working memory, playing the vanilla RNN’s old role).
Let \(\vect{\gamma}_t := \partial L/\partial\vect{c}_t\) denote the loss derivative at the cell-state node. In the LSTM of Equation 12.5, the gates depend on \(\vect{h}_{t-1}\) and \(\vect{x}_t\), and only indirectly on \(\vect{c}_{t-1}\). With the previous hidden state and the current input held fixed, the direct cell-state Jacobian is diagonal. The contribution propagated from \(\vect{\gamma}_t\) along this path for \(\ell\) steps is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left.
\frac{\partial\vect{c}_t}{\partial\vect{c}_{t-1}}
\right|_{\vect{h}_{t-1},\,\vect{x}_t\,\mathrm{fixed}}
&= \operatorname{diag}(\vect{f}_t),\\
\vect{\gamma}_{t-\ell}^{\mathrm{direct}}
&= \left(\prod_{j=t-\ell+1}^{t}\vect{f}_j\right)
   \odot\vect{\gamma}_t .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.6}\]
The product is elementwise. Forget-gate values near one reduce attenuation along this direct path. The full gradient also includes paths through hidden states, candidate updates, and gates, so this contribution is only one part of the full recurrent Jacobian. A positive forget-gate bias increases retention at initialization, all other gate inputs held fixed. The experiments below test how this choice affects training.
PyTorch stores separate input-hidden and hidden-hidden bias vectors, then adds them. The code sets their sum to \(+1\); setting both slices to \(+1\) would silently create an effective bias of \(+2\). Figure 12.4 repeats the measurement of Figure 12.2 for this LSTM: at \(T=60\) its input gradient is about ten orders of magnitude larger than the vanilla RNN’s.



Build a seeded nn.LSTM and set its two forget-gate bias slices to sum to +1.
Measure the LSTM gradient norm across lag.



# [1]
torch.manual_seed(0)
lstm = nn.LSTM(4, 32, batch_first=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    n = lstm.bias_ih_l0.shape[0] // 4
    lstm.bias_ih_l0[n:2 * n].fill_(1.0)
    lstm.bias_hh_l0[n:2 * n].zero_()             # the two bias slices sum to +1
# [2]
g_lstm = grad_at_first_input(lstm, lags)










Figure 12.4: The gradient measurement of Figure 12.2, rerun on the same input sequences with an LSTM with the same input and hidden widths (4 inputs, 32 hidden units) whose effective forget-gate bias is initialized to \(+1\). The vanilla RNN’s input gradient decays exponentially with \(T\), and the LSTM’s decays much more slowly and arrives at lag 60 attenuated, about ten orders of magnitude stronger.

      Scope and caveats

This panel simplifies further on purpose: one constant f, multiplied 80 times. Nothing here is trained, and nothing here is a claim about training. title: 12  Sequences and Recurrence
text:
12.5 GRU: gating with one state
The Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014) implements the same ideas with fewer parts: cell and hidden state merged into one \(\vect{h}_t\), forget and input gates merged into a single update gate \(\vect{z}_t\) (what is kept is not overwritten, and vice versa), plus a reset gate \(\vect{r}_t\) that scales the previous state before it enters the candidate:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vect{z}_t &= \sigma\!\left(\matr{W}_z [\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_z\right), \qquad
\vect{r}_t = \sigma\!\left(\matr{W}_r [\vect{h}_{t-1}, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_r\right),\\
\tilde{\vect{h}}_t &= \tanh\!\left(\matr{W}_h [\vect{r}_t \odot \vect{h}_{t-1},\, \vect{x}_t] + \vect{b}_h\right), \qquad
\vect{h}_t = \vect{z}_t \odot \vect{h}_{t-1} + (1 - \vect{z}_t) \odot \tilde{\vect{h}}_t .
\end{aligned}
\tag{12.7}\]
This follows Cho et al.’s original convention: \(\vect{z}_t\) weights the old state, so it reads as keep. Some later references reverse the convention and let \(\vect{z}_t\) weight the candidate instead. Compare the interpolation equation, not the gate’s name alone.
The GRU has two gates instead of three and one state instead of two. The memory test below compares PyTorch’s version with the LSTM under one training protocol, and Exercise 3 builds one by hand. Figure 12.5 draws the cell on the layout of Figure 12.3.








Figure 12.5: The GRU cell on the LSTM cell’s layout. One state travels: the update gate \(z_t\) keeps a fraction of \(h_{t-1}\), and the same dial’s complement \(1 - z_t\) writes in the candidate \(\tilde{h}_t\). The reset gate \(r_t\) scales \(h_{t-1}\) before the candidate reads it, as in Equation 12.7.

      Scope and caveats
        The two values are round numbers inside the range of tanh, which shapes every candidate; the chapter trains its gates and prints no state values. A real state is a vector, and every coordinate of \( \vect{z}_t \) is a keep of its own, so one coordinate can hold its value while its neighbor is overwritten.
        The reset gate decides how much of the old state the candidate reads: it shapes the candidate before the blend and is not drawn. PyTorch’s reset-after candidate changes how the candidate is computed, not this blend.
        This panel follows the chapter’s convention: \( \vect{z}_t \) weights the old state, so it reads as keep. Some references swap the roles; compare the interpolation equation, not the gate’s name.
        Blue marks every value the cell carries: the filled circle is the old state, the hollow diamond the candidate, the ring the new state, and the arrows their kept and written shares, filled and hollow like the marks they come from. The keep and write bar and the dial are neutral ink: a gate weighs values and carries none. The bar puts write on the left and keep on the right, the sides where the candidate and the old state sit on the line and where the dial writes all or keeps all, and each share is named beside its value's mark.
      
    
    Check yourself. A GRU starts from h0 = 0, and every candidate it writes is a tanh output inside (−1, 1). Can a coordinate of its state ever reach 1.2, whatever the gates do?

    Transcript and keyboard help

        The keep halves to 0.5: the bar splits into write on the left and keep on the right, half each, and the new state leaves the picture. Predict: where does it land?

        The candidate becomes an arrow from 0 to 0.30. What is not kept is written: it shrinks to 0.5 × 0.30 = 0.15 and slides onto the tip of the kept arrow, and the new state lands at that tip, 0.40 + 0.15 = 0.55.
        The segment from the candidate to the old state is marked. With equal shares, 0.55 sits halfway along it.
        The dial turns up to full keep. The kept arrow grows back to 0.80, the written arrow shrinks to nothing, and the new state slides along the segment to 0.80.
        The dial turns down to keep 0. The kept arrow shrinks to nothing and the written arrow carries the whole candidate: the new state slides the length of the segment to 0.30, overwritten.
