The original Transformer normalized after each residual addition:
\[
\vect{x}\leftarrow\operatorname{LN}(\vect{x}+\operatorname{MHA}(\vect{x})),\qquad
\vect{x}\leftarrow\operatorname{LN}(\vect{x}+\operatorname{FFN}(\vect{x})).
\]
Our implementation adopts the now-standard pre-LayerNorm design:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vect{x}&\leftarrow \vect{x}+\operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LN}(\vect{x})),\\
\vect{x}&\leftarrow \vect{x}+\operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LN}(\vect{x})).
\end{aligned}
\]
Post-LayerNorm normalizes the aggregated representation after each residual addition, analogous to applying an activation function after the shortcut merge in early ResNets (Chapter 10). Pre-LayerNorm moves normalization into the function branch, mirroring pre-activation ResNets. Pre-LayerNorm keeps an unobstructed identity path along the residual stream, and in the experiments of Xiong et al. it trained without the learning-rate warmup (Chapter 4) that post-LayerNorm needed.
RMSNorm retains the rescaling but omits mean centering:
\[
\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\vect{x})
=\vect{g}\odot
\frac{\vect{x}}
{\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}x_\ell^2+\epsilon}}.
\]
It divides each token by its root-mean-square magnitude and applies a learned per-feature gain \(\vect{g}\). Prior to modulation by \(\vect{g}\), it rescales \(\vect{x}\) to a sphere of radius approximately \(\sqrt d\) without shifting the representation into the zero-mean subspace. This omits one reduction operation per token. Whether this computational saving translates into empirical gains depends on model scale, precision format, and memory bandwidth.


The position-wise feedforward network
Once tokens exchange information through attention, the same two-layer feedforward network processes each sequence position independently:
\[
\operatorname{FFN}(\vect{z})
=\matr{W}_2\operatorname{ReLU}(\matr{W}_1\vect{z}+\vect{b}_1)+\vect{b}_2,
\]
where \(\matr{W}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}\times d}\), \(\vect{b}_1\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}}\), \(\matr{W}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times
d_{\text{ff}}}\), and \(\vect{b}_2\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\).
With \(\vect{w}_{1j}^\top\) as row \(j\) of \(\matr{W}_1\) and \(\vect{u}_j\) as column \(j\) of \(\matr{W}_2\), the transformation decomposes as
\[
\operatorname{FFN}(\vect{z})
=\sum_j [\vect{w}_{1j}^\top \vect{z}+b_{1j}]_+\,\vect{u}_j+\vect{b}_2.
\]
This decomposition highlights an interpretation of the feedforward network as a key–value associative memory. Each row of \(\matr{W}_1\) acts as a pattern detector, testing whether the input falls within a learned half-space, and its rectified activation determines the degree to which the value vector \(\vect{u}_j\) is written to the representation. While Transformer feedforward layers can exhibit associative-memory behavior empirically, this remains an operational analogy: the activations are unnormalized, graded half-space responses rather than localized kernel weights that sum to one.
The complete block therefore alternates between two complementary operations:

causal multi-head attention routes information between sequence positions; and
the feedforward network transforms representations within each individual position.

Residual connections add the results of both operations to a single residual stream that persists across the depth of the network.






NoteWhat attention alone does to a stack of tokens



Within each attention head, every output is a convex combination of that head’s value vectors, so it lies within their convex hull. The multi-head output concatenates these averages and applies the output projection, a linear map that can move the result outside the hull of the original value vectors. Without residual shortcuts or feedforward layers, stacked attention layers apply such averaging again and again and can contract the token representations toward a single shared representation.
Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas formalized this rank collapse for unmasked attention. When the projection matrices are small enough in norm and the token embeddings are clustered, the authors’ bound on the distance from the token matrix to a rank-one subspace shrinks doubly exponentially with depth, with the exponent tripling at every layer. Their empirical evaluations reproduced this collapse across pretrained language models when residual connections were removed.
The residual update \(\vect{x}\leftarrow \vect{x}+F(\vect{x})\) provides a bypass around every attention layer. The identity branch propagates token differences forward directly without averaging, so the collapse is no longer forced. A shared position-wise FFN cannot restore distinctions once token representations are identical. It maps identical inputs to identical outputs. Feedforward layers can dilate existing token differences and slow the collapse, and residual connections provide a path that bypasses the repeated averaging. The cited collapse result holds under its stated assumptions. It does not describe every attention architecture without residual connections.

16.6 Character-level language modeling with a causal Transformer
To compare the causal Transformer directly against the recurrent baseline of Chapter 12, the experiment holds fixed every training setting that both architectures share. Chapter 12 trained on a committed snapshot of Chapters 1–6 and 8–10 with executable code cells and HTML comments removed: 148,594 characters, vocabulary 104, a contiguous 90/10 split, 100-character windows, batch size 64, and 2,501 updates with Adam at learning rate 0.002 and gradient clipping at norm 1. Freezing this text snapshot keeps the benchmark invariant across subsequent manuscript edits. The held-out evaluation scores each fixed window independently.
Although the two architectures differ in structure (recurrent gates versus attention blocks), their training inputs and parameter budgets can be matched. The code below reconstructs Chapter 12’s exact random-window schedule, then gives both Transformer variants the same initial parameter tensors and all 16,006,400 target characters in the same order.



Implement the tiny Transformer: positions, block, model.



# [1]
def sinusoidal_positions(length: int, width: int) -> torch.Tensor:
    position = torch.arange(length, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
    frequency = torch.exp(
        torch.arange(0, width, 2, dtype=torch.float32)
        * (-math.log(10_000.0) / width)
    )
    table = torch.zeros(length, width)
    table[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(position * frequency)
    table[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(position * frequency)
    return table

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.attention = CausalMultiHeadAttention(WIDTH, HEADS)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.ff = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(WIDTH, FF_WIDTH),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(FF_WIDTH, WIDTH),
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, return_weights: bool = False):
        if return_weights:
            attended, weights = self.attention(self.norm1(x), True)
            x = x + attended
            return x + self.ff(self.norm2(x)), weights
        x = x + self.attention(self.norm1(x))
        return x + self.ff(self.norm2(x))

class TinyTransformerLM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab: int, positions: bool) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.positions = positions
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab, WIDTH)
        nn.init.normal_(
            self.token_embedding.weight,
            mean=0.0,
            std=1 / math.sqrt(WIDTH),
        )
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
            [TransformerBlock() for _ in range(BLOCKS)]
        )
        self.final_norm = nn.LayerNorm(WIDTH)
        self.output = nn.Linear(WIDTH, vocab)
        self.register_buffer(
            "position_table",
            sinusoidal_positions(CONTEXT, WIDTH),
            persistent=False,
        )

    def forward(self, tokens: torch.Tensor, return_weights: bool = False):
        length = tokens.shape[1]
        x = self.token_embedding(tokens) * math.sqrt(WIDTH)
        if self.positions:
            x = x + self.position_table[:length]
        maps = []
        for block in self.blocks:
            if return_weights:
                x, weights = block(x, True)
                maps.append(weights)
            else:
                x = block(x)
        logits = self.output(self.final_norm(x))
        return (logits, maps) if return_weights else logits


To match the window sequence of Chapter 12, an isolated generator steps through the same random state that produced the LSTM’s minibatches and precomputes the start indices for every update before training begins. Both Transformer variants then load the same saved initial parameter snapshot:



Redraw Chapter 12’s window schedule, clone one Transformer initialization, and hash both.
Implement the paired protocol: shared schedule, identical initial tensors.

The architecture contains 132,488 trainable parameters, 736 fewer than the LSTM of Chapter 12 (133,224 parameters), so the parameter counts match to within 0.55%. Its model dimension is \(d=84\), divided into \(N_h=4\) heads of width \(D_h=21\). Each of the two feedforward sublayers expands to \(d_{\text{ff}}=168\) features, with a ReLU between its two linear layers. We initialize token embeddings with coordinate standard deviation \(1/\sqrt d\) prior to the \(\sqrt d\) scaling, ensuring embedding features and sinusoidal coordinates begin on comparable scales. ModuleList registers the two repeated blocks with the model. The position table is registered as a non-persistent buffer: it moves with the module across devices but is neither optimized nor included in the state-dictionary fingerprint, as its entries derive deterministically from the closed-form formula. With dropout disabled, resetting the parameter tensors and window sequence makes the positional ablation reproducible.






TipOne shared seed does not guarantee identical minibatches



Setting the same random seed before two training runs does not guarantee that both models encounter identical minibatches. Module instantiation consumes random draws, so differing architectural graphs silently shift the stream of random draws for all subsequent operations. To enforce a controlled ablation, we precompute the full window-index tensor with an isolated generator and initialize both models from an identical parameter snapshot, logging SHA-256 fingerprints for both artifacts.


We reuse the training and evaluation harnesses of Chapter 12 unchanged. The trainer’s signature:



Reuse the shared trainer through its explicit model, data, schedule, and optimization interface.

from dlbook.training import fit_next_token      # Listing 12.1, Ch. 12
from dlbook.evaluation import fixed_window_loss  # Listing 12.2, Ch. 12

# [1]
def train_transformer(
    positions: bool,
) -> tuple[nn.Module, list[tuple[int, float]]]:
    net = TinyTransformerLM(len(chars), positions=positions)
    net.load_state_dict(initial_state, strict=True)  # paired start: same tensors
    assert state_digest(net.state_dict()) == initial_hash
    return fit_next_token(
        net, train_data, vocab=len(chars),
        schedule=starts,                 # minibatch order is protocol, not chance
        log_every=250, log_decimals=4,
    )

@torch.no_grad()
def transformer_sample(
    net: nn.Module,
    prompt: str,
    n: int = 300,
    temperature: float = 0.8,
) -> str:
    net.eval()
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1_406_050)
    tokens = [stoi.get(char, 0) for char in prompt]
    for _ in range(n):
        context = torch.tensor(tokens[-CONTEXT:]).unsqueeze(0)
        probabilities = F.softmax(
            net(context)[0, -1] / temperature, dim=-1
        )
        next_token = torch.multinomial(
            probabilities, 1, generator=generator
        ).item()
        tokens.append(next_token)
    return "".join(chars[index] for index in tokens)

Figure 16.8 plots both training curves alongside held-out losses: the curves separate within the first 250 updates, and the gap persists throughout training. The positional model has a loss of 1.1132 on a full deterministic pass over the training corpus and 1.9190 on the held-out tail. Removing positional encodings raises these values to 1.8672 and 2.3405, respectively. Positional encodings lower held-out loss by 0.4214, or 18.0% relative to the variant without them.






WarningTrap: overinterpreting a single controlled run



The causal mask inherently leaks ordinal information: row \(i\) attends only to a prefix of length \(i+1\), allowing stacked layers to infer position from expanding receptive fields. That is why the model without positional encodings performs better than an orderless model would. Haviv et al. trained causal language models up to 1.3 billion parameters without positional encodings and found that held-out perplexity closely approached that of sinusoidal baselines as scale increased. A small probe network trained on internal activations recovered approximate token positions, and the authors conjectured that the causal mask supplies this signal through the count of predecessors. At our compact scale, however, explicit sinusoidal encodings provide a substantial empirical advantage.
Yet the LSTM of Chapter 12 still has a held-out loss 0.0309 (1.64%) lower than that of the positional Transformer. In this regime, with 100 characters of context and approximately 133,000 parameters, the sequential inductive bias of recurrence remains competitive. This experiment matches corpus, parameter count, gradient updates, minibatch order, and optimization settings, but it does not imply that either architecture reached its tuned optimum. Because the experiment uses a single initialization seed, these results are a controlled case study rather than an average over random trials.



What did the heads route?
An attention map records internal routing weights, not causal explanations, predictive confidence, or mechanistic justifications. Nonetheless, inspecting learned weight distributions can verify the mask and reveal the patterns that emerged during training.     learned.sum(dim=-1),
    torch.ones_like(learned.sum(dim=-1)),
    atol=1e-6,

# [2]

print(
    "maximum row-sum error:",
    (learned.sum(dim=-1) - 1).abs().max().item(),
)

Figure 16.9: Learned attention weights in the second block for the prompt “The gradient ”. The maps are real routing distributions, not explanations or named head roles.





The learned maps satisfy both specifications: future positions receive identically zero weight, and each query row sums to one within single-precision floating-point tolerance. While the four heads exhibit distinct routing behaviors, labeling them as “the previous-character head” or “the word head” from a single prompt exceeds what the evidence establishes. Attention weights merely indicate where representations were pooled. Downstream feedforward layers and residual connections can transform, modulate, or neutralize what was retrieved.


Autoregressive sampling and qualitative evaluation
Both Transformer variants can generate text autoregressively: at each step, the model truncates the context to the most recent 100 characters, evaluates a categorical distribution over the vocabulary, samples a character, and appends it to the prefix. Unlike the LSTM of Chapter 12, this baseline implementation maintains no persistent recurrent state. It evaluates the entire context window afresh at every generation step.






TipPractice bridge (optional): decoding is another model choice



For next-token logits \(z_i\), temperature is the dial from Chapter 2: it divides each logit by \(T\) before the softmax:
\[
p_i(T)=\frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j\exp(z_j/T)},\qquad T>0.
\]
Lower \(T\) concentrates probability; higher \(T\) flattens it. Top-\(k\) sampling keeps the \(k\) largest logits, sets the rest to negative infinity, then renormalizes. Nucleus (top-\(p\)) sampling first sorts the model probabilities and keeps the smallest prefix whose cumulative mass reaches \(p\), then renormalizes. The former fixes a candidate count; the latter lets that count adapt to the distribution’s shape. Neither changes the trained weights, and neither guarantees a better sample.
Keeping a set of tokens and renormalizing, as top-\(k\) and nucleus sampling do, is what the causal mask does to each attention row (zero the excluded entries, divide the rest by their sum), with next tokens in place of keys. It gives the distribution over the next token conditioned on that token lying in the kept set. Enforcing a rule that forbids tokens, such as characters that would break the ISO date format of Chapter 13, conditions the distribution at each step in the same way. A sampler that does this at every step need not return the outputs the rule allows in proportion to their probabilities under the model (Exercise 9 of Chapter 13).
For evaluation, if \(L\) is mean token negative log-likelihood in natural-log units, perplexity is \(\exp(L)\). It is an exponentiated loss, not a fluency score. Compare it only under the same tokenization, data, and per-token averaging.

title: 16  Self-Attention and the Transformer
section: 16.7 Architectural trade-offs: gains and costs of self-attention
text:
16.7 Architectural trade-offs: gains and costs of self-attention
During autoregressive generation, exact attention converts past context into both a memory footprint and a computational bottleneck: every newly generated query must attend over all preceding keys and values. A key–value (KV) cache stores the projected key and value tensors from earlier steps, allowing new queries to attend over the prefix without recomputing historical activations. In the nonparametric regression framework of Chapter 14, the KV cache serves as the estimator’s dataset: an incoming query at step \(t\) reads a table that grows with \(t\), but earlier rows no longer require recomputation. In contrast, our sampler re-evaluates a sliding 100-character window with absolute slot encodings: when the window slides, every retained token shifts to a new slot index, changing its input representation. Caching past the window limit therefore requires a new positional or memory policy, not a drop-in speedup. Appendix C separates KV caching from FlashAttention’s I/O-aware kernel scheduling.
Self-attention leaves position and visibility to the modeler. Chapter 18 modifies visibility itself, while Chapter 19 explores what occurs when global routing trades away an image model’s locality bias.
Varying the kernel, predictor class, or update rule within this regression perspective yields alternative memory formulations. The following interlude contrasts the growing KV cache with finite sufficient statistics and delta updates.
Readers seeking deeper mathematical analysis of these architectures will find kernel geometry, exact I/O-aware algorithms, parallel recurrence, and feature-learning regimes in Shakeri (2026), “Beyond This Volume”.

title: 16  Self-Attention and the Transformer
section: 16.8 Okay, so: the Transformer routes, then transforms
text:
16.8 Okay, so: the Transformer routes, then transforms

Self-attention reuses the scaled dot-product operator within a single sequence. Queries, keys, and values \(\matr{Q},\matr{K},\matr{V}\) all derive from the same input \(\matr{X}\), and one learned comparison rule is shared across every permitted query–key pair. All sequence positions can be evaluated in parallel during training, while autoregressive generation remains sequential.
Without positional signals or a mask, self-attention is permutation equivariant, not invariant. \(\operatorname{SA}(\matr{P}\matr{X})=\matr{P}\operatorname{SA}(\matr{X})\). Sinusoidal clocks supply the order that global routing lacks (and that the convolutions of Chapter 9 built in), while sine–cosine coordinate pairs express relative displacements as planar rotations.
Multi-head attention routes in parallel through partitioned subspaces. The computation partitions \((B,n,d)\to(B,N_h,n,D_h)\), scales scores by \(\sqrt{D_h}\), forms \((B,N_h,n,n)\) routing weights, concatenates, and projects. At fixed \(d\), the four projection matrices hold \(4d^2\) weights regardless of head count \(N_h\).
The causal mask defines visibility, not computational cost. Future compatibility scores are set to \(-\infty\) prior to softmax. The underlying operator remains quadratic in sequence length.
The block alternates routing across positions and transformation within them. The attention and feedforward sublayers both add corrections to the residual stream of Chapter 10, and layer normalization standardizes the features of each token independently.
Position lowers held-out loss in this controlled benchmark. Explicit positional encodings reduce held-out loss from 2.3405 to 1.9190. Under this matched protocol, the compact LSTM has a slightly lower held-out loss than the small Transformer (1.8881 versus 1.9190). An architecture changes inductive bias but does not guarantee lower loss in every scale and data regime.

title: 16  Self-Attention and the Transformer
text:
Sources and further reading

Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need: multi-head attention, sinusoidal position, and the original post-LayerNorm encoder–decoder.
Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding: rotates queries and keys so their positional interaction is expressed through relative offset.
Ba, Kiros, and Hinton, Layer Normalization: normalization within one example and identical train/evaluation computation.
Zhang and Sennrich, Root Mean Square Layer Normalization: RMSNorm’s scale-only normalization and empirical study. 
Xiong et al., On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture: a qualified comparison of pre- and post-LayerNorm optimization: post-LayerNorm’s gradient growth near the output layers at initialization, and pre-LayerNorm training without warmup. 
Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas, Attention Is Not All You Need: Pure Attention Loses Rank Doubly Exponentially with Depth: bounds the distance of a pure-attention stack’s output from a common row. For small projection norms and clustered tokens the bound shrinks doubly exponentially with depth. Residual connections remove this forced collapse, and FFNs can slow it.
Geva et al., Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories: empirical evidence behind the associative-memory interpretation of FFNs. 
Haviv et al., Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information: causal language models trained without positional encodings come close to models with them in held-out loss and still carry each token’s approximate position, and the authors conjecture that the causal mask supplies it.
Jain and Wallace, Attention Is Not Explanation: an important limit on reading attention maps as explanations. 
Tsai et al., Transformer Dissection: An Unified Understanding for Transformer’s Attention via the Lens of Kernel: attention written as a kernel smoother, with a comparison of kernel choices that includes a symmetric kernel made by tying the query and key projections.
Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration: nucleus sampling and the distinction between likely continuations and useful generation behavior. 
Park et al., Grammar-Aligned Decoding: shows that a sampler that forbids, at each step, every token that cannot lead to a grammatical output can return grammatical outputs at rates not proportional to the model’s probabilities, as in Exercise 9 of Chapter 13.
Shakeri, Deep Learning: Making It Trainable (2026), “Beyond This Volume”: kernel geometry, exact I/O-aware algorithms, parallel recurrence, and feature-learning regimes.

title: 17  Interlude: Attention as Test-Time Regression
text:
17.1 Three memory constructions through regression
During autoregressive generation, a causal Transformer can retain the keys and values of earlier tokens in a key–value (KV) cache, described in the architectural trade-offs section of Chapter 16, so that each new query attends to all prior tokens without recomputing them. This interlude compares three ways to construct that memory computation: a query-local fit over stored pairs, running statistics for a factorized kernel, and an online linear predictor updated by the delta rule.
Read this way, attention is an online regression estimator at test time. The constructions share a regression perspective, but they need not solve the same optimization problem. Softmax attention, linear attention, state-space models and DeltaNet differ in the kernel, the predictor class, the regularization and the update rule, and these choices determine both the answer and the information that must be retained.
The recurrent networks of Chapter 12 compressed the history into a fixed-size state. The Transformer resolved that bottleneck by keeping the visible key–value rows available. Reading those rows becomes more expensive as the prefix grows, and across a complete sequence dense routing has quadratic cost. There is another resolution: return to the regression perspective of Chapter 14 and change the kernel, the predictor class, or the update rule. Some of these choices permit a state of fixed size.
Recent sequence models make that move under names such as test-time regression, test-time training, fast weights, linear attention, DeltaNet, Titans, MesaNet, and state-space sequence models. Each solver is characterized by what information it retains and what computational trade-offs it accepts.

title: 17  Interlude: Attention as Test-Time Regression
text:
Choices within the regression framework
At time \(t\), let learned projections turn each token representation \(\vect{x}_\tau\) into two views,
\[
\vect{k}_\tau=\matr{W}_K\vect{x}_\tau,
\qquad
\vect{v}_\tau=\matr{W}_V\vect{x}_\tau.
\]
Following Wang, Shi, and Fox (2025), we describe memory construction as a weighted regression problem. A memory layer builds an online predictor \(M_t:\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_v}\):
\[
M_t
=\arg\min_{M\in\mathcal{M}}
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau\le t}w_{t,\tau}
\norm{M(\vect{k}_\tau)-\vect{v}_\tau}^{2}
+\Omega(M),
\qquad
\vect{y}_t=M_t(\vect{q}_t),
\quad \vect{q}_t=\matr{W}_Q\vect{x}_t.
\]
The display specifies a reference fitting problem. An online update need not attain its minimizer. Query-local attention also makes the observation weights depend on the query, as the next construction shows.
Here the keys and values are computed from the input sequence. The memory state changes during the forward computation, while the projection parameters are held fixed during that evaluation. The frame exposes four design choices.
The views. \(\matr{W}_Q,\matr{W}_K,\matr{W}_V\) are the learned projections of Chapter 16: queries and keys are compared, and values are what the comparison passes on. The token is not assigned one permanent meaning. The three projections give it a query, a key that provides the features used for comparison, and a value.
The history weights. \(w_{t,\tau}\) determine how much an older residual matters to the fitting problem. The forget gates of Chapter 12 already made retention depend on time and content. A geometric schedule can privilege recent errors; an input-dependent schedule can keep some tokens longer than others.
The model and regularizer. The class \(\mathcal{M}\) determines whether the predictor is a local constant, a linear map, or something richer. \(\Omega\) brings back ridge penalties from Chapter 1 and weight decay from Chapter 4. Regularization controls the fitted map. It is not, by itself, the same operation as forgetting old observations.
The solver. A closed-form local fit, a running sufficient statistic, and one gradient step do different work and preserve different information. A layer may compute a closed-form solution or execute an iterative or approximate update, whose rule may itself be learned.
This objective is an umbrella, not an equivalence theorem. Its methods can restrict different function classes, use different weights, and stop at different approximations.


Solver 1: keep the data and fit at the query
Softmax attention instantiates the framework as a query-local constant estimator. For a query \(\vect{q}\), the predictor class \(\mathcal{M}\) is restricted to constant vectors \(\vect{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}\), and observation weights are the query-dependent affinities, yielding the local-constant problem
\[
\vect{c}^{*}(\vect{q})
=\arg\min_{\vect{c}}
\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau\le t}
\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k}_\tau)
\norm{\vect{c}-\vect{v}_\tau}^{2}.
\]
Write \(\kappa_\tau=\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k}_\tau)\). Differentiation gives
\[
\nabla_{\vect{c}}=
\sum_{\tau\le t}\kappa_\tau(\vect{c}-\vect{v}_\tau)=\vect{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\vect{c}^{*}=
\frac{\sum_\tau\kappa_\tau\vect{v}_\tau}{\sum_\tau\kappa_\tau}.
\]
Choose \(\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k})=\exp(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k}/\sqrt{d_k})\) and the normalized coefficients form a row of scaled dot-product softmax. The kernel supplies the weights, and the constant fit supplies the average. An unrestricted \(M\) with unit observation weights and no regularizer would instead interpolate compatible training pairs and be undetermined away from them.
We can check numerically that the gradient vanishes at the weighted average. Subtracting the largest score rescales every \(\kappa_\tau\) by the same positive constant and leaves the minimizer unchanged.



Draw 12 seeded key-value pairs and a query, then form the weighted average, softmax output, and gradient.
Verify softmax attention’s local-constant optimum.
Print the largest absolute entry of the stationarity gradient.



# [1]
ms_rng = np.random.default_rng(6050)
ms_d, ms_T = 8, 12
ms_K = ms_rng.standard_normal((ms_T, ms_d))
ms_V = ms_rng.standard_normal((ms_T, 3))
ms_q = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d)
ms_scores = ms_K @ ms_q / np.sqrt(ms_d)
ms_kappa = np.exp(ms_scores - ms_scores.max())
ms_c = (ms_kappa[:, None] * ms_V).sum(0) / ms_kappa.sum()
ms_attention = (ms_kappa / ms_kappa.sum()) @ ms_V
ms_gradient = (ms_kappa[:, None] * (ms_c - ms_V)).sum(0)
# [2]
assert np.allclose(ms_c, ms_attention)
# [3]
print(f"max |stationarity gradient|: {np.abs(ms_gradient).max():.3e}")

max |stationarity gradient|: 3.053e-16



This solver retains the key–value rows because a future query may weight every row differently. That is why dense causal attention carries a growing dataset forward.


Solver 2: collapse a factorized kernel into sufficient state
Suppose the kernel factors through a finite feature map \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{r}\):
\[
\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k})
=\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}).
\]
Assume the resulting kernel is nonnegative on the pairs being used and that the normalization denominator is positive. The positive feature map used below satisfies these conditions. Substitute that factorization into the weighted average and regroup terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vect{y}_t(\vect{q})
&=\frac{\sum_{\tau\le t}
\bigl[\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)\bigr]\vect{v}_\tau}
{\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)} \\
&=\frac{\matr{S}_t^\top\phi(\vect{q})}
     {\vect{z}_t^\top\phi(\vect{q})},
\qquad
\matr{S}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_v},
\quad
\vect{z}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{r},
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\matr{S}_t=\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)\vect{v}_\tau^{\top},
\qquad
\vect{z}_t=\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau).
\]
The sufficient state is the pair \((\matr{S}_t,\vect{z}_t)\), not \(\matr{S}_t\) alone: the numerator needs accumulated value-weighted features and the denominator needs its normalizer. Each new pair updates that fixed-size state once. For this factorized kernel, any later query gets the same answer from the state as from a full traversal of all pairs.



Define the reusable ms_phi helper.
Initialize the sufficient-state pair, ms_S and ms_z, as zero arrays.
Compare a factorized-kernel traversal with its running state.
Check the claimed identities, shapes, or invariants.
Print whether ms_streaming matches ms_traversal and their largest absolute difference.



# [1]
def ms_phi(x):
    return np.where(x > 0, x + 1, np.exp(x))

# [2]
ms_S = np.zeros((ms_d, ms_V.shape[1]))
ms_z = np.zeros(ms_d)
# [3]
for ms_key, ms_value in zip(ms_K, ms_V, strict=True):
    ms_S += np.outer(ms_phi(ms_key), ms_value)
    ms_z += ms_phi(ms_key)
ms_streaming = (ms_S.T @ ms_phi(ms_q)) / (ms_z @ ms_phi(ms_q))
ms_weights = ms_phi(ms_K) @ ms_phi(ms_q)
ms_traversal = (ms_weights[:, None] * ms_V).sum(0) / ms_weights.sum()
# [4]
assert np.allclose(ms_streaming, ms_traversal)
# [5]
print("streaming equals traversal:", np.allclose(ms_streaming, ms_traversal))
print(f"max |difference|: {np.abs(ms_streaming-ms_traversal).max():.3e}")

streaming equals traversal: True
max |difference|: 3.469e-17



The identity is exact in real arithmetic. In floating point the two results can differ slightly, because the sums are accumulated in a different order. The traversal of the full dataset has collapsed into two running sums. With \(r\) and \(d_v\) fixed, storage no longer grows with the prefix. Causal linear attention can therefore run as a recurrence: its state stores the sufficient statistics of this regression.
This construction has a limitation. Ordinary softmax’s exponential dot-product kernel does not have a finite exact feature map like the one used above. With the scale \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) absorbed into \(\vect{q}\), the kernel has the Taylor series \(\exp(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})=\sum_{m\ge0}(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{m}/m!\). Each power \((\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{m}\) is a dot product of features built from all products of \(m\) coordinates, as in \((\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{2}=\sum_{a,a'}(q_a q_{a'})(k_a k_{a'})\), so the series gives an exact feature map with such features for every \(m\), infinitely many in all. Changing to a finite factorization changes the kernel, or approximates it.1 The state preserves the chosen kernel’s readout for every query, but not the individual stored pairs: a discarded row cannot be revisited. The traversal equality is exact for the chosen factorized kernel, not a proof that finite-state linear attention reproduces exact softmax for arbitrary prefixes.


Solver 3: take one gradient step and get the delta rule
Now restrict the predictor to a scalar linear map \(M(\vect{q})=\vect{h}^{\top}\vect{q}\) and let the solver take one SGD step on only the newest pair. Its instantaneous loss and gradient are
\[
\ell_t(\vect{h})
=\frac{1}{2}(\vect{h}^{\top}\vect{k}_t-v_t)^2,
\qquad
\nabla_{\vect{h}}\ell_t
=\vect{k}_t(\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{h}-v_t).
\]
Substituting the gradient into the update gives the delta recurrence in two lines:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vect{h}_t
&=\vect{h}_{t-1}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t
  (\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{h}_{t-1}-v_t)\\
&=(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})\vect{h}_{t-1}
  +\eta_t v_t\vect{k}_t.
\end{aligned}
\]



Set ms_eta to 0.3, draw a weight vector, key, and scalar value, and compute both update forms.
Verify that one SGD step is the delta recurrence.
Print whether the two updates agree and their largest absolute difference.



# [1]
ms_eta = 0.3
ms_h = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d)
ms_k = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d)
ms_v = ms_rng.standard_normal()
ms_sgd = ms_h - ms_eta * ms_k * (ms_k @ ms_h - ms_v)
ms_delta = ((np.eye(ms_d) - ms_eta * np.outer(ms_k, ms_k)) @ ms_h
            + ms_eta * ms_v * ms_k)
# [2]
assert np.allclose(ms_sgd, ms_delta)
# [3]
print("SGD equals Delta recurrence:", np.allclose(ms_sgd, ms_delta))
print(f"max |difference|: {np.abs(ms_sgd-ms_delta).max():.3e}")

SGD equals Delta recurrence: True
max |difference|: 4.441e-16



For vector values, store \(\matr{H}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}\), read a query as \(M(\vect{q})=\matr{H}_t\vect{q}\), and replace the update by
\[
\matr{H}_t
=\matr{H}_{t-1}
+\eta_t(\vect{v}_t-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{k}_t)\vect{k}_t^{\top}.
\]
Each outer product writes the residual left by the current key. The update changes a query’s readout in proportion to its inner product with that key, \(\matr{H}_t\vect{q}-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{q}=\eta_t(\vect{v}_t-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{k}_t)(\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{q})\), so a query orthogonal to the key reads the same value before and after the update. DeltaNet turns that classical online least-squares step into a sequence layer. Expanding the update gives \(\matr{H}_t=\matr{H}_{t-1}(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})+\eta_t\vect{v}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top}\), where the transition matrix acts on the state from the right. In transposed form, \(\matr{H}_t^{\top}=(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})\matr{H}_{t-1}^{\top}+\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{v}_t^{\top}\), exposing a state-space form where \(\matr{A}_t=\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top}\) acts on the key space from the left and the input write is the outer product \(\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{v}_t^{\top}\). The state transition is therefore determined by the current token’s learned key.
Exponential history weights \(w_{t,\tau}=\gamma^{t-\tau}\) introduce forgetting into the least-squares objective, but its exact minimizer generally requires a recursive least-squares covariance state. Writing \(\gamma\matr{H}_{t-1}\) into a one-step delta recurrence is a fading-memory solver choice, not an algebraic consequence of those weights. Gates can make that retention and the step size depend on the current token.
Such gates link this recurrence to the wider state-space model (SSM) family (connected to the parallel-recurrence bridge of Exercise 8 of Chapter 12). Mamba makes parts of its state transition, input injection, and readout depend on the token; in the regression frame, those mechanisms play roles analogous to a learnable schedule for what to keep and what to write. Gated DeltaNet adds learned gating around delta-style updates. That reading is an analogy, not a claim that Mamba is literally obtained by differentiating the shared regression objective. Structured SSMs also use different state parameterizations and can cost less, in retained state and per-token work, than the dense outer-product recurrence here.


Retained state and per-token work















Figure 17.1: The solver map compares retained state and per-token work. Its positions are qualitative; the formulas and direct labels give the asymptotic costs for the stated dense setup.



The asymptotic labels in Figure 17.1 describe this dense setup, not every implementation. Feature width \(r\), head dimensions, low-rank structure, convolutions, and hardware schedules change the constants and sometimes the order of growth.






WarningTrap: attention’s memory is a dataset, not a hidden box



Attention does not have a separate memory in the recurrent sense. The attention operation is the estimator. During causal decoding, the KV cache is the observed key–value dataset it must retain. A nonparametric query rule keeps a growing dataset so it can form a new local fit. A parametric state instead compresses those data into a fixed-size object. FlashAttention changes how the uncompressed fit is scheduled, but it does not compress the history into a fixed-size state. “Retains every row” does not mean “recalls every association without error.” Softmax still returns a convex mixture whose quality depends on keys, temperature, and interference.




Mechanism test: recall under a fixed capacity
The storage comparison motivates a recall experiment to evaluate how the one-pass delta update behaves as more associations are written into a state of fixed dimension. We store \(N\) random unit key–value pairs, query every stored key, and decode each retrieved vector to the nearest stored value. Exact softmax attention keeps all pairs. A dense delta state has \(d^2\) numbers regardless of \(N\). A selective delta arm receives one extra priority bit and writes ordinary pairs at only one-tenth strength, so the bit marks the pairs that the arm favors.
We developed the study on two groups of seeds. On those groups we fixed \(\eta=0.20\), the 25% priority rate, the 0.10 ordinary write gate, dimensions \((8,16,32)\), and loads \(N/d\in(0.5,1,2,4,8)\). After fixing these settings, we evaluated a third, disjoint group, the held-out group, with 30 repetitions for each dimension and load. All methods in a trial receive the same keys, values, order, queries, and decoder. The code below is the frozen protocol; it runs on CPU in under a second on the reference machine.



Fix the seed, step size, ordinary write gate, three dimensions, five loads, and 30 repetitions.
Define the reusable helpers: ms_unit and ms_decode.
Define the reusable helpers: ms_trial and ms_panel.
Run the sealed synthetic recall-under-capacity study.



# [1]
MS_SEED, MS_ETA, MS_GATE = 6050, 0.20, 0.10
MS_DIMS, MS_LOADS, MS_REPEATS = (8, 16, 32), (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), 30

# [2]
def ms_unit(x):
    return x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)

def ms_decode(prediction, values):
    return np.argmax(prediction @ values.T, axis=1)

# [3]
def ms_trial(rng, repeat, d, load):
    n = max(4, round(load * d))
    keys = ms_unit(rng.standard_normal((n, d)))
    values = ms_unit(rng.standard_normal((n, d)))
    priority = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)
    priority[rng.permutation(n)[:max(1, round(0.25 * n))]] = True

    scores = 32.0 * (keys @ keys.T)
    scores -= scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    weights = np.exp(scores); weights /= weights.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    attention = weights @ values

    def delta(write_gate):
        state = np.zeros((d, d))
        for key, value, gate in zip(keys, values, write_gate, strict=True):
            state += MS_ETA * gate * np.outer(value - state @ key, key)
        return keys @ state.T

    plain = delta(np.ones(n))
    selective = delta(np.where(priority, 1.0, MS_GATE))
    truth = np.arange(n)
    correct = lambda pred: ms_decode(pred, values) == truth
    a_ok, d_ok, s_ok = correct(attention), correct(plain), correct(selective)
    ordinary = ~priority
    return [repeat, d, n, load, a_ok.mean(), ((attention-values)**2).mean(),
            d_ok.mean(), d_ok[priority].mean(), d_ok[ordinary].mean(),
            s_ok.mean(), s_ok[priority].mean(), s_ok[ordinary].mean()]

def ms_panel(tag, repeats):
    seeds = np.random.SeedSequence([MS_SEED, tag]).spawn(
        repeats * len(MS_DIMS) * len(MS_LOADS))
    rows, index = [], 0
    for repeat in range(repeats):
        for d in MS_DIMS:
            for load in MS_LOADS:
                rows.append(ms_trial(np.random.default_rng(seeds[index]),
                                     repeat, d, load))
                index += 1
    return np.asarray(rows)

# Tags 0 and 1 were development; tag 2 remained sealed until settings were fixed.
ms_development = np.vstack([ms_panel(tag, 5) for tag in (0, 1)])
assert np.all(ms_development[:, 4] == 1.0)
ms_endpoint = ms_panel(2, MS_REPEATS)
assert np.all(ms_endpoint[:, 4] == 1.0)

print("study_seed=6050; development_tags=(0, 1); sealed_endpoint_tag=2")
print("endpoint_trials=30 x 3 dimensions; d=(8, 16, 32); "
      "N/d=(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)")
print("fixed: eta=0.20; priority_fraction=0.25; ordinary_write_gate=0.10")
print("load  attention  Delta  gated-all  gated-priority  gated-ordinary")
# [4]
for load in MS_LOADS:
    block = ms_endpoint[ms_endpoint[:, 3] == load]
    means = block[:, [4, 6, 9, 10, 11]].mean(0)
    print(f"{load:>4.1f}   " + "  ".join(f"{value:.3f}" for value in means))

hard = ms_endpoint[ms_endpoint[:, 3] == 8]
priority_gain = hard[:, 10] - hard[:, 7]
ordinary_gain = hard[:, 11] - hard[:, 8]
print(f"N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta priority: {priority_gain.mean():+.3f} "
      f"(SD {priority_gain.std(ddof=1):.3f})")
print(f"N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta ordinary: {ordinary_gain.mean():+.3f} "
      f"(SD {ordinary_gain.std(ddof=1):.3f})")
print(f"attention top-1 failures=0/{int(ms_endpoint[:, 2].sum())}")
print(f"mean value MSE={ms_endpoint[:, 5].mean():.2e}; "
      f"max trial MSE={ms_endpoint[:, 5].max():.2e}")

study_seed=6050; development_tags=(0, 1); sealed_endpoint_tag=2
endpoint_trials=30 x 3 dimensions; d=(8, 16, 32); N/d=(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)
fixed: eta=0.20; priority_fraction=0.25; ordinary_write_gate=0.10
load  attention  Delta  gated-all  gated-priority  gated-ordinary

 1.0   1.000  0.910  0.352  0.992  0.139
 2.0   1.000  0.657  0.282  0.982  0.048
 4.0   1.000  0.338  0.228  0.848  0.022
 8.0   1.000  0.134  0.138  0.522  0.010
N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta priority: +0.387 (SD 0.156)
N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta ordinary: -0.124 (SD 0.065)
attention top-1 failures=0/26040
mean value MSE=5.43e-06; max trial MSE=4.55e-04


















Figure 17.2: A sealed synthetic mechanism test. The uncompressed table keeps perfect top-1 identification in this sharp-softmax construction, while the fixed delta state loses associations as \(N/d\) grows. The selective arm receives a priority bit that the other arms lack and trades ordinary recall for priority recall. Keys, values, order, queries, decoder, and feature dimension \(d\) are matched; stored data, side information, and inference arithmetic are not.



At \(N/d=8\), the gate raises priority recall over the plain delta state by 0.387 on average and lowers ordinary recall by 0.124. The gate favors the retention of priority pairs at the expense of ordinary pairs, and total recall barely moves. Overall gated recall is 0.138 while plain delta recall is 0.134 at that load. Given an extra signal, a fixed state can allocate its capacity differently.
These results show interference under the specified delta update as the number of stored pairs grows. They do not establish a universal recall limit for fixed-size recurrent states. Now we can compare the three solvers. Keeping the dataset provides uncompressed access at growing cost. Sufficient statistics give exact streaming evaluation for the chosen factorized kernel. Delta updates instead maintain a fixed-size predictor whose stored associations can interfere. The RNN state has returned as one of these statistical choices.






NoteCheck yourself



Close the book for one minute and list what each solver keeps.

Which solver retains the original key–value rows?
Why does a factorized kernel need both \(\matr{S}_t\) and \(\vect{z}_t\)?
What information can a fixed delta state overwrite as its load grows?

title: 17  Interlude: Attention as Test-Time Regression
section: 17.2 Okay, so: the solver is part of the architecture
text:
17.2 Okay, so: the solver is part of the architecture

The objective alone does not specify the memory system. Views, history weights, function class, regularizer, and solver jointly define the result.
Softmax attention keeps the dataset for query-dependent reads. It preserves every key–value row, and its read cost grows with the prefix.
A finite kernel feature map admits sufficient state. The pair \((\matr{S}_t,\vect{z}_t)\) reproduces the chosen factorized-kernel traversal without retaining raw rows.
One SGD step yields a delta update. Its fixed matrix writes residuals online, which makes capacity and interference explicit.
Selective retention reallocates a fixed capacity. The sealed recall study shows a gate trading ordinary recall for priority recall, without establishing a universal architecture ranking.

Sources and further reading

Katharopoulos et al., Transformers Are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention: the recurrent sufficient-state form for causal linear attention. 
Choromanski et al., Rethinking Attention with Performers: positive random features whose dot product equals softmax’s exponential kernel in expectation.
Schlag, Irie, and Schmidhuber, Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers: the connection among linear attention, fast weights, and the delta update.
Gu and Dao, Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces: input-dependent state-space parameters, related to the regression frame by analogy rather than exact equivalence.
Yang et al., Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule: learned gating around delta-style associative updates.
Wang, Shi, and Fox, Test-Time Regression: A Unifying Framework for Designing Sequence Models with Associative Memory: the shared regression objective and solver-design perspective.
Sun et al., Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States: a sequence model’s hidden state as a learner updated by a self-supervised objective during the forward pass.
Behrouz et al., Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time: a learned long-term memory updated at test time.
von Oswald et al., MesaNet: Sequence Modeling by Locally Optimal Test-Time Training: sequence layers derived from locally solved test-time objectives.
Wang et al., Beyond Test-Time Memory: State-Space Optimal Control for LLM Reasoning: the objective changed from regression to finite-horizon optimal control, a reformulation that the epilogue treats as a research proposal rather than an established equivalence.

title: 18  The BERT Moment: Pretraining as the New Regime
text:
18.1 Separate controls, not one mask
In Chapter 10, we compared training from scratch with adapting features learned on another task. For language, task-specific labels can be scarce while unlabeled text is available. Can that text provide a useful training signal before we introduce a downstream task?
Masked language modeling constructs such a signal from the sequence itself. Replace bank in “the boat reached the bank” or “the bank approved the loan” and predict the original token from the corrupted input. Both examples have the same target word, but different contexts. The task provides token targets without requiring separate labels for word senses.
That move depends on what Chapter 16 showed: visibility is a modeling decision. A next-token model used a causal triangle because attending to future positions would reveal its target. A representation model can instead let every nonpadding token consult both sides, provided enough selected positions are masked or replaced in the input that copying cannot solve the whole task. Full visibility over a corrupted input, scored on the original selected tokens, gives masked language modeling (MLM). Pretraining on raw text changed the default workflow from “initialize and train” to “pretrain, then adapt.”
Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) uses a few special tokens. [CLS] is a learned summary placeholder, [SEP] marks a boundary, and [PAD] fills unused batch slots. Consider six positions:
\[
[\text{CLS}],\quad \text{the},\quad \text{bank},\quad \text{rose},\quad
[\text{SEP}],\quad [\text{PAD}].
\]
There are four distinct decisions in play.
Figure 18.1: Visibility and supervision are separate controls. A causal decoder permits a lower triangle (left). BERT-style attention permits every nonpadding key (center). The MLM selector marks one selected target position (right).
The center matrix contains no future-blocking triangle. Every nonpadding query can route from every nonpadding key, including itself. That is what bidirectional means here: a token’s representation can jointly use left and right context in every layer. It does not mean running two separate recurrent networks, and it does not define a left-to-right probability for the whole sentence.
Only padding keys are blocked in the drawing. A [PAD] query row can still produce an output, which downstream computation ignores; real queries, however, can never retrieve padding as information.
Now suppose bank is selected and replaced:
\[
[\text{CLS}]\ \text{the}\ [\text{MASK}]\ \text{rose}\ [\text{SEP}]\ [\text{PAD}].
\]
Every ordinary token may attend to [MASK], because [MASK] is an input token, not an attention prohibition. Only the selector says that position 2 contributes MLM loss. The padding mask separately blocks the final slot as a key. Reusing mask for visibility, selection, corruption, and padding is convenient shorthand, and a common source of bugs.

title: 18  The BERT Moment: Pretraining as the New Regime
text:
Attention visibility determines which key positions each query may use. A causal decoder blocks future keys, whereas a BERT encoder permits all nonpadding keys.
The MLM target selector chooses which ordinary positions contribute loss.
The corruption branch replaces some selected tokens by [MASK], replaces some by random tokens, and deliberately leaves some unchanged.
The padding mask prevents real tokens from routing information from placeholder slots used only to make batch shapes rectangular.




Construct causal and full visibility beside a separate MLM selector.



# [1]
import copy
import itertools

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

tokens = ["[CLS]", "the", "bank", "rose", "[SEP]", "[PAD]"]
nonpadding = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0], dtype=bool)
causal = np.tril(np.ones((6, 6), dtype=int)) * nonpadding[None, :]
full = np.ones((6, 6), dtype=int) * nonpadding[None, :]
selector = np.zeros((1, 6), dtype=int)
selector[0, 2] = 1














WarningThe copy trap



If full attention received the original token at every selected position, the model could copy answers through the residual stream. BERT assigns 90% of selected positions to the mask or random-replacement branches, so copying cannot solve the whole task; the deliberate 10% unchanged branch has a separate purpose, explained below. Conversely, replacing a token by [MASK] does not make it invisible. Its neighbors still attend to the placeholder and one another. Always audit visibility, selection, corruption, and padding separately.

title: 18  The BERT Moment: Pretraining as the New Regime
text:
18.2 Text supplies supervision
In ordinary supervised learning, an external label \(y\) accompanies an input \(x\). Masked language modeling derives both from one unlabeled sequence: the corrupted sequence is the input, and the original selected tokens are the targets. This is self-supervised learning: the supervision is constructed from the data rather than supplied by a human annotator.






NoteSelf-supervised does not mean target-free



The method still has labels and a loss. What changes is their origin. The clean text supplies a target for every selected position, so a large corpus can create many training examples without a task-specific annotation campaign.


This idea was part of a broader 2018 convergence, not a solitary invention. Table 18.1 sets four of its works side by side.



Table 18.1: Four 2018 works, with the pretraining signal of each and what moved downstream.





Work
Pretraining signal
What moved downstream




ELMo
Forward and backward LSTM language models
Fixed contextual features


ULMFiT
Causal language modeling
The entire adapted language model


GPT
Causal Transformer language modeling
A pretrained Transformer plus task head


BERT
Masked tokens in full context, plus next sentence prediction
A deeply bidirectional Transformer encoder plus task head






The workflow mattered as much as the architecture: learn broadly from raw text first, then spend scarce labels on adaptation.

title: 18  The BERT Moment: Pretraining as the New Regime
text:
18.3 The masked-language-model objective
Let a tokenized sequence be
\[
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_T),\qquad x_t\in\{1,\ldots,V\},
\]
where \(T\) is the sequence length and \(V\) is the vocabulary size. Choose a random set \(\mathcal{S}\) of eligible positions, then apply a corruption operator \(c\) to obtain \(\widetilde{x}=c(x,\mathcal{S})\). A bidirectional encoder with parameters \(\theta\) produces
\[
\matr{H}=f_\theta(\widetilde{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}.
\]
An output head maps each selected hidden state to vocabulary logits. The MLM loss is
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLM}}(\theta)
=-
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}
\sum_{t\in \mathcal{S}}
\log p_\theta\!\left(x_t\mid \widetilde{x}\right).
\]
Every term conditions on the same jointly corrupted sequence \(\widetilde{x}\), not on its own clean sequence with only \(x_t\) removed. For a batch, let \(\mathcal{S}\) denote the selected example–position pairs across all sequences. Token IDs have shape \((B,T)\), hidden states \((B,T,d)\), and dense vocabulary logits \((B,T,V)\). Boolean selection gathers \(|\mathcal{S}|\) rows, so cross-entropy receives a logit matrix of shape \((|\mathcal{S}|, V)\) and a target vector of \(|\mathcal{S}|\) token indices. Unselected positions can affect the representations but contribute no direct MLM loss.

Fifteen percent, then 80/10/10
Original BERT selects 15% of eligible tokens. Conditional on selection:

80% are replaced by [MASK];
10% are replaced by a random vocabulary token;
10% remain unchanged.

For 1,000 eligible positions, the expected flow is therefore
\[
1000\longrightarrow150\longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
120 & [\text{MASK}],\\
15 & \text{random tokens},\\
15 & \text{unchanged}.
\end{cases}
\]
All selected positions, 150 in expectation in this example, are scored against their original tokens. The 120 expected mask replacements constitute 12% of eligible positions, while the supervision rate is the full 15%: every selected position is scored, whether masked, replaced or unchanged. Random ordinary-looking replacements force the encoder to cross-check a token against its context rather than trusting the visible identity. The unchanged branch prevents the opposite shortcut: the assumption that every selected ordinary-looking token must be wrong. It also reduces the mismatch between pretraining, where [MASK] exists, and downstream inputs, where it ordinarily does not. An unchanged selected token exposes its answer on purpose. Only about 1.5% of all eligible positions follow that branch, and no input marker indicates which ordinary-looking tokens were selected.



Compute the expected two-stage policy counts.
Build and audit the five Boolean rows on one illustrative sequence.
Report the policy totals.



# [1]
eligible_count = 1_000
selected_count = round(0.15 * eligible_count)
branch_counts = np.array([120, 15, 15])

# [2]
ledger_tokens = [
    "[CLS]", "the", "quiet", "bank", "rose", "after",
    "the", "rain", "today", "[SEP]", "[PAD]", "[PAD]",
]
eligible = np.array([False] + [True] * 8 + [False] * 3)
selected = np.array(
    [False, False, True, False, True, False, False, True, True, False, False, False]
)
mask_sites = np.array(
    [False, False, True, False, False, False, False, True, False, False, False, False]
)
random_sites = np.array(
    [False, False, False, False, True, False, False, False, False, False, False, False]
)
unchanged_sites = selected & ~mask_sites & ~random_sites
assert np.all(selected <= eligible)
assert np.array_equal(selected, mask_sites | random_sites | unchanged_sites)
assert not np.any(mask_sites & random_sites)

# [3]
print(f"direct loss targets: {branch_counts.sum()}")
print(f"[MASK] share of all eligible positions: {branch_counts[0] / 1000:.1%}")

section: 18.4 From a Transformer encoder to BERT
text:
18.4 From a Transformer encoder to BERT
The original BERT input at position \(i\) adds three learned vectors:
\[
z_i=e_{\text{tok}}(x_i)+e_{\text{pos}}(i)+e_{\text{seg}}(s_i),
\]
where \(x_i\) is the token identifier, \(i\) is the sequence position, and \(s_i\) is the segment index. The token comes from a WordPiece vocabulary: frequent character sequences are stored whole, while rarer words can be assembled from reusable subword pieces. The optional example below uses the related byte pair encoding to show how a subword vocabulary is built from data.






TipPractice bridge (optional): make the vocabulary learnable



Chapter 12 fixed its vocabulary at individual characters. A full-word vocabulary shortens sequences but gives every rare spelling its own entry. Subword tokenization sits between the two. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) begins with small symbols, counts adjacent pairs in the training corpus, merges the most frequent pair, and repeats until it reaches a chosen vocabulary budget.
This original toy implementation starts from characters plus an end-of-word marker. Corpus frequencies weight the pair counts; lexicographic order breaks exact ties so the result is reproducible.

Define the reusable merge_pair helper.
Split the four counted words into characters plus </w>, and start an empty merges list.
Learn five subword merges from weighted word counts.
Print each merge with its weighted pair count, then the pieces that now spell lower.



from collections import Counter

# [1]
def merge_pair(
    symbols: tuple[str, ...], pair: tuple[str, str]
) -> tuple[str, ...]:
    merged: list[str] = []
    index = 0
    while index < len(symbols):
        if index + 1 < len(symbols) and symbols[index:index + 2] == pair:
            merged.append("".join(pair))
            index += 2
        else:
            merged.append(symbols[index])
            index += 1
    return tuple(merged)

# [2]
corpus = {"low": 5, "lower": 2, "newest": 6, "widest": 3}
words = {tuple(word) + ("</w>",): count for word, count in corpus.items()}
merges: list[tuple[tuple[str, str], int]] = []
# [3]
for _ in range(5):
    counts: Counter[tuple[str, str]] = Counter()
    for symbols, frequency in words.items():
        for pair in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            counts[pair] += frequency
    maximum = max(counts.values())
    best = min(pair for pair, count in counts.items() if count == maximum)
    merges.append((best, maximum))
    words = {merge_pair(symbols, best): count for symbols, count in words.items()}

# [4]
print("merges:", [("+".join(pair), count) for pair, count in merges])
print("lower:", " | ".join(next(word for word in words if "r" in word)))

NoteReading the learned pieces (optional)



The first three merges build est</w> from nine weighted occurrences; the next two build low from seven. The word lower is therefore represented as low | e | r | </w> even though the whole word was never granted its own token. This is the mechanism, not BERT’s tokenizer: WordPiece uses a different merge-scoring criterion, and practical byte-level tokenizers begin from bytes rather than the toy character alphabet. All three share one idea: a learned vocabulary trades sequence length against reusable coverage.


Returning to BERT’s input representation, learned absolute position embeddings replace the fixed sinusoidal table of Chapter 16. Segment A/B embeddings mark which of two packed text spans supplied a token; they do not block cross-segment attention. [CLS] begins the sequence, and [SEP] ends each span:
\[
[\text{CLS}]\ A\ [\text{SEP}]\ B\ [\text{SEP}].
\]
The resulting sequence passes through a stack of full-context Transformer encoder blocks. Original BERT uses post-LayerNorm, as did the original Transformer in Chapter 16. Table 18.2 gives the two published sizes of BERT.
