WarningTrap: independent data is not automatically the right data



A perfectly independent test set from \(P\) estimates performance under \(P\). Without further assumptions, it does not estimate risk under another deployment distribution \(Q\). Independence from model selection cannot repair a population mismatch.

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
section: E.2 Name the distribution that carries the claim
text:
E.2 Name the distribution that carries the claim
If deployment follows \(Q\) rather than \(P\), then the target quantity is
\[
R_Q(\theta)
=\E_{(X,Y)\sim Q}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(X),Y\bigr)\right].
\tag{E.3}\]
Chapter 6 uses a controlled transformation to make this distinction visible. For a label-preserving input map \(T\), the shifted risk is
\[
R_{T_\#P}(\theta)
=\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right],
\tag{E.4}\]
where \(T_\#P\) denotes the distribution produced by applying \(T\) to inputs drawn from \(P\). Keeping \(Y\) unchanged is part of the assumption. A horizontal shift may preserve a garment label; the same statement would be false for a transformation that changes the semantic target.
When \(T\) is itself drawn from a declared augmentation distribution \(\mathcal A\), the population objective becomes
\[
R_{\mathcal A}(\theta)
=\E_{(X,Y)\sim P}
\E_{T\sim\mathcal A}
\left[\ell\bigl(f_\theta(T(X)),Y\bigr)\right].
\tag{E.5}\]
Sampling one fresh transformation per example is a Monte Carlo estimator of the inner expectation. It optimizes average behavior under \(\mathcal A\), but it does not prove exact invariance to every transformation, including those outside the declared support.
The reusable audit is short: name the training distribution, the validation and test distributions, the deployment distribution, and every transformation relating them. If two of those happen to be equal, say so rather than leaving the equality implicit.

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
section: E.3 Deriving losses from conditional distributions
text:
E.3 Deriving losses from conditional distributions
Suppose a model specifies a conditional distribution \(p_\theta(y\mid\vect{x})\). Under conditionally independent observations, its likelihood and mean negative log-likelihood are
\[
\mathcal L(\theta)
=\prod_{i=1}^{n}p_\theta(y_i\mid\vect{x}_i),
\qquad
\operatorname{NLL}(\theta)
=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\log p_\theta(y_i\mid\vect{x}_i).
\tag{E.6}\]
Maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing NLL. The target space and conditional distribution determine the familiar loss (Table E.2).



Table E.2: Four conditional distributions and the familiar losses their negative log-likelihoods give











Conditional distribution
Model parameterization
NLL, up to constants or scale
Familiar loss




\(Y\mid X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(X),\sigma^2)\) with fixed \(\sigma\)
\(\mu_\theta\in\R\)
\((y-\mu_\theta)^2\)
Squared error


\(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_\theta(X))\)
\(p_\theta=\operatorname{sigmoid}(o_\theta)\)
\(-y\log p_\theta-(1-y)\log(1-p_\theta)\)
Binary cross-entropy


\(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\vect{p}_\theta(X))\)
\(\vect{p}_\theta=\operatorname{softmax}(\vect{o}_\theta)\)
\(-\log p_{\theta,y}\)
Categorical cross-entropy


\(Y\mid X\sim\operatorname{Laplace}(\mu_\theta(X),b)\) with fixed \(b\)
\(\mu_\theta\in\R\)
\(|y-\mu_\theta|\)
Absolute error






The four distributions in this table are illustrative, not exhaustive. They show what to ask: what kind of target is modeled, which parameters must stay in a valid domain, and which deviations the loss treats as plausible. Counts, angles, intervals, censored values, and structured outputs may need other conditional distributions.
Each row also determines what the model is trained to predict about the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X\). To find out, replace \(f_\theta\) in Equation E.2 by any function \(f\) of the input. Because \(f(\vect{x})\) can then be chosen separately at each input value \(\vect{x}\), the best \(f(\vect{x})\) minimizes the average loss over \(Y\) given \(X=\vect{x}\). Squared error is minimized by the conditional mean \(\E[Y\mid X=\vect{x}]\), the regression function \(f^*(\vect{x})\) of Equation 1.5. Absolute error is minimized by a median of \(Y\) given \(X=\vect{x}\). Cross-entropy is minimized by the true class probabilities \(P(Y=k\mid X=\vect{x})\), one for each class \(k\). Averaged over \(Y\) given \(X=\vect{x}\), the loss is the cross-entropy of Chapter 2 with these probabilities as the target distribution: their entropy, which no model changes, plus the KL divergence from them to the model’s probabilities. That divergence is never negative and is zero when the two agree.
These minimizers do not depend on whether the Gaussian or Laplace row is correct. If the true conditional distribution is skewed, squared error is still minimized by its mean and absolute error by its median. The two can differ, and then the choice of loss determines which one the model predicts. A trained network approaches these minimizers only as far as its architecture, data, and optimizer allow.
The squared-error case is a projection like the least-squares fit of Chapter 1, with the sum over training examples replaced by an average over the population and the feature columns replaced by every function of the input. There, least squares left a residual orthogonal to every feature column. Here, if \(\E[Y^2]<\infty\), the residual \(Y-f^*(X)\) is orthogonal to every function \(g\) of the input with finite second moment, \(\E[g(X)^2]<\infty\), in the sense \(\E[(Y-f^*(X))\,g(X)]=0\), so no such function has a smaller expected squared error than \(f^*\) (Exercise 7). The denoisers of Chapter 11 and Chapter 22 are trained toward such conditional means.

Why the Gaussian is plausible, and where it is not
The Gaussian assumption is mathematically convenient, but convenience is not its only motivation. If a residual is the sum of many small, weakly dependent perturbations with finite variance, a central-limit argument can make a Gaussian approximation plausible. Among distributions on \(\R\) with a fixed mean and variance, the Gaussian also has maximum differential entropy: it adds no further shape constraint beyond those two moments.
Neither argument proves that a particular residual is Gaussian. A few dominant causes, heavy tails, changing variance, dependence, truncation, or multimodality can break the approximation. Check it in four steps:

state the conditional residual assumption;
derive the loss it implies;
inspect residuals and relevant slices;
revise the likelihood or estimator when the mismatch changes the claim.

The maximum-entropy claim also assumes a known mean and variance and support \(\R\). Other supports or constraints give other maximum-entropy distributions.

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
section: E.4 Three ways to compare distributions
text:
E.4 Three ways to compare distributions
Chapters 21 and 22 compare distributions for different reasons. The word “distance” can hide distinct geometries, so start with the question rather than the formula.
For distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) with densities or mass functions \(p\) and \(q\), the Kullback–Leibler divergence is
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)
=\E_{X\sim P}\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right].
\tag{E.7}\]
It is nonnegative and equals zero only when the distributions agree almost everywhere under the usual conditions. It is not symmetric, does not satisfy the triangle inequality, and becomes infinite when \(P\) puts positive mass where \(Q\) puts none. Its direction matters: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) averages a log density ratio under \(P\).
Let \(M=\tfrac12(P+Q)\). The Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) is
\[
D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P\|Q)
=\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|M)
+\tfrac12D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|M).
\tag{E.8}\]
It is symmetric and lies between \(0\) and \(\log 2\) when natural logarithms and equal mixture weights are used. The mixture prevents the support failure that can make a KL term between \(P\) and \(Q\) infinite. JSD still compares probability mass, not the physical distance between locations.
Given a ground metric \(d\) on the sample space, a rule for the distance between two points, the Wasserstein-1 distance is
\[
W_1(P,Q)
=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi(P,Q)}
\E_{(X,Y)\sim\gamma}[d(X,Y)],
\tag{E.9}\]
where \(\Pi(P,Q)\) is the set of couplings with marginals \(P\) and \(Q\). Each coupling is a transport plan: it says how much probability mass moves from each source point to each destination point. On the real line with ground metric \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\), matching quantiles in order gives an optimal plan. For distributions with finite first moments, the distance then becomes
\[
W_1(P,Q)
=\int_0^1\left|F_P^{-1}(u)-F_Q^{-1}(u)\right|\,\dd u,
\tag{E.10}\]
where \(F_P^{-1}\) and \(F_Q^{-1}\) are the quantile functions of \(P\) and \(Q\).
Wasserstein distance uses the geometry of the sample space and inherits the units of the ground metric. That can be valuable, but it also means the answer depends on whether the chosen ground metric represents meaningful movement. Table E.3 sets the three quantities side by side.



Table E.3: Three ways to compare distributions, what each makes visible, and the boundary to remember










Quantity
What it makes visible
Boundary to remember




\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\)
Expected log-density mismatch in a declared direction
Asymmetric; support mismatch can make it infinite


\(D_{\mathrm{JS}}(P\|Q)\)
Symmetric mass disagreement with a shared mixture
Ignores how near two points are


\(W_1(P,Q)\)
Amount and distance of mass movement
Requires a meaningful ground metric; estimation can be difficult in high dimensions






No row certifies sample quality, fairness, or deployment safety by itself. The metric must be paired with a population, an estimator, and the substantive property the measurement is meant to probe.

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
text:
E.5 What the code estimates
Monte Carlo turns an expectation into an average. If \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_B\) are independent draws from the same distribution as \(Z\), and \(g(Z)\) has finite variance, then
\[
\hat\mu_B=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}g(Z_b),
\qquad
\E[\hat\mu_B]=\E[g(Z)],
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_B)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(g(Z))}{B}.
\tag{E.11}\]
The \(1/B\) variance law assumes independent draws. Dependence changes the variance of the average, and positive covariance can increase it.
Section 4.6.1 distinguishes three cases that recur across the book:

Decomposable per-example objective. If each example’s loss term does not depend on the rest of its batch, a batch mean estimates an average: the dataset mean when batches come from a fixed dataset, or the population mean for fresh draws. Squared error and cross-entropy belong to this case.
Nonlinear functional of an aggregate. If the target is \(R(\E[g(Z)])\), plugging in the batch mean gives \(R(\hat\mu_B)\), which is generally biased. Jensen’s inequality gives a direction when \(R\) is convex or concave. More optimization steps do not remove fixed-batch plug-in bias, whereas larger or restructured estimators may.
Batch-defined objective. The batch supplies candidates or negatives and is part of the objective itself. Changing batch size changes the target, not merely its Monte Carlo noise.

The code audit is therefore not “does this line contain .mean()?” It is the five fields of Table E.4.



Table E.4: The five fields of a code audit and the question each asks









Field
Question




Target
Which population quantity or protocol-defined objective do we want?


Estimator
Which random quantity does the code compute?


Reduction
Which axes and examples enter the sum, mean, or denominator?


Validity
Which sampling and independence assumptions let it estimate the target?


Boundary
What bias, dependence, missing support, or protocol change remains?

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
section: E.6 Standard deviation is not standard error
text:
E.6 Standard deviation is not standard error
Uncertainty must name what was repeated. Suppose we run a complete training protocol with \(K\) independently chosen seeds and obtain metrics \(M_1,\ldots,M_K\).

The seed standard deviation \(s\) describes spread among those \(K\) optimization runs under the fixed dataset and protocol.
The standard error of the seed mean, often estimated as \(s/\sqrt K\), describes uncertainty in that mean under an idealized population of comparable independent runs. For small \(K\), both \(s\) and the resulting interval are unstable.
Neither quantity automatically measures variation across new datasets, deployment populations, annotator groups, prompts, or future time periods.

When two methods use the same data split, initialization family, and minibatch schedule, analyze paired differences \(D_k=M_{A,k}-M_{B,k}\). Pairing can remove shared variation and answer the comparison more directly than two unrelated marginal SDs. If several observations come from one prompt, person, subject, or source document, that cluster may be the sampling unit. With positive within-cluster dependence, treating those rows as independent can understate uncertainty.






NoteA compact statistical audit



Before interpreting a reported number, name five things:

Population: which \(P\), \(Q\), slice, or transformed distribution?
Estimand: risk, accuracy, divergence, or calibration error?
Estimator: what calculation and denominator produced the number?
Variation: data, optimization, sampling, annotation, or deployment?
Boundary: which tempting conclusion does this evidence not establish?

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
text:
Sources and further reading

Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics: likelihood.
Geman, Bienenstock, and Doursat, Neural Networks and the Bias/Variance Dilemma: classical bias and variance. 
Gneiting, Making and Evaluating Point Forecasts: squared error is minimized in expectation by the mean, and absolute error by any median.
Kullback and Leibler, On Information and Sufficiency: KL divergence.
Lin, Divergence Measures Based on the Shannon Entropy: Jensen–Shannon divergence.
Jaynes, Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics: maximum entropy under declared constraints.
Metropolis and Ulam, The Monte Carlo Method: Monte Carlo estimation.
Villani, Optimal Transport: Old and New: transport geometry.
Prince, Understanding Deep Learning: further background on probability models and loss functions in deep learning.

title: Appendix E — Statistical Learning Contracts
text:
Exercises

(Pencil.) At a fixed \(\vect{x}\), write \(\hat f_{\mathcal D}(\vect{x})-Y\) as the sum of the mean-prediction error, the training-set fluctuation, and the fresh-outcome noise. Expand the square. State the zero-mean and conditional-independence assumptions that remove the cross terms and recover Equation 1.5.
(Pencil.) Derive the Gaussian and Laplace rows of the likelihood table (Table E.2) by taking negative logarithms. Which constants may be dropped when the scale parameters are fixed, and what changes if they are learned?
(Code.) Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and estimate \(\log\E[e^Z]\) with \(\log(B^{-1}\sum_b e^{Z_b})\). Sweep \(B\) with many repetitions. Measure the plug-in bias, predict its sign from Jensen’s inequality, and distinguish it from the Monte Carlo variance within one \(B\).
(Audit.) A team trains on \(P\), tunes repeatedly on a validation set from \(P\), and reports accuracy on an independent shifted set from \(T_\#P\) as “test accuracy.” Name the three questions the label hides and propose a split and report for each.
(Audit.) Two scalar generators have similar JSD but different Wasserstein-1 distance under the usual Euclidean metric. Give one configuration where this is plausible. Explain which conclusion would change if the coordinate units were rescaled, and why neither number alone establishes perceptual fidelity.
(Code.) Compare two methods across five matched seeds. Report the five paired differences, their mean and SD, and the two unpaired marginal SDs. Then break the pairing by shuffling one method’s five outcomes, and repeat the summary. Explain which source of variation the paired summary removes and which sources remain outside the experiment. 
(Pencil.) Assume \(\E[Y^2]\) is finite, and write \(f^*(X)\) for the regression function of Equation 1.5 evaluated at the random input. (a) Show that \(\E[(Y-f^*(X))\,g(X)]=0\) for every function \(g\) with \(\E[g(X)^2]\) finite. Fix \(X=\vect{x}\) first: \(g(\vect{x})\) is then a constant, and \(Y-f^*(\vect{x})\) has average zero given \(X=\vect{x}\). Then average over \(X\). (b) Write \(Y-f(X)=(Y-f^*(X))+(f^*(X)-f(X))\), expand the square, and use (a) to show \(\E[(Y-f(X))^2]=\E[(Y-f^*(X))^2]+\E[(f^*(X)-f(X))^2]\) for any function \(f\) with \(\E[f(X)^2]\) finite. Why does no function of the input have a smaller expected squared error than \(f^*\)? (c) Figure 1.9 fits straight lines to a curved \(f^*\). In the split of (b), which term is the irreducible noise of Equation 1.5, averaged over \(X\), and which term stays positive for every straight line \(f\)?
